- Goldman Sachs (Maggie Wei): measures won't lift growth from the 3% it projects; growth "will remain sluggish". Nomura (Lu Ting): not "game-changers". JLL's Bruce Pang: "Don't expect massive additional stimulus".
- Property slump and Covid lockdowns put the "around 5.5%" GDP goal out of reach; Bloomberg-polled economists project growth under 4%.
- State Council said it won't flood the economy with stimulus or "overdraw".

wikis.title: Westinghouse announces AP300 small nuclear reactor (CNBC)
wikis.summary: CNBC, May 4, 2023: Westinghouse launches the AP300, a scaled-down AP1000 targeting availability in 2027 at about $1 billion per unit.
wikis.body:
- Published Thu, May 4 2023 by Catherine Clifford.
- AP300: about 300 MW, powering roughly 300,000 homes, versus 1,200 MW for the AP1000; aims to be available in 2027; approx. $1 billion per unit per David Durham, president of energy systems.
- Durham cites a 2022 MIT study of about $6.8 billion for an AP1000; Vogtle (Georgia, two AP1000s) estimates reached past $30 billion, which he says include borrowing interest.
- Needs NRC approval by end of 2027; Durham: "the NRC has already licensed every bit of this technology".
- Passive safety: a water pool above the reactor cools fuel about three days with no operator action; Durham: "If the AP1000 had been in operation at Fukushima, it would have been a total non-event."
- Jeffrey Merrifield (former NRC commissioner, speaking generally): smaller reactors suit more utilities and can supply industrial heat; a 300 MW unit is comparable to a typical coal plant, easing grid connection.
- Demand for large reactors remains strong overseas.

wikis.title: Westinghouse launches AP300 SMR (press release)
wikis.summary: Westinghouse's May 4, 2023 release unveiling the AP300, a 300-MWe single-loop pressurized water reactor scaled from the AP1000.
wikis.body:
- Cranberry Township, PA, May 4, 2023. AP300 is a 300-MWe single-loop pressurized water reactor using identical AP1000 technology (major equipment, structure, passive safety, fuel, I&C); "the only SMR truly based on an Nth-of-a-kind operating plant".
- Draws on 18 reactor years of AP1000 operation; 80+ year design life; Gen III+ tech with regulatory approval in the U.S., Great Britain and China, and EUR compliance.
- Passive safety shuts down without operator action, no backup power or cooling.
- Design certification anticipated by 2027, then site-specific licensing and first-unit construction "toward the end of the decade".
- Uses: electricity, district heating, water desalination, hydrogen; fast load-follow suits renewables.
- CEO Patrick Fragman quoted. Dr. Rita Baranwal (CTO, former DOE Assistant Secretary of Nuclear Energy) named SVP in Energy Systems to lead the AP300 team.

wikis.title: Westinghouse unveils AP300 small modular reactor (World Nuclear News)
wikis.summary: WNN, 4 May 2023: Westinghouse's AP300 SMR, a one-loop AP1000, with NRC approval sought by 2027 and first power about ten years out.
wikis.body:
- Thursday, 4 May 2023. Westinghouse calls AP300 a "game-changer"; goal is first unit delivering power within a decade.
- CEO Patrick Fragman: rounds out the portfolio; "no more and no less than an AP1000 with one loop instead of two"; fuel and constructability lessons identical.
- Press conference: footprint about 25% of a football pitch; target cost USD1 billion per unit; NRC licensing by 2027, then three years for site-specific permissions and three for construction.
- Possible uses: hydrogen, district heating, desalination, data centre power. David Durham: NRC design certification first, other countries within a couple of years.
- Rita Baranwal to lead the team. AP300 sits between AP1000 and eVinci microreactor.
- Upwards of 50 different SMRs are in development worldwide.

wikis.title: April 2023 jobs report: 253,000 jobs added (CNBC)
wikis.summary: CNBC, May 5, 2023: nonfarm payrolls rose 253,000 in April, beating the 180,000 estimate, with unemployment at 3.4%.
wikis.body:
- Published Fri, May 5 2023 by Jeff Cox. Payrolls +253,000 vs estimate 180,000; unemployment 3.4% vs 3.6% estimate, tied for lowest since 1969; broader rate 6.6%.
- Average hourly earnings +0.5% (est. 0.3%), +4.4% year over year (est. 4.2%).
- Gains: professional and business services 43,000; health care 40,000; leisure and hospitality 31,000; social assistance 25,000; finance 23,000; government 23,000.
- Revisions: March cut to 165,000 (down 71,000); February to 248,000 (down 78,000). Household survey showed 139,000 jobs.
- Participation 62.6%; labor force 166.7 million. Unemployment for Blacks 4.7% (record low), Hispanics 4.4%, Asians 2.8%, adult women 3.1%.
- Markets: Dow up nearly 400 points at open; Treasury yields jumped; a June Fed hike was seen as a small probability. Context: bank turmoil and slowing economy.

wikis.title: BLS Employment Situation, April 2023 (household and establishment data)
wikis.summary: BLS release of May 5, 2023 reporting nonfarm payrolls up 253,000 and unemployment at 3.4 percent, with household and industry detail.
wikis.body:
- Embargoed until 8:30 a.m. ET Friday, May 5, 2023 (USDL-23-0871).
- Payrolls +253,000 (average of 290,000 over prior 6 months); unemployment rate 3.4 percent, unemployed 5.7 million; rate has ranged 3.4 to 3.7 percent since March 2022.
- Rates: men 3.3, women 3.1, teens 9.2, Whites 3.1, Blacks 4.7, Asians 2.8, Hispanics 4.4 percent.
- Long-term unemployed 1.2 million (20.6 percent). Participation 62.6 percent and employment-population ratio 60.4 percent, below February 2020 (63.3 and 61.1). Part time for economic reasons 3.9 million; want a job but not in labor force 5.3 million; discouraged workers 364,000.
- Industries: professional and business services +43,000 (temp help -23,000); health care +40,000; leisure and hospitality +31,000 (still 402,000 below Feb 2020); social assistance +25,000; financial activities +23,000; government +23,000; mining +6,000.
- Average hourly earnings +16 cents (0.5 percent) to $33.36, +4.4 percent over 12 months; production/nonsupervisory +11 cents to $28.62. Average workweek 34.4 hours.

wikis.title: Used vehicle wholesale prices fall 3% in April 2023 (CNBC)
wikis.summary: CNBC, May 5, 2023: Cox Automotive's Manheim index fell 3% from March to April, its first monthly decline of 2023.
wikis.body:
- Published Fri, May 5 2023 by Michael Wayland. Cox Automotive's Manheim Used Vehicle Value Index fell 3% March to April, first decline this year; still up 5.2% from December, down 4.4% from April 2022.
- Chris Frey (Cox): eight straight months of year-over-year declines averaging 8.3%, "likely not over yet".
- Cause cited: automakers increasing production of new cars and trucks. Retail prices traditionally follow wholesale.
- Average listed used price was $26,086 in February, down slightly from January. Charlie Chesbrough: tight supply may support prices; "unlikely a massive decline".
- Used prices are watched by investors and the Biden administration as an inflation barometer.

wikis.title: Cox Automotive: wholesale used-vehicle prices decline in April 2023
wikis.summary: Cox Automotive's May 5, 2023 Manheim Used Vehicle Value Index report: prices down 3.0% in April to 230.8, with sales, supply and fleet data.
wikis.body:
- MUVVI fell 3.0% in April from March (mix, mileage and seasonally adjusted) to 230.8, down 4.4% year over year. Non-adjusted price rose 0.1% from March, down 5.6% year over year.
- Chris Frey: values rose 8.6% in Q1 from December; eight straight months of yearly declines averaging 8.3%; financial crisis had 16 months averaging 5.8%; "a second, and more rapid, decent off the pandemic peak of January 2022".
- Daily MMR retention averaged 98.7%; sales conversion 60.9% (63.6% in April 2019).
- Used retail sales estimated down 8% from March and year over year; retail days' supply 42; wholesale supply 25 days.
- New-vehicle sales up 9.0% year over year; SAAR 15.9 million (14.3 million a year earlier, 14.8 million in March). Fleet share 17.5%; rental fleet sales +64% year over year.
- Rental risk prices +5.8% year over year, average mileage 59,600.
- Conference Board confidence down 2.6%; Michigan index up 2.4%. AAA gas average $3.61 on April 30, down 14% year over year.
- Full April data released June 7, 2023; next quarterly call Monday, July 10 at 11 a.m. EDT.

wikis.title: Manheim index falls below 200 in April 2024 (Auto Remarketing)
wikis.summary: Auto Remarketing, May 7, 2024: Cox's Manheim index hit 198.4 in April 2024, down 14.0% year over year.
wikis.body:
- Tuesday, May 7, 2024. Manheim Used Vehicle Value Index fell below 200 for the first time in over three years, at 198.4, lowest since March 2021 (195.4).
- Down 14.0% year over year and 2.3% month over month (adjusted); unadjusted down 11.9% year over year and 0.6% from March.
- Yearly declines by class: compact cars 17.6%, midsize cars 16.8%, pickups 15.2%, SUV/CUV 14.6%, luxury 12.9%. Non-electric vehicles down 13.1%, EVs down 17.5% from April 2023.
- Note: this page is about April 2024, not 2023.

wikis.title: Post on X: June 25bps hike probability doubled (May 8, 2023)
wikis.summary: A May 8, 2023 post by J Cole (@J_Cole789) saying the probability of another 25bps hike in June doubled that day.
wikis.body:
- Post text: "Probability for another 25bps hike in June doubled today" with an attached image (not described in the text).
- Dated May 8, 2023. No figures given in the text.

wikis.title: Ukraine counteroffensive: when will the mud season end? (DW)
wikis.summary: DW, April 1, 2023: a former US Air Force meteorologist forecasts when Ukraine's spring mud (rasputitsa) will dry, shaping counteroffensive timing.
wikis.body:
- April 1, 2023, by Frank Hofmann. Kyiv plans a spring counteroffensive; David Helms, a retired US Air Force meteorologist who formerly worked for NOAA, posts forecasts under #NAFOWeather.
- Helms: "The loss of moisture from the soil really picks up by May 1st and beyond." Southern Ukraine dry from around mid-April, Donetsk about two weeks later, Russian-occupied Luhansk from mid-May.
- If correct, Russian tanks may still be stuck in eastern mud while Ukraine could attack south toward Melitopol.
- Rasputitsa makes fields and unpaved roads impassable for around a month in fall and spring; soil strength falls as moisture rises, logarithmically. Vehicle weight matters. Flat land and black earth contribute.
- Helms also flags "optimal optical satellite intelligence opportunities" so activists can buy imagery (e.g. Maxar) for Ukrainian commanders.
- Zelenskyy and his defense minister have referred to the planned counteroffensive; tanks from UK and Germany and German Marder vehicles are mentioned.

wikis.title: Zelensky says Ukraine needs more time for counter-offensive (BBC, 11 May 2023)
wikis.summary: BBC interview report: Zelensky says brigades are ready but more equipment is needed before the expected counter-offensive.
wikis.body:
- 11 May 2023, Hugo Bachega, Kyiv. Zelensky (Eurovision News interview): brigades, some NATO-trained, are "ready" but need "some things" including armoured vehicles "arriving in batches". "With [what we already have] we can go forward... But we'd lose a lot of people. I think that's unacceptable. So we need to wait."
- Timing and place are secret. Russian forces have fortified a 900-mile (1,450km) frontline; the war is in its 15th month; nearly a fifth of Ukraine is under Russian control.
- A senior official said the assault should not be seen as a "silver bullet". Zelensky warned of a "frozen conflict", which Russia was "counting on". A disappointing result could reduce Western support and increase pressure to negotiate.
- Zelensky: no pressure can make Ukraine surrender territory; expects to "win by" the 2024 US election; bipartisan support in Congress.
- His 10-point peace proposal (return of territory, reparations, special tribunal) was rejected by Moscow. Sanctions are depleting Russian missile stocks; he called the alleged Kremlin drone attack possibly a false flag.

wikis.title: Why Ukraine's counteroffensive still hasn't begun (AP via PBS, May 19, 2023)
wikis.summary: AP analysis of weather, training and weapons deliveries delaying Ukraine's spring counteroffensive.
wikis.body:
- May 19, 2023, Tara Copp (AP). Officials insist the counteroffensive is coming; preliminary shaping moves have begun, a U.S. official said.
- Weather: extended wet cold spring left deep mud, "like a soup".
- Training: U.S. has trained more than 10,700 Ukrainians; over 41,000 more via programs of 30+ partner nations; Abrams training to start at Grafenwoehr, Germany. Defense Minister Reznikov said Ukraine won't wait for it.
- Weapons: U.S. announced over $14 billion in the past five months. Ben Barry (IISS): of about 300 pledged tanks only about 100 arrived; of about 700 fighting vehicles only about 300. Ukraine fires 6,000 to 8,000 155mm rounds per day (Oleksandra Ustinova).
- Russia has about 200,000 troops along a 1,000-km line, dug in with ditches, minefields and dragon's teeth.
- Zelenskyy said last week it was delayed by insufficient Western weapons.

wikis.title: Musk announces Cybertruck delivery event timing (Electrek, Apr 19, 2023)
wikis.summary: Electrek: on the Q1 2023 call Musk said a Cybertruck handover event would be held at the 'end of the third quarter'.
wikis.body:
- Apr 19 2023, Fred Lambert. Musk: Tesla plans a "handover event" toward "the end of the third quarter", putting first deliveries around September 2023 - the most precise timing yet. Cybertruck was unveiled in 2019.
- Reservation holders should expect updated specs and pricing at that event; Tesla previously said pricing would differ from 2019.
- Electrek expects only a few trucks delivered, likely to insiders, with months before customer deliveries, depending on production ramp.
- Musk earlier indicated a top-of-the-line quad-motor variant.

wikis.title: Cybertruck handover event expected in Q3 2023 (InsideEVs)
wikis.summary: InsideEVs, Apr 20, 2023: Musk said on the Q1 2023 call that the first Cybertruck deliveries come at a handover event around the end of Q3.
wikis.body:
- Apr 20, 2023, Dan Mihalascu. Musk: event "toward the end of the third quarter", likely September 2023. Reservation holders likely get spec and pricing updates.
- Musk: "we continue to build Alpha versions of the Cybertruck on our pilot line... completing the installation of the volume production line at Giga Texas, and we're anticipating a great delivery event, probably in Q3."
- Q1 letter said production starts "later this year" versus earlier "this summer".
- Ramp follows an "S-curve"; "a very radical product. It's not made in the way that other cars are made."
- InsideEVs notes past Model Y handover events delivered few vehicles, mostly to insiders.

wikis.title: Tesla Cybertruck deliveries set for November 30 (TechCrunch, Oct 18, 2023)
wikis.summary: TechCrunch: Musk said the Cybertruck delivery event will be November 30 at Giga Texas, as Q3 profits fell 44%.
wikis.body:
- Oct 18 2023, Rebecca Bellan. Musk posted the delivery event will be held November 30 at the Austin gigafactory; usually a few select customers. Number to be delivered not shared.
- Same day as Q3 earnings: profits down 44% year over year. Report noted pilot production started at Giga Texas and the truck "remains on track for initial deliveries this year". Earlier promises of summer 2023 and then Q3 were missed.
- Production ramp expected 2024; capacity under 125,000 per year at mass production, which Musk said should be reached in 2025. Operating expenses up 43% to $2.4 billion, partly Cybertruck.
- Musk: "enormous challenges in reaching volume production"; about 18 months until cash-flow positive.
- Tesla also raised AI spending for its Dojo supercomputer.

wikis.title: How DC became obsessed with a potential 2027 Chinese invasion of Taiwan (Defense News)
wikis.summary: Defense News, May 7, 2024: traces how the '2027' timeline for a Chinese move on Taiwan, from Adm. Davidson's 2021 testimony, shaped US policy and spending.
wikis.body:
- May 7, 2024, Noah Robertson; first of a two-part series.
- At a November (2023) summit near San Francisco, an American official said Xi told Biden of reports of 2027 or 2035 plans: "There are no such plans."
- US intelligence: Xi told the PLA to be ready to invade Taiwan by 2027; officials stress "ready to invade is different than will invade" and the year is not a deadline.
- Origin: at a 2021 hearing, retiring INDOPACOM head Adm. Phil Davidson said "The threat is manifest during this decade, in fact, in the next six years" - the "Davidson window". Gen. Mark Milley later said it was based on a Xi speech about moving capabilities to seize Taiwan "from 2035 to 2027"; the text was not shared.
- Spending: INDOPACOM's latest priorities list is $26.5 billion, of which about $11 billion missed the fiscal 2025 request (about $15 billion made it); $1 billion annual authority to send Taiwan weapons; supplemental with almost $2 billion to replace stocks and $2 billion in financing.
- CIA Director Bill Burns (Feb 2023): Xi wants readiness by 2027 "but that doesn't mean that he's decided to invade". Blinken (fall 2022): "much faster timeline". Gen. Mike Minihan memo: "I hope I am wrong... we will fight [China] in 2025." Pentagon line since: conflict "neither imminent nor inevitable".
- David Finkelstein (CNA): the military option "hangs over the Taiwan Strait like Damocles' sword".

wikis.title: Post on X by Alexander Stahel: 'Some context' (April 24, 2023)
wikis.summary: An April 24, 2023 post by Alexander Stahel (@BurggrabenH) reading only 'Some context' with an image.
wikis.body: - Post text: "Some context" plus an attached image (not described in the text). Dated April 24, 2023. No other facts.

wikis.title: China's $23 trillion local debt mess (Bloomberg via Japan Times, May 22, 2023)
wikis.summary: Teaser of a Bloomberg feature on China's local government debt, using the restructured coal city of Hegang as a warning sign.
wikis.body:
- May 22, 2023. Headline: China's $23 trillion local debt mess is about to get worse. Text is truncated by a paywall.
- In 2021 Hegang, a coal town of nearly a million people near the Russian border, was forced into an "unprecedented financial restructuring"; its debt was more than double its fiscal income. It was the first time a city took official emergency steps since the State Council's 2016 rules on local government debt risks.
- Other heavily indebted municipalities "look set to follow suit", an ominous sign for Xi Jinping.
- Residents cite no indoor heating in winter, more traffic fines, rumored teacher job cuts and two-month salary delays for street cleaners.

wikis.title: UC San Diego adding 3,310 dorm beds (San Diego Union-Tribune, Jan 21, 2022)
wikis.summary: UCSD received Regents approval for Pepper Canyon West and Thurgood Marshall College housing to lift capacity to 22,260 beds.
wikis.body:
- Jan 21, 2022, Gary Robbins and Phillip Molnar. New dorms will hold 3,310 students, raising capacity to 22,260. Regents approved two projects that week.
- Pepper Canyon West: 1,310 transfer and upper-division students, two 22- or 23-story towers near the Blue Line trolley station, $350 million, with retail; construction begins this summer, completes in 2024; delayed by the pandemic.
- Thurgood Marshall College: about 2,000 beds; Regents gave about $33 million for planning; tentative completion 2025; cost not yet announced.
- Context: record enrollment left nearly 3,300 students on housing waiting lists; about 43,000 students, up more than 14,000 in a decade. Theater District Living and Learning Neighborhood (2,000 beds) starts fall 2023.

wikis.title: UC San Diego plans 3,310 new dorm beds
wikis.summary: Erudera reports that UC San Diego is pursuing two housing projects adding about 3,310 beds, expected to start in summer 2022 and finish by 2024.
wikis.body:
- Published Jan 24, 2022 by Erudera News, citing the San Diego Union Tribune.
- Two projects would house some 3,310 students: **Thurgood Marshall College Undergraduate Student Housing** and **Pepper Canyon West**. Both were approved by the Board of Regents "last week".
- Projects "are expected begin this summer and be completed by 2024". The 3,310 beds would raise capacity to a total of 22,260 beds.
- Pepper Canyon West: about 1,316 transfer and upper-division undergraduates, near the newly opened Blue Line trolley station; two towers of 22 or 23 stories, the tallest buildings in UTC. $350 million allocated; the plan was delayed by the pandemic.
- Around 3,300 students needed rooms in fall 2021. Enrollment is 43,000, up more than 14,000 over the previous decade, with another increase projected for fall.
- Regents also let the university begin plans for some 2,000 beds for Marshall College students (about $33 million).
- Theater District Living and Learning Neighborhood, near La Jolla Playhouse, is to house 2,000 students in fall 2023.
- Statista: 2.66 million US student beds in 2018, projected 2.84 million in 2021.
- UC San Diego was founded in 1960.

wikis.title: Sagrada Família: history, design and completion of the Tower of Jesus Christ (Wikipedia, part 1)
wikis.summary: First part of Wikipedia's Sagrada Família article covering its history from 1882, construction, the spires (including the central tower finished 20 February 2026) and the design of the basilica.
wikis.body:
## Overview
- Catholic church in the Eixample district of Barcelona, designed by Antoni Gaudí; "the tallest church in the world". Consecrated as a basilica by Pope Benedict XVI on 7 November 2010 (6,500 in the congregation, 50,000 more outside).
- Nativity façade and Crypt are a UNESCO World Heritage Site (1984 inscription, extended 2005) under "Works of Antoni Gaudí".
- Construction began 19 March 1882 under Francisco de Paula del Villar; Gaudí took over in 1883 (Architect Director 28 March 1884). At his death in 1926 it was between 15 and 25 percent complete. Funded by private donations; Spanish Civil War (July 1936 fire in the crypt, workshop and plans partly destroyed) interrupted work.
- Construction passed the midpoint in 2010. In 2014 completion was anticipated for 2026 (centenary of Gaudí's death); COVID-19 slowdowns threatened that.

## Tower of Jesus Christ
- Reached structural completion on 20 February 2026 when the final piece was installed; height 172.5 m (566 ft).
- Became world's tallest church on 30 October 2025 at 162.91 m, surpassing Ulm Minster (161.53 m).
- Inaugurated and blessed by Pope Leo XIV on 10 June 2026 during his visit to Spain, coinciding with the centenary of Gaudí's death.
- Gaudí designed it to be shorter than Montjuïc hill, believing his creation should not surpass God's. Completion of the spire's interior is expected in 2028.
- Uses post-tensioned stone panels pre-assembled before incorporation.

## Spires
- Design calls for 18 spires (12 Apostles, 4 Evangelists, Virgin Mary, Jesus Christ); fourteen completed as of 2026. A 7 m illuminated star was installed on the Virgin Mary tower on 29 November 2021.

## Later history
- Jordi Faulí i Oller became architect in 2012. October 2015: 70 percent complete. As of a 2017 estimate, decorative elements complete by 2030 or 2032. Entrance fees of €15 to €20 fund an annual construction budget of €25 million.
- AVE high-speed train tunnel beneath the site opened 8 January 2013 amid controversy over stability.
- Stone from Withnell Quarry, Brinscall, England since 2018.

## Façades
- Nativity (east, built before 1935), Passion (west, from Gaudí's 1917 design, begun 1954, steeples finished 1976), Glory (south, incomplete).

wikis.title: Central tower of Sagrada Família completed
wikis.summary: Vatican News reports that the upper arm of the cross on the Tower of Jesus Christ was installed on 20 February 2026, completing the tower's external works.
wikis.body:
- Upper arm of the cross installed **20 February 2026**, completing the external works of the central tower, the basilica's highest point (172.5 m). Interior work continues through 2027 and 2028. The six central towers are now externally complete.
- Tower: twelve-sided plan, 12 levels of panels begun 16 October 2018 at 85 m using pre-compressed stone and steel; final panel completed 4 December 2024 at 142.5 m. Terminal section 29 m tall (begun May 2025), with inscription "Tu solus Sanctus, tu solus Dominus, tu solus Altissimus".
- Cross: 17 m high, 13.5 m wide, glass and white glazed ceramic; lower arm installed 27 October 2025 at 162.91 m. Manufactured in Germany in 2025, delivered in modules, pre-assembled on a platform 54 m above the central nave, hoisted in seven sections. The 4.5 x 4.5 x 4.9 m element became the highest point.
- An Agnus Dei sculpture by Andrea Mastrovito will be installed inside the upper arm.
- Coincides with the centenary of Gaudí's death; commemorative events planned. Chief Architect Jordi Faulí: "a concrete commitment to the future, making possible the completion of the Sagrada Família."
- Published 21 February 2026.

wikis.title: Final piece of Sagrada Família central tower installed
wikis.summary: ArchDaily reports the cross section installed on 20 February 2026 brought the Sagrada Família to its maximum height of 172.5 m.
wikis.body:
- Published 24 February 2026 by Antonia Piñeiro. The upper section of the 17 m, four-sided steel and glass cross was winched into place at 11 a.m. on Friday 20 February, completing the tower dedicated to Jesus Christ, bringing the church to 172.5 m.
- Construction began 144 years earlier; Gaudí took over in 1883. Announced in March 2024 as an anticipated 2026 completion marking the centenary of Gaudí's death.
- October 2025: recognised as the world's tallest church, surpassing Ulm Minster, when the first section of the cross reached 162.91 m.
- Expected to feature eighteen towers. 2026 is "expected to mark the completion of the main building"; work on the Glory Façade projected to last another 10 years. Doubts remain about the grand entrance stairway, which would require demolishing apartments and rehousing residents.
- About 5 million visitors a year; tourism generates roughly €150 million annually, about half of which (per The Guardian) has been spent on construction.
- A completion ceremony is set for 10 June, the centenary of Gaudí's death and 16 years since consecration by Pope Benedict XVI.
- Context: Barcelona is UNESCO World Capital of Architecture 2026; UIA World Congress of Architects 28 June to 2 July 2026.

wikis.title: Blessing and inauguration of the Tower of Jesus Christ, 10 June 2026
wikis.summary: Sagrada Família's announcement of the 10 June 2026 event at which Pope Leo XIV will bless and inaugurate the central Tower of Jesus Christ on the centenary of Gaudí's death.
wikis.body:
- Announced at a press conference (publish date 5/21/26) held in the Crossing Room, 80 m above ground inside the tower (65 m above the Temple floor), by General Director Xavier Martínez and Head Architect Jordi Faulí.
- **10 June 2026**, hundredth anniversary of Gaudí's death: floral offering at his tomb in the crypt at 10:00 am; Solemn Mass at 7:30 pm led by Pope Leo XIV with cardinals, bishops, priests and Catalan choirs; afterwards the Pope goes outside and blesses the tower. The King and Queen of Spain, the president of the Spanish Government and the president of the Generalitat de Catalunya confirmed attendance.
- More than 4,000 attend the Mass by invitation; an additional 4,000 invitations to follow from Carrer de la Marina in front of the Nativity façade (3,080 for parish communities, 920 institutional). 4,200 tickets donated via parishes. Live broadcast on TV, social media and city screens.
- Commemoration: 31 events between autumn 2025 and Christmas 2026 (12 held, 19 to come); €3.2 million budget funded entirely by a patronage plan. Sponsors named include CaixaBank, Telefónica, Endesa, Henkel, Prosegur, GetYourGuide, Tiqets and others.
- Tower milestones: work began 16 October 2018 with first panels at 85 m; final piece of the cross installed 20 February 2026. Internal cladding under way, the Lamb of God figure recently installed, lift installation in progress, crane bracing due to be removed shortly.
- More at sagradafamilia2026.org.

wikis.title: Sagrada Família to inaugurate Tower of Jesus Christ on June 10, 2026
wikis.summary: May 21, 2026 press release giving the programme for Pope Leo XIV's blessing and inauguration of the Sagrada Família's central tower on the centenary of Gaudí's death.
wikis.body:
- PR Newswire release from Sagrada Família, May 21, 2026, Barcelona.
- Pope Leo XIV will preside over the Solemn Mass and bless the central Tower of Jesus Christ on **June 10, 2026**, exactly 100 years after Gaudí's death. The King and Queen of Spain, the Spanish Government president and the Generalitat president will attend.
- Programme: 10:00 am floral offering at Gaudí's tomb in the crypt; 7:30 pm Solemn Mass; then the blessing outside marking the formal inauguration.
- More than 4,000 guests inside; 4,000 invitations to follow from Carrer de la Marina (3,080 parish communities, 920 institutional). Live broadcast on institutional TV, social media and city screens.
- €3.2 million commemoration budget, funded through a patronage plan.
- Tower work began October 16, 2018; final cross piece installed February 20, 2026; internal cladding continues, The Lamb of God figure recently installed, lift installation under way, crane bracing expected to be removed shortly.
- Construction began March 19, 1882. The tower brings the basilica to 172.5 meters, making it the tallest church in the world.

wikis.title: Western Sydney Airport: plans, construction and opening timeline (Wikipedia, part 1)
wikis.summary: Part 1 of Wikipedia's Western Sydney Airport article, covering its location, flight-path controversy, Stage 1 construction and the milestone timeline through the 2026 opening.
wikis.body:
## Overview
- Western Sydney International (Nancy-Bird Walton) Airport, IATA WSI, ICAO YSWS, at Luddenham and Badgerys Creek, NSW; owned by the Australian Government, operated by WSA Co Limited; elevation 80 m.
- Opened 27 July 2026 for cargo flights; passenger flights scheduled to open 25 October 2026 (per ABC News, 9 June 2026).
- Linchpin of Aerotropolis Western Sydney (aerospace, defence, manufacturing, health, freight, agribusiness, education and research); the Western Parkland City was gazetted in 2023 as the city of Bradfield.

## Stage 1
- Single 3.7 km runway (05/23), terminal up to 90,000 m2, parking for about 11,500 cars. Initial cost estimated at A$2.4 billion (as of 2012); phase originally planned for 2025, later delayed to 2026.

## Flight paths
- Draft EIS 19 October 2015 showed flights merging over Blaxland; after backlash the final EIS (15 September 2016) marked paths "indicative only". Flight paths released June 2023; noise insulation grants for some residents. Airspace changes took effect 9 July 2026. (Section flagged "neutrality disputed", January 2026.)
- Sydney Airport Curfew Act 1995: BAe-146 freight exemption at Sydney Airport ends once WSI can be used for night movements.

## Timeline
- 15 April 2014 Badgerys Creek designated; 2 May 2017 Sydney Airport declines to build it; 9 May 2017 up to A$5.3 billion committed via WSA Co; 4 March 2019 named after Nancy Bird Walton; 15 March 2023 IATA code WSI; 8 June 2023 Qantas/Jetstar agreement; 27 August 2024 Singapore Airlines first international carrier.
- Construction: Stage 1 began 24 September 2018; Bechtel delivery partner (30 June 2018); terminal awarded to Multiplex 4 June 2021, begun 21 November 2021; runway completed 29 January 2024; terminal complete 11 June 2025, with a year of testing to follow; 28 October 2025 first commercial-sized jet (an RFS Boeing 737) landed.
- 22 June 2026 bus terminal opened; 9 July 2026 Class C airspace in effect; 27 July 2026 cargo operations began.

wikis.title: Western Sydney Airport opening dates announced
wikis.summary: Prime Minister's media release of 10 June 2026 setting passenger opening for 25 October 2026 and freight for 26 July 2026, with airline start dates.
wikis.body:
- Media release, Wednesday 10 June 2026, Anthony Albanese and Catherine King. "After 15 years of planning, seven years of construction and a year of testing", WSI welcomes first passengers on **25 October 2026**.
- Full-service, curfew-free, serving up to 10 million passengers annually with scalable expansion.
- Jetstar operates the first commercial flight (Airbus A320 to the Gold Coast, 11am Sunday 25 October); from launch up to 14 flights a week to Melbourne, four weekly to the Gold Coast, three weekly to Brisbane.
- Qantas (QantasLink Embraer E190) from 28 March 2027: four weekly to Brisbane, four to Melbourne. Air New Zealand to Auckland from 26 October; Singapore Airlines daily to Changi from 23 November 2026.
- Freight starts Sunday 26 July (Qantas Freight regular flights the following evening). 1 November 2026 is the intended gazettal date for night movements under the Sydney Airport Curfew Act 1995, ending overnight freight at Kingsford Smith.
- Part of a near $18 billion investment in Western Sydney (Sydney Metro Airport rail, Elizabeth Drive, Fifteenth Avenue, Mamre Road). Over 12,800 jobs, about half local; over $500 million to more than 360 local businesses.
- Minister King: passenger flights "in just 137 days".

wikis.title: Western Sydney Airport set to open
wikis.summary: Department of Infrastructure notice that WSI opens for freight on 27 July 2026 and passengers on 25 October 2026.
wikis.body:
- Published 11 June 2026. Freight flights 27 July 2026; passenger flights 25 October 2026.
- Jetstar first passenger flights to the Gold Coast on 25 October, plus Melbourne and Brisbane; Air New Zealand to Auckland 26 October; Singapore Airlines daily to Singapore from 23 November 2026.
- Qantas Freight regular services from 27 July 2026. From 1 November 2026 WSI is intended to become Sydney's airport for overnight freight movements under the Sydney Airport Curfew Act 1995.
- Project created more than 12,800 jobs (about half local); more than $500 million invested in 360 Western Sydney businesses. Part of investment including road upgrades and the future Sydney Metro Airport connection.

wikis.title: Grand Paris Express: lines, history, costs and opening schedule (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia overview of the Grand Paris Express, Europe's largest public transport project, with four new automated metro lines plus extensions, staged openings from June 2024 to 2031.
wikis.body:
- Megaproject in Île-de-France: four new Paris Metro lines (15, 16, 17, 18) plus extensions of lines 11 and 14; a total of 200 km of new track and 68 stations, projected 2 million passengers a day. "Europe's largest public transport project". Built by Société des Grands Projets (SGP, until 2023 Société du Grand Paris); operators chosen by Île-de-France Mobilités. Lines open in stages between June 2024 (Line 14 extension, opened 24 June 2024) and 2031.
- History: Grand Paris law 3 June 2010; state and region merged plans 26 January 2011; master plan approved by decree 24 August 2011; recast as "Nouveau Grand Paris" in March 2013. Line 15 South construction began 2015. Schedule revised repeatedly (February 2018; further slippages in February and December 2025). Line 15 South, once expected around 2020, is "now due in early 2027 at best".
- **Line 15**: ring line, planned to open in phases 2027 to 2031; southern section (Pont de Sèvres to Noisy-Champs) tunnels completed 2021, expected 2027. Alstom Metropolis MR6V trains.
- **Lines 16 and 17**: Line 16 planned 2027-2028; Line 17 in phases 2027-2030 (its traffic forecasts contested). Alstom MR3V trains.
- **Line 18**: Orly to Versailles-Chantiers via Saclay plateau, phases 2026-2030, starting with Massy-Palaiseau to the plateau; Vinci consortium won a €799 million package in May 2020.
- Line 11 extension to Rosny-Bois-Perrier opened 13 June 2024; a further extension towards Noisy-Champs postponed indefinitely. Line 19 studies launched November 2023, could open around 2040.
- Costs: about €20 billion (2009), €27 billion (2013 recast), €38.5 billion (Cour des comptes, January 2018); a 2020 Senate report estimated €35.6 billion in 2012 prices, around €42 billion current.
- Trains driverless, platform screen doors, average commercial speed about 65 km/h, headways as short as 85 seconds; expected 20 to 30 percent load reduction in the core network. Operators: RATP (11, 14), ORA (RATP Dev, Alstom, ComfortDelGro) for Line 15 South, Keolis for 16, 17, 18.

wikis.title: Grand Paris Express Line 15 South postponed to summer 2026 (Sortiraparis)
wikis.summary: Sortiraparis article, updated November 29, 2024, saying commissioning of Line 15 South slipped from end 2025 to summer 2026 because of testing delays, with East and West sections due in 2031.
wikis.body:
- Updated November 29, 2024. Line 15 will be France's longest metro line: 75 km around Paris, crossing 45 communes and four départements, 36 stations (East, West, South sections), over 1.5 million passengers daily.
- Southern section (Pont de Sèvres to Noisy-Champs) was announced for end of 2025; postponed to **summer 2026**, announced 28 November by Société des grands projets, "delays in testing". Chairman Jean-François Monteils: "We need to deepen our test phases...".
- History of slips: initially 2020, then 2023, 2024, end of December 2025, now summer 2026. East (Champigny Centre to Saint-Denis-Pleyel) and West (Pont de Sèvres to Saint-Denis Pleyel) sections scheduled for 2031.
- Travel example: Arcueil-Cachan to Pont de Sèvres in 11 minutes versus 48 minutes today. Almost 95% of stations connect with existing transport.
- Noteworthy stations: Noisy-Champs (interchange with Line 16, platforms 13.5-21 m deep), Le Vert de Maisons (35 m), Saint-Maur-Créteil (52 m, deepest in France).
- Lists connections at each station (e.g. Saint-Denis Pleyel: line 14 and RER D; La Défense: T2, line 1, RER A and E, lines L and U).

wikis.title: Delhi-Mumbai Expressway: route, packages and opening timeline (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on India's 1,350 km access-controlled Delhi-Mumbai Expressway, partially operational, with its packages, cost and staged openings through 2026.
wikis.body:
- Under construction, partially operational, 1,350 km, eight-lane (expandable to 12), access-controlled greenfield expressway (NE 4) connecting Delhi and Mumbai, cutting travel from 24 hours to 12. Runs through Delhi (12 km), Haryana (129), Rajasthan (373), Madhya Pradesh (244), Gujarat (426) and Maharashtra (171). Main length Sohna to Virar is 1,198 km; extensions DND-Faridabad-KMP (59 km) and Virar-JNPT (92 km); spurs Faridabad-Jewar (32 km) and Bandikui-Jaipur (67 km) take the network to 1,450 km.
- Cost: around ₹1,00,000 crore (~US$13.1 billion) including land; NHAI SPV DME Development Limited. 52 packages to about 20 contractors; about 15,000 hectares acquired (status as of 28 March 2026).
- Timeline: Package-1 awarded 20 March 2018 to IRB Infrastructure; foundation stones March 2019 (then "about 3 years" to complete); 12 February 2023 PM Modi inaugurated 246 km Sohna-Dausa-Lalsot; 244 km Madhya Pradesh section opened 20 September 2023; Vadodara-Bharuch 22 February 2024; November 2024 24 km Mithapur-Ballabhgarh; December 2024 80 km Kota-Laban; April 2025 756 km open; June 2026 a 63.5 km stretch Kim to Enna opened.
- Expectations: Aug 2025 - Delhi-Vadodara "expected to be completed by December 2026", Vadodara-Mumbai fully operational "in 2027-28". Bandikui-Jaipur spur operational Aug 2025; Faridabad-Jewar spur expected end of 2026. Godhra-Dahod under construction, expected by end of 2026.

wikis.title: Delhi-Mumbai Expressway: Delhi-Vadodara targeted June 2026, Gujarat packages March 2028
wikis.summary: Swarajya report (26 March 2026) on Nitin Gadkari's Rajya Sabha reply: Delhi-Vadodara section targeted for June 2026 while three Gujarat packages slip to March 2028.
wikis.body:
- Swarajya Staff, Mar 26, 2026, reporting a written reply in the Rajya Sabha on Wednesday 25 March by Road Transport and Highways Minister Nitin Gadkari.
- Under Bharatmala Pariyojana: 54 construction packages, 1,445 km including spurs, of which 929 km operationalised.
- Delhi-Vadodara section: 912 km, 697 km operationalised, 215 km under implementation; "targeted for its completion by June 2026".
- Vadodara-Mumbai: Packages 8, 9 and 10 in Gujarat delayed "mainly due to delays on part of Contractor"; now targeted for March 2028; other packages in 2026.
- Sanctioned cost Rs 96,547 crore; expenditure Rs 77,558 crore up to December 2025.

wikis.title: Delhi-Mumbai Expressway approaching completion in November 2026 (VahanBazaar)
wikis.summary: VahanBazaar explainer (May 9, 2026) saying the 1,362 km expressway's last section is due in November 2026, halving Delhi-Mumbai travel to about 12 hours.
wikis.body:
- Published May 9, 2026. Claims 1,362 km length, ~12 hours travel (vs ~22-24 on old NH48), 120 km/h design speed, six states, 50+ exits; built by NHAI under Bharatmala Phase 1. Runs from Dwarka in Delhi to Bhiwandi near Mumbai; "the world's longest access-controlled highway upon completion".
- Says the last section opens in **November 2026**; remaining sections (mainly Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat-Maharashtra border, final approach to Mumbai) "on track for completion by November 2026".
- State lengths given: Delhi ~24 km, Haryana ~129, Rajasthan ~373, Madhya Pradesh ~244, Gujarat ~426, Maharashtra ~166. Spurs to Jaipur, Vadodara, Surat, Bhopal connector.
- Newest sections use barrier-free Multi-Lane Free Flow (MLFF) tolling read via FASTag; toll for the full route "to be announced".
- Comparison: old route ~1,420 km; estimated fuel saving of 3-4 litres per trip; EV trips need 3-4 charging stops. Also discusses used-car market implications.

wikis.title: Jeddah Tower: design, history and construction status (Wikipedia, part 1)
wikis.summary: First part of Wikipedia's Jeddah Tower article covering the megatall skyscraper's specs, planning history, halt in 2018 and restart, reaching 113 floors by 2 September 2026.
wikis.body:
- Megatall skyscraper under construction in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, centrepiece of Jeddah Economic City; planned as the first 1 km building, at least 1,008 m (at least 180 m taller than the Burj Khalifa). 167 floors, 252 levels, 57 Kone lifts, observatory at 630/638 m; estimated completion August 2028; architect Adrian Smith + Gordon Gill; contractor Saudi Binladin Group; owner Kingdom Holding Company; developer Jeddah Economic Company.
- Status: "As of 2 September 2026, the tower reached 113 floors"; 100th floor by May 2026. Construction halted January 2018 with about one third complete (contractor labour issues after the 2017-2019 Saudi purge, then COVID-19). New request for proposals September 2023; restarted January 2025; "expected to be completed as early as 2028".
- Jeddah Economic City: 5.2 km2, designed by HOK, at least SR75 billion (US$20 billion), about ten years. Tower to house a Four Seasons hotel, offices, luxury condominiums and the world's highest observation deck.
- History: 2008 soil tests raised doubts and reports of scaling back; 2009 reports of being on hold denied; March 2010 Adrian Smith selected; October 2010 agreement with Emaar; August 2011 Langan foundation design (piles up to 200 m deep, pad over 90 m across, weight over 900,000 tonnes).

wikis.title: Jeddah Tower construction and August 2028 completion target (Newsweek)
wikis.summary: Newsweek piece (updated 08/19/25) quoting Adrian Smith + Gordon Gill Architecture that construction has ramped up with completion scheduled for August 2028.
wikis.body:
- The architects AS+GG told Newsweek: "The construction schedule reflects August of 2028 completion". Tower constructed to Core Level 69 "this week"; wings five to 10 floors behind; "50 percent of the concrete has been placed".
- Exact floors and height "will be unveiled upon completion"; "more than 130 floors" and over 3,281 feet; at least 568 feet taller than the Burj Khalifa. Sky terrace on the 157th level would be the world's highest observatory.
- Centrepiece of the $20 billion Jeddah Economic City (formerly Kingdom City), northern Obhur. Mixed-use: luxury hotel, offices, apartments, condominiums.
- Design inspired by palm fronds; three sides with notches creating shaded terraces. 59 elevators (54 single-deck, five double-deck) plus 12 escalators; observatory elevators at 10 m per second.
- Construction began around 2013, was halted for years; "officially began again in January this year". Gordon Gill: "No changes have occurred since the restart"; a new bridge over the creek is planned to link to the city core. Total cost "confidential"; the firm's website says $1.2 billion to construct.

wikis.title: Jeddah Tower to overtake Burj Khalifa by 2028 (The Week)
wikis.summary: The Week India (August 16, 2026) says Jeddah Tower, expected to be unveiled in August 2028, has reached 106 levels and about 430 m.
wikis.body:
- Published August 16, 2026 by Meera Suresh. Tower expected completed August 2028, beating Burj Khalifa by at least 172 m (about 564 ft).
- Latest reports: 430 m and 106 levels, exceeding half the Burj Khalifa's height; "107 floors at present". Work restarted January 2025 after stalling for several years.
- About 530,000 m2 built area (residential, hospitality, office, observation). 59 elevators (54 single-deck, five double-deck) and 12 escalators. "11 times the height of the Statue of Liberty".
- Construction started 2013, paused 2018 due to labour shortages and the detention of prominent Saudi businessmen during the 2017 anti-corruption campaign.

wikis.title: Fehmarn Belt fixed link tunnel (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the under-construction 17.6 km immersed road-rail tunnel between Lolland (Denmark) and Fehmarn (Germany), now due to open in 2031.
wikis.body:
- Immersed tunnel under the 18 km wide Fehmarn Belt; owner Femern A/S; length 17.6 km, four lanes and two electrified tracks (200 km/h), tolled. Work began 1 January 2021; opens 2031 (NDR, Jan 2026: "Schwieriger als geplant"). Planned as the world's longest combined road and rail tunnel; replaces the Scandlines ferry.
- Ferry crossing of 45 minutes becomes 10 minutes by car and seven by train. Hamburg-Copenhagen rail journey from 4 h 40 to 2 h 30.
- Approved 2015 with a construction budget of 52.6 billion krone (US$8.2 billion), largest traffic investment in Danish history; Germany plans a further €800 million for connections. Earlier: 2009 estimate 42 billion DKK (€5 billion); 2011 €5.5 billion; bridge option abandoned in December 2010 in favour of a tunnel.
- Completion date revisions: 2021 (2012), 2024 (2014), 2028 (2015), 2029 (2020), 2032 (2026 per the article).
- 79 standard elements of 217 m plus ten 85.7 m service elements. EU awarded €589 million (June 2015). Fehmarn Sound Tunnel to replace the Fehmarn Sound Bridge on the German side.

wikis.title: Fehmarnbelt tunnel project status, summer 2026 (Femern)
wikis.summary: Femern's project status page (summer 2026) describing the tunnel factory, work harbours, dredging and the first tunnel elements immersed from May 2026.
wikis.body:
- Tunnel factory: site equal to 300 football pitches, largest in Europe, over 2,000 people from more than 40 countries; three halls (A, B, C) with five standard-element lines and a sixth line for 10 special elements.
- Tunnel built from 79 elements, each 217 m long, each of nine segments; designed for a 120-year lifespan. Panel Factory (about 25,000 m2, about 100 employees) assembles rebar grids.
- Work harbours run by Blue Water Harbor Management; a cargo vessel arrives about every third day in Denmark, about two per week in Germany.
- Work at sea began June 2020; 2 million tonnes of Norwegian granite for the new coastline. Trench dredging completed in 2024, almost 15 million m3 of material reused for about 300 hectares of nature and recreation areas at Rødbyhavn.
- Immersion vessels: Maya, Ivy 1 and Ivy 2, NP460, Wismar.
- "In May 2026, the first element was immersed off the Danish coast and connected to the Danish tunnel portal. Until August 2026, two additional elements have been immersed."
- Puttgarden: German portal has a 450 m cut and cover section and about 150 m transition zone; two of three new bridges completed. Construction began 2020 in Denmark, 2021 in Germany.

wikis.title: Fehmarn Belt tunnel delayed until 2031 (DPA via Yahoo)
wikis.summary: DPA report of 16 January 2026 that the Denmark-Germany Fehmarn Belt tunnel will open no earlier than 2031, two years behind schedule.
wikis.body:
- Fri, January 16, 2026. Sund & Bælt Holding CEO Mikkel Hemmingsen: lowering of tunnel segments delayed by two years, "two years behind schedule"; last target had been 2029.
- 18 km rail and road tunnel between Fehmarn and Lolland, aimed to cut Copenhagen-Hamburg travel times.
- Cause: immersion method only tested in the Øresund (15 m deep) versus 45 m depth here. "It was more difficult than planned... You have to lower the segments with a precision of half a centimetre."
- Schleswig-Holstein premier Daniel Günther: largest construction site in Northern Europe. A further tunnel between Fehmarn and the German mainland is also expected to be delayed beyond 2029.

wikis.title: The B1M: building the Fehmarn Belt fixed link
wikis.summary: The B1M's video article (23 November 2022, narrated by Fred Mills) explaining why the Fehmarn Belt link became an immersed tunnel and how the tunnel elements are built.
wikis.body:
- Published 23 November 2022 by The B1M (Ian Parkin; video presented by Fred Mills); page lists 15,324,897 video views.
- Context: the Scan-Med corridor (5,000 km, Malta to Finland) has a 150 km detour through Denmark at the Fehmarn Belt. Sweden pushed for a fixed link as a deal for helping build the Øresund Bridge; Denmark and Germany signed a treaty in 2008. Crossing: four-lane motorway plus two rail lines, funded by Denmark (which collects tolls); Germany upgrades the route and builds another tunnel under the Fehmarn Sound.
- Options rejected: a cable-stayed bridge (spans over 700 m, pylons just under 300 m, sea foundations to 25 m depth, poor soil) and a bored tunnel (would need up to five tunnels; the belt is about 40 m deep and trains climb only about 1 in 40). Chosen: immersed tube tunnel, five times longer than the 4 km Drogden Tunnel.
- Construction site at Rødbyhavn run by Femern A/S; factory of half a million m2 (around 200 football pitches) producing, per the video, 89 elements each 220 m long, 12 m high, 40 m wide, running 24/7 for three and a half years. Each element is nine segments, each taking 36 hours to cast; elements weigh 73,000 tonnes and are lowered to within 15 mm of target.
- Discusses opposition (e.g. AGFF) and the Fehmarn Sound Bridge (1963). Femern technical director Jens Ole Kaslund: "My hope is just that a year after it opens, no one can remember that it was not there."

wikis.title: Hinkley Point C nuclear power station: history, cost and schedule (Wikipedia, part 1)
wikis.summary: First part of Wikipedia's Hinkley Point C article covering the two-EPR Somerset plant's history, approval, financing and delays, with Unit 1 projected to start in 2030.
wikis.body:
- Under construction at Hinkley Point, Somerset: two EPR pressurized water reactors (2 x 1,630 MWe, 3,260 MWe planned); owners EDF Energy 76.69% and China General Nuclear Power Group 23.31%; operator NNB Generation Company; 6,300 on-site construction workers; cooling with Severn Estuary sea water.
- Construction began March 2017 when completion was expected in 2025. As of 2026, Unit 1 projected online 2030; cost £35 billion in 2015 prices (c. £48 billion in 2026 prices), "almost double the estimated cost when the project was approved" (initially £18 billion in 2015 prices).
- History: 1981 plans and opposition (Stop Hinkley Expansion campaign; 1988-89 inquiry); 1995 plans abandoned; January 2008 white paper; EDF bought British Energy for £12.4 billion (2009); site named one of eight on 18 October 2010; site licence November 2012; Centrica withdrew February 2013; Development Consent Order March 2013; October 2013 contract for difference at £89.50 per MWh; December 2013 EU state-aid investigation; EDF board approved July 2016 and UK government September 2016.
- Delays attributed to COVID-19, Brexit and budget overruns.

wikis.title: Hinkley Point C first reactor start-up pushed back to 2030 (Construction Enquirer)
wikis.summary: Construction Enquirer report that mechanical and electrical delays moved Hinkley Point C Unit 1 start-up to 2030 and raised the cost to £48bn at today's prices.
wikis.body:
- By Aaron Morby (URL dated 2026/02/22). EDF confirmed lower than expected productivity on electromechanical installation: Unit 1 now scheduled to start up in **2030**, a year after the previous best case (2029), two years behind the earlier 2027 revised timetable and five years after the original 2025 date set when approved in 2016.
- Cost: £35bn in 2015 prices, equivalent to £48bn today, up £1.4bn.
- EDF annual results: Unit 1 civil works 94% by concrete volume at end of last year; 24 primary loop welds finished in January; major safety injection pumps installed. Unit 2 dome lifted and reactor pressure vessel delivered. MEH programme still behind despite better installation rates in H2 2025; recent momentum is "a reasonable foundation" for the revised timetable.
- Hinkley received £1.6bn from Sizewell C for expertise; Sizewell C projected at £38bn at 2024 prices.

wikis.title: Hinkley Point C M&E productivity hit pushes Unit 1 start-up to 2030
wikis.summary: Industrialised Construction (March 2, 2026) report that EDF delayed Hinkley Point C Unit 1 to 2030 and put cost at £48bn.
wikis.body:
- Published March 2nd, 2026. EDF pushed the first reactor start-up back a further year on lower-than-expected productivity in electromechanical installation; Unit 1 now due in 2030 (previous best-case 2029; 2027 revised timetable; original 2025).
- Cost £35bn in 2015 prices, "£48bn at today's prices", up £1.4bn.
- From EDF's annual results: Unit 1 civil works 94% by concrete volume at end of last year; 24 primary loop welds completed in January; safety injection pumps installed; Unit 2 dome lifted, reactor pressure vessel delivered. MEH programme remains behind schedule.
- £1.6bn payment from Sizewell C for expertise; Sizewell C projected at £38bn at 2024 prices.

wikis.title: Rogun Dam, Tajikistan (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the Rogun (Roghun) Dam on the Vakhsh River, begun in 1976, restarted in 2016, with two units commissioned and the 335 m dam still under construction.
wikis.body:
- Under-construction dam in southern Tajikistan on the Vakhsh River; built by Webuild (formerly Salini Impregilo); owner Government of Tajikistan. Planned height 335 m; reservoir 13.3 km3; six 600 MW turbines (3,600 MW planned, 240 MW installed), 17.1 TWh a year expected. Listed cost US$2-5 billion; opening date "2018-2029".
- History: proposed 1959; construction began 1976, abandoned in 1993 after the Soviet collapse; RUSAL agreement 2004; suspended August 2012 pending World Bank studies (ESIA published 16 June 2014, TEAS July 2014); 2010 IPO raised US$184 million of US$1.4 billion target; 1 July 2016 Salini Impregilo chosen for $3.9 billion; 29 October 2016 President Rahmon launched construction; first unit commissioned November 2018, second September 2019; concrete pouring on the main dam core began mid-July 2022.
- Uzbekistan opposed it over cotton irrigation (Karimov called it a "stupid project" in 2010) but dropped opposition in 2018.
- Said to have been the world's highest dam only as a projected height; in reality about 60.96 m until destroyed in a flood in 1993.

wikis.title: Webuild: Rogun Dam takes shape in Tajikistan
wikis.summary: Webuild press note (August 28, 2025) on progress at the 335 m Rogun Dam and a visit by Tajikistan's President.
wikis.body:
- Press note dated August 28, 2025. The dam is nearing 1,110 m above sea level, a milestone that lets the reservoir level rise and increases energy production.
- President Emomalī Rahmon visited the site with PM Qohir Rasulzoda and the client OJSC Rogun HPP. Around 70% of Tajikistan's population experiences power outages, especially in winter.
- At completion: 335 m high, installed capacity "equivalent to three nuclear reactors", supplying about 10 million people and doubling Tajikistan's energy production.
- Over the last year the dam rose up to 100 m, placing about 13 million m3 of embankment material (about 3.5 million m3 of loam for the impermeable core); more than 180,000 linear metres of injections carried out.
- Webuild says it has built over 300 dams and hydro projects; also mentions the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam inauguration scheduled for September and Snowy 2.0.

wikis.title: On the road to Rogun Dam (Al Jazeera reporter's notebook)
wikis.summary: Al Jazeera's 29 May 2026 visit to the Rogun Dam site, Tajikistan's 'Project of the Century', describing its scale, tunnels and turbines.
wikis.body:
- By Mustafa Rezk, 29 May 2026. About two hours' drive from Dushanbe.
- The "$5bn Rogun project", launched in the mid-1970s to tackle chronic energy shortages, described by President Emomali Rahmon as a matter of "life or death"; hopes to reduce winter shortages and perhaps export surplus.
- Includes hydraulic tunnels 1,100 to 1,500 m long and an underground power station with six units, about 3,600 MW; dam with clay core.
- Italian engineer Andres of Webuild (main works contractor): the dam will be 335 m (1,100 ft) high, "one of the tallest in the world".
- Called the "Project of the Century"; needs massive funding and a balance with downstream countries watching water flows.

wikis.title: Ontario Line, Toronto: history, cost and contracts (Wikipedia, part 1)
wikis.summary: First part of Wikipedia's Ontario Line article: a 15.6 km Toronto rapid transit line now estimated at about $34 billion with opening in the early 2030s.
wikis.body:
- Under construction in Toronto: 15.6 km, 15 stations (six connecting to other lines), from Exhibition GO Station to Eglinton Avenue and Don Mills Road (Don Valley station, Line 5 Eglinton). To be designated Line 3 on opening.
- Announced by the Government of Ontario on April 10, 2019 at CA$10.9 billion with completion by 2027; in 2026 estimated around $34 billion, opening in the early 2030s. Groundbreaking March 27, 2022; tunnelling began April 20, 2026 with two TBMs.
- Origins: Downtown Relief Line plans (1980s), TTC 2012 study, Relief Line South (est. $6.8 billion). Metrolinx prepared the Ontario Line plan in three months based on Michael Schabas's proposal (lighter, shorter trains); Doug Ford approved after a February 26, 2019 presentation. October 2019 deal with Mayor Tory; council approved 22-3.
- Contracts: RSSOM to Connect 6ix (Hitachi Rail, Transdev, Plenary Americas, Webuild), awarded November 17, 2022, valued at $9 billion, in-service 2031. South civil to Ontario Transit Group (Ferrovial, Vinci), November 9, 2022, $6 billion, completion 2030. North (Gerrard to Don Valley Bridge) to Pape North Connect (Webuild and FCC), awarded January 17, 2024; signed August 2026 at $4.3 billion. Northernmost to Trillium Guideway Partners (Acciona, AMICO), February 20, 2024; value not announced as of August 2026.

wikis.title: Ontario Line cost jumps to $34B (CBC)
wikis.summary: CBC News (Aug 11, 2026) reports Metrolinx confirming the Ontario Line's cost has climbed to about $34 billion, more than triple the $10.9 billion first projected.
wikis.body:
- Olivia Piercey, CBC, posted Aug 11, 2026. Cost was $10.9 billion when announced in 2019; now around $34 billion per Metrolinx, and could be higher since no contract is yet awarded for the elevated parts. Baseline was roughly $29.8 billion as of June (Metrolinx report).
- Metrolinx CEO Michael Lindsay cited supply chain shocks and trade uncertainty: "we lived in a different world in respect of major capital project delivery."
- 15.6 km line, above- and below-ground, 15 stations, 40+ transit connections. Completion once 2027, then 2030, then 2031, now "sometime in the early 2030s".
- Last week two European companies (Webuild and FCC) awarded $4.32 billion for twin tunnels and two underground stations. Tunnelling on the downtown segment started April 16 (Premier Doug Ford).
- Transportation minister Prabmeet Sarkaria called it a "legacy project". Researcher Jonathan English: not out of the ordinary versus US projects, but far above Montreal's REM (about $10 billion, about 64 km); little transparency on line items.

wikis.title: Sydney Metro West: planning, stations and contracts (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the 24 km, nine-station Sydney Metro West line between Hunter Street and Westmead, under construction and planned to open in 2032.
wikis.body:
- Underground rapid transit under construction; owner Transport for NSW; 24 km, nine stations (Hunter Street, Pyrmont, The Bays, Five Dock, Burwood North, North Strathfield, Sydney Olympic Park, Parramatta, Westmead), depot at Clyde. Work began November 2020; tunnelling from 2023; planned opening 2032. Twin tunnels, fully automated, 25 kV overhead.
- Announced 14 November 2016; $6.4 billion funding in March 2019; total cost not released, with 2021 Sydney Morning Herald reports suggesting $27 billion and 2033 opening. Planning approvals March 2021. A Rosehill station proposal was rejected by Australian Turf Club members in May 2025.
- Contracts: Central Tunnelling to Acciona/Ferrovial (July 2021, $1.96 billion); Western Tunnelling to Gamuda/Laing O'Rourke (March 2022, $2.16 billion); Eastern Tunnelling to John Holland/CPB/Ghella (November 2022, $1.63 billion); Station Package West to Gamuda (January 2025, $2.85 billion); Hunter Street station and development to Metropolis Consortium (Lendlease, Mirvac, Coombes) at $1.5 billion. Trains and Systems contract covers 16 trains.

wikis.title: Metro West to supercharge housing supply (NSW Government, 7 December 2023)
wikis.summary: NSW Government release resetting Sydney Metro West to a 2032 completion and adding scoping of up to two new stations to drive housing supply, following the Sydney Metro Independent Review.
wikis.body:
- Ministerial media release, 7 December 2023, from the Premier and Minister for Transport (Minns Labor government): an enhanced Metro West with potential new stations linked to housing uplift.
- "The project will be reset to a more sustainable timeline, with the project expected to be completed by 2032." Extra time avoids paying a premium and allows exploring additional stations.
- The previous government left a 7 km gap between Sydney Olympic Park and Parramatta; scoping studies for up to 2 new stations west of Sydney Olympic Park.
- Independent reviewers Amanda Yeates and Mike Mrdak recommended committing to the current 9-station alignment at a minimum, targeting 2032, calling the earlier date "arbitrary"; also a property and placemaking strategy and a bus/active transport business case. Housing and Productivity Contributions to help fund infrastructure.
- Premier Chris Minns: "the biggest public transport project in the country". Minister Jo Haylen: will cut crowding by 30% at stations like Strathfield, Redfern and Burwood. Sydney Metro CEO Peter Regan: 4 of 6 tunnel boring machines in the ground on the 24 km line from Westmead to the CBD.

wikis.title: Sydney Metro West project overview
wikis.summary: Sydney Metro's overview of the 24 km Metro West line, its nine stations, features, planning approvals and 2032 target opening.
wikis.body:
- New 24 km underground metro that will "double rail capacity between Parramatta and the Sydney CBD"; about 10,000 direct and 70,000 indirect jobs during construction. Page lists an April 2026 project update.
- Confirmed stations: Westmead, Parramatta, Sydney Olympic Park, North Strathfield, Burwood North, Five Dock, The Bays, Pyrmont, Hunter Street. "Sydney Metro West will target an opening date of 2032."
- Features: driverless trains with platform screen doors, level-access, continuous mobile coverage.
- Planning: work started at The Bays in 2020; first major approval March 2021 (Westmead to CBD concept and Westmead-The Bays tunnelling); second September 2022 (The Bays to CBD); third (rail infrastructure, stations, precincts, operations) approved 2023. Over/adjacent station development approved in 2024 at Parramatta, Sydney Olympic Park, Pyrmont and Hunter Street East and West; an amending application lodged to raise residential dwellings at Sydney Olympic Park.

wikis.title: Brenner Base Tunnel (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the 64 km Brenner Base Tunnel between Innsbruck and Franzensfeste, scheduled to open in 2032, with the main tunnels completed on 29 July 2026.
wikis.body:
- Under construction rail tunnel through the Alps (Austria-Italy), twin tube, double track, 64 km overall, scheduled opening 2032; part of the Berlin-Palermo TEN-T axis, funded by Austria and Italy with large EU contributions. Passenger 250 km/h, freight 120 km/h; max elevation 840 m; up to 1,720 m below surface.
- Aim: relieve Brenner Pass road traffic (about three-quarters of traffic is road); Innsbruck-Bolzano travel time from about 2 hours to 50 minutes; max gradient 0.4-0.7%. About 21 million m3 of rock to excavate; bore diameter about 8.1 m.
- Cost: final estimate €8.384 billion at 2018 levels. Timeline slips: 2015 target (2005), 2022 (2007 memorandum), now 2032. Exploratory work from 2007; main tunnel construction 2011.
- 6 July 2019 unbroken 36 km tunnel; 18 September 2025 exploratory tunnel breakthrough joined Italian and Austrian sections; "two main tunnels were completed almost simultaneously at 10:35 on 29 July 2026". At least three workers died as of March 2025.
- Approaches: Lower Inn Valley high-speed line opened 9 December 2012 (Munich-Innsbruck 1:50 to 0:55); 180 km new line to Verona in eight sections; northern Brenner Nordzulauf lacks local support.

wikis.title: Brenner Base Tunnel (Austria-Italy rail tunnel)
wikis.summary: Railway Technology project page describing the Brenner Base Tunnel between Innsbruck and Fortezza: specs, construction lots, financing, benefits and contractors.
wikis.body:
- Rail tunnel beneath the Brenner Pass connecting Fortezza (Italy) and Innsbruck (Austria); core of the 425km Brenner railway line from Munich to Verona. Page dated August 11 2022.
- Length 56km (page also says 55km); with the Inn Valley Tunnel the combined length is 64km. About 230km of tunnels in total; excavation completed along 152km of the 230km.
- Approved 2009, construction begins 2011; the fact box says completion 2025, but the text says "expected to be completed by 2032" / operational by 2032.
- Estimated cost: fact box says €6bn; text says "more than €8bn ($11.53bn)". EU contributes up to 50%, remainder split equally by Austria and Italy.
- Two single-track tubes (8.1m diameter, 40-70m apart), exploratory tunnel (5m diameter, 12m below), cross passages every 333m, four lateral access tunnels (Mules, Wolf, Ahrental, Ampass), emergency stops at Innsbruck, St. Jodok and Trens.
- Design speed 120km/h freight, 250km/h passenger; 25kV 50Hz; ERTMS/ETCS Level 2 and GSM-R. About 50% excavated by TBM, 50% drill and blast.
- Benefit: travel time Innsbruck-Fortezza cut from 80 to 25 minutes. Developer BBT SE: ÖBB 50%, TFB (Italy) 50%.
- Lots: H21 Sill Gorge (expected end 2024), H41 (22.5km of main tubes and 38 cross passages by Summer 2028; €651m contract awarded November 2021), H33 Tulfes-Pfons (completed September 2021), H52 Hochstegen (ground-breaking May 2022), H53, H61 Mules 2-3, H71 Isarco river underpass.
- Contractors named: Herrenknecht (TBMs), Webuild, Strabag, Implenia, Porr, Swietelsky, Amberg, Lombardi, SYSTRA SWS and others.

wikis.title: Rail Baltica railway project
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Rail Baltica, the standard-gauge rail line linking Tallinn, Riga, Kaunas and Warsaw: route, parameters, organization, funding, cost growth and progress.
wikis.body:
- Under-construction rail infrastructure to integrate the Baltic states into the European rail network; Tallinn to Warsaw via Pärnu, Riga and Kaunas, with branches to Riga International Airport and Vilnius. 870km in the Baltic states (213km Estonia, 265km Latvia, 392km Lithuania).
- Standard gauge 1,435mm (region otherwise mostly 1,520mm Russian gauge), 25kV 50Hz AC, ERTMS L2; design speed 249km/h passenger (operational 234km/h), 120km/h freight; max freight train 1,050m, 25 tonne axle load.
- As of 2025, phase 1 single-track completion from Tallinn through Riga to the Lithuania-Poland border is "scheduled for 2030", double track "dependent on funding".
- Cost: €5.8bn in 2017 estimate; by 2024 the estimate rose to €23.8bn (2023 prices), phase 1 single track €15.3bn. A 2024 joint review by Baltic audit institutions found a funding shortfall of €10.1bn for phase 1 and €18.9bn overall. A 2026 European Court of Auditors report suggested the estimate may not be accurate.
- Implemented by Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania through joint venture RB Rail AS (est. 2014); Finland announced in February 2019 it would join. Funded by member states, EU TEN-T/CEF and cohesion funds; about €1.2bn received, plus a €928m CEF grant announced October 2023.
- A Helsinki-Tallinn tunnel was proposed; in February 2024 Finnish minister Lulu Ranne judged it unrealistic.
- Milestones: Saustinõmme viaduct cornerstone in Estonia 2019; spatial plans approved 2016-2018; Inter-Governmental Agreement ratified 2017.

wikis.title: Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2025/1332 on Rail Baltica
wikis.summary: EU legal text of 9 July 2025 setting priorities and a two-phase timetable for building Rail Baltica and repealing Decision (EU) 2018/1723.
wikis.body:
- Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2025/1332 of 9 July 2025, published OJ L 10.7.2025, in force; repeals Implementing Decision (EU) 2018/1723; based on Regulation (EU) 2024/1679.
- Recitals: geostrategic value has increased; contribution to defence and military mobility to be considered; COVID and Russia's war against Ukraine disrupted the project. The line should connect the three Baltic countries to the European network "in 2030".
- Member States are to complete the core network by 31 December 2030, but "the Rail Baltica project will not be completed before the end of 2030"; so it is built in two phases.
- Phase 1 (until 31 December 2030): prioritise Tallinn-Pärnu-Salaspils-Misa-Panevėžys-Kaunas-Warszawa; Riga and Vilnius linked via existing network; single track allowed Tallinn-Kaunas provided a double-track embankment and enough passing loops are built; Lithuania may install energy, control-command and signalling on existing standard-gauge track between Poland and Kaunas.
- Phase 2 covers further elements needed for full potential.
- RB Rail AS continues as project coordinator; a Rail Baltica Task Force chaired by the European Coordinator steers Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Finland and the Commission. Commission to update the decision every four years or on request.

wikis.title: Commission adopts milestones for completion of Rail Baltica
wikis.summary: European Commission news item of 9 July 2025 announcing an implementing decision setting milestones for Rail Baltica.
wikis.body:
- News article, 9 July 2025, DG Mobility and Transport: the Commission adopted an implementing decision setting key milestones and deadlines for completing Rail Baltica.
- "Unanimously supported by all Member States"; a step toward fully integrating Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania into the European railway network by 2030.
- European Coordinator Catherine Trautmann: "In the current geopolitical environment, building Rail Baltica is a necessity."
- Part of efforts to accelerate cross-border projects under the revised TEN-T Regulation. Finland "recently announced its intention to adapt its rail gauge to the European standard".
- Decision is Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2025/1332.

wikis.title: High Speed 2 (HS2): overview, history and cancellation of Phase 2
wikis.summary: First part of the Wikipedia article on HS2, the English high-speed railway under construction since 2020, covering its scope, opening dates, cost, history and the cutting back of the project.
wikis.body:
- HS2 is a high-speed railway under construction in England since 2020, between Handsacre (southern Staffordshire) and London, with a branch to Birmingham; stations at Old Oak Common, Birmingham Interchange and Birmingham Curzon Street (and London Euston).
- When proposed in 2010, Phase 1 was expected to open by December 2026; "as of May 2026, passenger services are not expected to begin before 2036".
- As of May 2026 expected cost £87.7 billion to £102.7 billion (2025 prices); Old Oak Common-Curzon Street services May 2036 to October 2039; London Euston services May 2040 to December 2043.
- Class 895 trains expected to reach 320 km/h (200 mph); 230 km line, 25 kV 50 Hz, ETCS Level 2.
- Timeline: 2009 DfT proposes second high-speed line; December 2010 Y-shaped route proposed; February 2017 Phase 1 Act; February 2021 Phase 2a Act; Oakervee Review published 11 February 2020; formal approval to start work 15 April 2020; Integrated Rail Plan 18 November 2021 curtailed the eastern leg.
- July 2023 IPA red rating; HS2 Ltd chief executive Mark Thurston resigned 13 July 2023. October 2023 Rishi Sunak announced Phase 2 abandoned and £36 billion redirected to "Network North"; Euston cut to six platforms.
- January 2024 Public Accounts Committee: "HS2 now offers very poor value for money to the taxpayer".
- December 2024 Mark Wild became chief executive; 31 March 2025 letter said the organisation "has failed in its mission to control costs and deliver to schedule" and the programme was about one third complete against a planned three-quarters. Stewart Review reported 18 June 2025; Transport Secretary called the situation "an appalling mess". Work between Birmingham and Handsacre deferred four years in October 2025 as part of a reset.

wikis.title: HS2 6-monthly report to Parliament, November 2023
wikis.summary: UK government written statement of 15 November 2023 on HS2 after the Network North announcement: cancelled later phases, Phase 1 cost estimates, Euston and construction progress.
wikis.body:
- Published 15 November 2023 by DfT, HS2 Ltd and Huw Merriman; delivered in the House of Commons.
- Network North command paper (4 October 2023): government will not extend HS2 beyond Birmingham; "we will not proceed with Phase 2a, 2b or HS2 East"; £36 billion (2023 prices) reallocated to other transport schemes, plus a further £12 billion earmarked to connect Manchester and Liverpool.
- Phase 1 completed London to West Midlands with two branches (central Birmingham, and Handsacre near Lichfield to the West Coast Main Line). Initial services Old Oak Common to Birmingham Curzon Street still "within the range of 2029 to 2033".
- Euston scaled back to a 6-platform station with a development-led "Euston Quarter" approach using private funding.
- Cost: HS2 Ltd board's updated Phase 1 estimate at completion £49 billion to £57 billion (2019 prices); government disagreed, DfT provisional range £45 billion to £54 billion. Main Work Civils £21.8 billion to £23.4 billion, up £6.1 billion.
- Delivery: 350 active construction sites; TBMs Florence and Cecilia over three quarters of the 10 mile Chilterns drive; Sushila and Caroline (2,000 tonne) started the 8.4 mile Northolt Tunnels in November 2022.
- Accounting Officer concluded Phase 1 benefit cost ratio above 1 in a range of scenarios; HS2 Ltd Executive Chair Sir Jon Thompson asked to update the estimate.

wikis.title: HS2 Phase 1 Accounting Officer Assessment summary (May 2026)
wikis.summary: DfT summary of the decision to continue HS2 Phase 1 after a programme reset, with new cost and schedule ranges and value-for-money conclusions.
wikis.body:
- Updated 19 May 2026. Government confirmed it will complete the current scope from Euston to the West Midlands "despite the very significant increases in cost and delays to delivery".
- In June 2025 the Transport Secretary announced a fundamental reset of HS2 covering cost, schedule, commercial arrangements and HS2 Ltd capacity.
- Phase 1 cost range £87.7 billion to £102.7 billion (mixed price base, excluding inflation). Schedule ranges: Old Oak Common to Curzon Street May 2036 to October 2039; Euston to the North West via Handsacre Junction May 2040 to December 2043.
- Operating speed to be reduced to 320 kph; initial assessment suggests possible savings of £1 billion to £2.5 billion, not yet included; impact on benefit cost ratio "minimal".
- Value for money: assuming 10 trains per hour vs cancellation and remediation, BCR for continuing "likely exceeds 1.5"; at 2020 Notice to Proceed with current costs it would be 0.3-0.4.
- Euston to be delivered partly privately financed by a new Euston Delivery Company. HS2 Ltd transformation plan being developed through 2026; regularity, propriety and feasibility tests met.

wikis.title: Second Avenue Subway: overview, phases and early history
wikis.summary: First part of the Wikipedia article on New York's Second Avenue Subway, covering its phases, service pattern, plans and the pre-war history of the proposal.
wikis.body:
- NYC Subway line under Second Avenue, Manhattan. Phase 1 (72nd, 86th and 96th Street stations, 1.8 mi tunnel, cost $4.45 billion) opened January 1, 2017; served by Q at all times, limited rush-hour N and R.
- Full line proposed: 10 miles, 19 stations, projected 724,000 daily riders, "more than $24.7 billion"; Harlem-125th Street to Hanover Square.
- Phase 2 (96th to 125th Streets, 1.5 miles, $6 billion) began construction in June 2026. Phase 3 south to Houston Street, Phase 4 to Hanover Square; a new T train (turquoise) would serve the full line.
- Design: 30 trains per hour (26 at Hanover Square); 125th Street station scaled down to two tracks in July 2018.
- History: proposed 1920 (Daniel L. Turner plan; 1929 approval with $98.9 million cost); Depression and WWII delays; Second Avenue El closed 1940/1942 (northern half June 11, 1940; southern June 13, 1942), Third Avenue el demolished 1955. Construction began 1972, halted 1975 by the fiscal crisis; restarted April 2007.
- Ridership listed as 45,367 weekday.

wikis.title: MTA to approve $1.97 billion tunneling contract for Second Avenue Subway Phase 2
wikis.summary: amNewYork article (August 15, 2025) on the MTA's planned $1.97 billion contract to bore tunnels and start two stations for Phase 2 in East Harlem.
wikis.body:
- Posted August 15, 2025 (Adam Daly). MTA board expected to vote Monday to award a $1.97 billion contract to Connect Plus Partners (joint venture of Halmar International and FCC Construction).
- Phase 2: a $6.99 billion project "slated to open in September 2032"; three new Q stations at 106th, 116th and 125th streets, about 110,000 daily riders, connecting to Metro-North at Harlem-125th Street; with Phase 1 the line is expected to carry about 300,000 passengers a day.
- Contract scope: convert a 2,500-foot 1970s tunnel between 116th and 125th into a station box, bore an 8,400-foot tunnel to Malcolm X Boulevard, mine the 125th Street station cavern, dig ancillary shafts.
- 1.5 million-pound German-made variable-density TBM; delivery expected early 2027; reduces crew 40%, saving an estimated $100 million in labor.
- Phase 2 about 10% cheaper than Phase 1; changes saved an estimated $1.3 billion; four of six cross passages eliminated; 32 "value engineering" proposals.
