- Published Tue 27 Aug 2024. San Miguel Corp confirmed a BusinessWorld report that completion of the New Manila International Airport in Bulacan would slip to 2028, mainly from difficulty sourcing sand used as backfill.
- Project cost: Php740 billion ($13.15 billion). The Manila Bay reclamation projects' suspension limited access to sand.
- SMC also expected MRT Line 7 in Bulacan to be delayed to 2028 over the alignment and location of San Jose del Monte Station. SMC's half-year net income jumped 66 per cent.

wikis.title: MetroLink enabling works could start in 2027, says Transport Minister
wikis.summary: Irish Times report (3 Oct 2025) on Transport Minister Darragh O'Brien's timeline for Dublin's MetroLink after planning permission was granted.
wikis.body:
- Published Fri 3 Oct 2025 by The Irish Times. Minister for Transport Darragh O'Brien said "enabling" works could start in two years (2027), with construction getting under way in 2028, "with a fair wind".
- Planning permission was granted "on Thursday"; he hoped there would be no legal challenge (judicial review). Absent one, MetroLink could be completed by 2035. He said the rail link from Swords (north Dublin) to Charlemont, near Ranelagh, could open in phases.
- He said: "This [project] is happening", after many previous announcements and cancellations.
- Funding: the Government pledged EUR 2 billion under the revised National Development Plan (announced in July), covering initial works over the next five years; "not a blank cheque". Previous cost estimates ranged from EUR 7 billion up to EUR 23 billion; the Minister did not believe it would be as high as EUR 23 billion and declined to give updated costs as the project would go to tender soon.
- Bidders: "two consortia that have already confirmed that they will be bidding"; market engagement events were held in Dublin and London. Many Irish jobs and firms expected to be involved.
- Latest cost-benefit analysis: EUR 1.40 return to the exchequer per EUR 1 invested.
- Fingal County Council / Mayor Tom O'Leary: 25-minute direct rail link between Swords and Dublin city, trains every three minutes, capacity up to 20,000 passengers per hour in each direction, rail access to Dublin Airport; plans to grow Swords to 100,000 people.

wikis.title: MetroLink procurement split into civil and rail-systems packages (ENR, May 2026)
wikis.summary: ENR report on Ireland launching procurement for the M401, M402 civil and M500 DBFOM packages of Dublin's MetroLink, with notice values near $18 billion.
wikis.body:
- Published May 12, 2026 (Engineering News-Record). Ireland launched procurement for all three major delivery packages, combined published notice values approaching $18 billion, following the October 2025 Railway Order approval of the 18.8-km alignment (16 stations, Swords - Dublin Airport - city centre - Charlemont).
- Contracting authority: Transport Infrastructure Ireland (TII). M401 and M402 civil design-and-build notices released in February; M500 DBFOM (design, build, finance, operate, maintain) released May 1.
- **M401** (~$5.4bn): southern urban section; bored tunnels, portals, shafts, station boxes up to 35 m deep. **M402** (~$3.9bn): northern section; bored tunnelling, cut-and-cover, retained cut, at-grade work, two viaducts. Combined ceiling ~$9.3bn; TII expects bids considerably below. NEC4 contracts; three bidders shortlisted per package; bidders may pursue both but win only one. M401 award targeted Q3 2027; M402 Q4 2027.
- **M500** (~$8.6bn net present value): availability-based PPP covering GoA4 driverless rolling stock, signalling, track, overhead contact system, platform screen doors, ventilation, lifts/escalators, M&E fit-out across 16 stations, depot, operations control centre, 3,000-space park-and-ride; ~7-year construction then 25 years of operation (about 32-year term). PQQ open; invitation to tender targeted early 2028; financial close expected Q4 2028; three bidders shortlisted for competitive dialogue. Interest signalled by consortia including Alstom, FCC, John Laing, Meridiam and RATP.
- Reference design led since 2018 by IDOM and Jacobs. Earlier enabling contracts (utility diversions, archaeology, Dublin Airport station box) already in procurement.
- Design targets: up to 20,000 passengers per direction per hour, initial 3-minute peak frequency, long-term 90-second headways, up to 53 million annual passengers.
- Quotes: TII CEO Lorcan O'Connor said M500 "has been carefully structured to allocate risk appropriately"; Program Director Dr. Sean Sweeney called the civil notices "a significant step forward".

wikis.title: NIED Large-scale Rainfall Simulator
wikis.summary: NIED facility page describing its Large-scale Rainfall Simulator and what it is used for.
wikis.body:
- The facility has "the world's largest rainfall area and sprinkling capacity" and can produce rainfall intensities between 15 and 300 mm/hr.
- Used to research landslides, debris flow, soil erosion, urban flooding, etc. Example experiment: reproducing a landslide by sprinkling water on a large model slope.
- Part of NIED's experimental facilities alongside the E-Defense Large-scale Earthquake Simulator and the Cryospheric Environment Simulator; NIED is at Tsukuba.

wikis.title: NIED outline and history timeline
wikis.summary: Timeline of Japan's National Research Institute for Earth Science and Disaster Resilience from 1959 to 2020.
wikis.body:
- Mission: protect lives and property from natural disasters through research on earthquakes, volcanoes, floods, landslides, meteorological changes, snow and ice damage.
- 1963.4: National Research Center for Disaster Prevention (NRCDP) established in Ginza, Tokyo under the Science and Technology Agency (after 1959 Ise Bay Typhoon).
- 1970.6: Large-scale Earthquake Simulator completed (first facility in Tsukuba Science City). 1974.3: Large-scale Rainfall Simulator completed. 1978.4: HQ moved to Tsukuba.
- 1990.6: renamed National Research Institute for Earth Science and Disaster Prevention. 1996.6: K-NET operation started. 1997.3: Cryospheric Environment Simulator completed (Shinjo). 1997.4: Hi-net, KiK-net, F-net construction started.
- 2001.4: became an Independent Administrative Agency. 2004.10: E-Defense (three-dimensional full-scale earthquake testing facility) started operation (Miki).
- 2010.4: V-net volcano network. 2011.8: S-net construction started. 2015.4: became a National Research and Development Agency. 2016.4: renamed National Research Institute for Earth Science and Disaster Resilience; DONET transferred from JAMSTEC.
- 2017.11: integrated MOWLAS operation began. 2019.2: N-net (Nankai Trough) construction started. 2020.6: 50th anniversary of the Large-scale Earthquake Simulator.

wikis.title: Palm Jebel Ali (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Dubai's Palm Jebel Ali artificial archipelago, from 2002 start through stalling to its 2023-2024 relaunch.
wikis.body:
- Artificial archipelago in Dubai; construction began October 2002, originally due mid-2008, on hold after the 2008 financial crisis, relaunched in 2024; "presently intended for completion in 2028". Described as 50 percent larger than Palm Jumeirah in the original plan.
- Original plan: six marinas, a water theme park, "Sea Village", stilt homes, boardwalks with an Arabic poem by Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum. Developer Nakheel planned to house 250,000+ people; theme parks "World of Discovery" (Busch Entertainment) planned.
- Breakwater completed December 2006; infrastructure work began April 2007. Property prices reportedly fell 40% in the two months to November 2008. Nakheel offered refunds in March 2011.
- October 2018: Nakheel CEO confirmed no immediate restart plans. July 2021: plans for villas announced. May 2022: reports of a Dubai court judgment cancelling the project, voiding 724 villa contracts (investors refunded original investment only). September 2022: Nakheel rebrand and relaunch plans; $4.6 billion debt restructuring; plans for 1,700 villas and 6,000 apartments.
- 31 May 2023: Sheikh Mohammed announced relaunch, up to twice the size of Palm Jumeirah, ~110 km added coastline, 80+ hotels, Gateway Tower, housing 35,000 families, a third of public facilities on renewable energy. 30 owners appealed the cancellation judgment. Construction restarted 2024; first properties planned for Q1 2027. In 2024 two investor groups issued trigger letters for international arbitration against Dubai Holdings (including Nakheel).

wikis.title: Nakheel awards $950m of villa contracts at Palm Jebel Ali
wikis.summary: The National (27 Apr 2026): Nakheel awarded more than Dh3.5 billion contracts for 544 villas at Palm Jebel Ali, completion targeted end of 2028.
wikis.body:
- Published April 27, 2026. Nakheel awarded contracts worth more than Dh3.5 billion ($950 million) for 544 villas: Ginco General Contracting builds 354 villas across Fronds A-D; United Engineering Construction (UNEC) builds 190 on Fronds E and F.
- Building scheduled to start "in the coming weeks" (this quarter); completion target Q4 / end of 2028.
- Khalid Al Malik, CEO of Dubai Holding Real Estate: "The awarding of these contracts signals tangible progress in the delivery of Palm Jebel Ali".
- When completed: twice the size of Palm Jumeirah, seven islands and 16 fronds, 90+ km of beachfront, homes for 35,000 families, 80 hotels and resorts. Master plan unveiled 2023 by Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid. Aligned with Dubai 2040 Urban Master Plan and D33 economic agenda.

wikis.title: Navi Mumbai International Airport starts flight operations with four airlines
wikis.summary: Aviation A2Z report (25 Dec 2025) on commercial operations beginning at Navi Mumbai International Airport with IndiGo, Air India Express, Akasa Air and Star Air.
wikis.body:
- Published December 25, 2025. Navi Mumbai International Airport (NMI) officially began commercial operations on December 25, 2025, with IndiGo (6E), Air India Express (IX), Akasa Air (QP) and Star Air (S5).
- Launch phase: 23 scheduled daily departures in the first month, flights 08:00-20:00, up to 10 aircraft movements per hour. Round-the-clock operations planned from February 2026, increasing to 34 daily departures.
- IndiGo: 13 destinations (Ahmedabad, Bengaluru, Cochin, Delhi, Hyderabad, Lucknow, Mangaluru, Nagpur, Goa Mopa, Jaipur, Chennai, Coimbatore, Vadodara), phased from 25 to 30 December 2025. First day included an inbound service from Bengaluru and outbound to Hyderabad. IndiGo says NMI complements Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj International Airport (BOM).
- Air India Express: initially Bengaluru (daily) and Delhi (five weekly, daily from January 1, 2026); NMI part of its dual-airport strategy in Mumbai.
- Akasa Air: Delhi, Goa, Kochi, Ahmedabad (Delhi and Kochi from 26 Dec 2025, Ahmedabad from 31 Dec 2025); targets 300 domestic and 50 international weekly departures over time.

wikis.title: Navi Mumbai International Airport (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Navi Mumbai International Airport: proposal in 1997, Adani/CIDCO-led construction from 2021, inauguration 8 Oct 2025 and commercial operations from 25 Dec 2025.
wikis.body:
- IATA NMI, ICAO VANM; in Ulwe, Navi Mumbai, Raigad district, Maharashtra. Owned by CIDCO (26%) and Mumbai International Airport Limited (74%); operator Navi Mumbai International Airport Limited (NMIAL). Second airport in the Mumbai Metropolitan Region.
- History: proposed November 1997; approved by Union cabinet August 2007; CIDCO nodal agency from 30 July 2008; cost estimate INR 167 billion (US$1.7 billion) in three phases, reaching 90 million passengers and 2.5 million tonnes of cargo per annum by 2032. GVK-led MIAL won the bid on 13 February 2017; groundbreaking 18 February 2018 (Modi); Zaha Hadid Architects appointed for terminal and ATC tower March 2018; Larsen & Toubro awarded construction September 2019; Adani took over 2021 (NMIAL SPV with CIDCO); construction began August 2021; 57% of first phase done by November 2023. 2,786 households relocated across ten villages.
- Inaugurated 8 October 2025 by Narendra Modi; commercial operations 25 December 2025 (first arrival an IndiGo flight from Bengaluru at 8 am). Dedicated freighter operations began 1 August 2026 (IndiGo Cargo to Sharjah).
- Facilities: 1,160 ha; single 3,700 m runway 08/26 with Category II ILS; eventually two parallel runways (third-runway feasibility study started 2025); terminal capacity 20 million passengers per annum after phase one, lotus-shaped design, 90 million when complete; cargo 0.8 million tonnes/year after phase one, target 3.2 million; FedEx developing a 300,000 sq ft automated cargo hub; temporary ATC tower.
- Statistics April 2025 - March 2026 (AAI): 638,394 passengers, 4,510 aircraft movements, 560.8 cargo tonnage.

wikis.title: Montparnasse Tower EUR 800 million renovation abandoned (Sortiraparis)
wikis.summary: Sortiraparis report (updated 23 July 2026) that co-owners abandoned the EUR 800 million Tour Montparnasse renovation at a 21 July 2026 general assembly, while asbestos removal proceeds.
wikis.body:
- Updated July 23, 2026. At a general assembly on Tuesday, July 21, 2026 the co-owners of Tour Montparnasse (Paris, 15th arrondissement) flagged the renovation as obsolete despite voting it months earlier; revelation from Le Figaro. A new project still needs to be drawn up.
- Trigger: asset manager LFPI, owning around 30%, said it no longer wished to fund the transformation as envisioned and favours a more modest, less costly intervention.
- Budget: EUR 624 million excl. taxes (summer 2025) -> EUR 727.7 million (March 2026) -> nearing EUR 800 million with asbestos. Banks reluctant to grant financial guarantees. In May 2026 several owners including Xavier Niel sued over decisions on floor-area exchanges; Frederic Lemos alleged conflicts of interest and refused to cede his 43rd-floor units, blocking the planned luxury hotel (floors 42-45).
- Project: designed by the Nouvelle AOM collective (Franklin Azzi Architecture, ChartierDalix, Hardel Le Bihan), 2017 competition winners: redesigned glass facade, rooftop agricultural greenhouse, luxury hotel, public spaces, partial demolition of the shopping centre. Construction was to start September 2026, reopening around 2030; Sefri-Cime and Vinci Construction were lined up.
- Asbestos removal first phase was kicked off at the July 21 meeting despite LFPI voting against. Tower empty since 31 March 2026; the 56th-floor Panoramic Observatory closed the same day after 50+ years. Current building permit expires in November 2026. No official statement from City of Paris, syndic or LFPI. Mayor of the 15th Philippe Goujon: "We don't want a watered-down renovation."

wikis.title: Montparnasse Tower renovation abandoned after ten years (Epoch Times FR)
wikis.summary: Epoch Times France (24 July 2026) on the abandonment of the EUR 800 million Tour Montparnasse renovation after LFPI withdrew support, with a first phase of works still agreed.
wikis.body:
- Published 24 juillet 2026. The renovation, priced near EUR 800 million, was abandoned after a co-owners' general assembly, per media that saw the minutes. Main co-owner LFPI no longer supported the transformation in its current form. Project had been under way since 2015.
- Costs (per Le Figaro): EUR 624 million excl. tax, then EUR 727 million, then nearing EUR 800 million with technical uncertainties including asbestos.
- The tower has been emptied of occupants since 31 March 2026; compliance works (technical, energy) remain needed.
- Frederic Lemos, former council president, said he was "astonished" by articles on total abandonment and called for a new general assembly to lift conditions precedent for the first phase.
- A first tranche was agreed: asbestos removal and removal of part of the facade; per Liberation it starts in September and lasts about two years. No new plan officially unveiled; no timetable for a redesign.

wikis.title: Nouvelle route du Littoral (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Reunion's Nouvelle route du Littoral (NRL), a 12.5 km sea-crossing road project with viaducts and causeway, its cost, delays and redesign.
wikis.body:
- NRL ("New Coastal Road") reroutes National route 1 over the sea in Reunion, ~12 km on viaducts and causeway, linking Saint-Denis and La Possession, replacing the coastal road exposed to rockfalls and waves. Faced technical, ecological and financial challenges; some contract awards subject to a legal inquiry.
- Cost EUR 1.6 billion (December 2011), ~EUR 130 million per km; nicknamed "the most expensive road in the world".
- 2019: rock supply (3 million tonnes) interrupted work; administrative court suspended quarry authorisations April 2019, Council of State confirmed 3 April 2020. Agreement between region and contractors 31 July 2020. Viaduct Grande Chaloupe-Saint-Denis completed 30 March 2021. 2021: incorrectly installed tetrapods caused further delays.
- Mid-February 2022 Huguette Bello announced La Possession-Grande Chaloupe section to be a viaduct not a causeway, adding EUR 500-700 million; opening estimated around 2029 or 2030. Cyclone Batsirai (February 2022) partially submerged the existing causeway.
- 28 August 2022: partially opened, one direction only, on 8.7 km between St Denis and La Grande Chaloupe.

wikis.title: Nouvelle Route du Littoral completion schedule to 2030 (La 1ere)
wikis.summary: La 1ere Reunion (21 Oct 2025): the Region presented the works calendar to finish the NRL, with the second viaduct delivered mid-2030.
wikis.body:
- Published 21 octobre 2025. Region president Huguette Bello and prefect Patrice Latron presented the calendar; final stage named "Dernier Viraz". About 70,000 users per day.
- 3.1 km of road missing, including 2.5 km of viaduct; cost EUR 846 million, with State subsidy of EUR 281 million and VAT compensation fund of EUR 400 million. Site to create 5,000 jobs.
- Calendar: mid-November 2025 dismantling of the temporary La Possession auto-pont (ramp closed from 18 November; dismantled night of 22-23 November 2025). Nov 2025-Feb 2026 connection/earthworks; Saint-Denis to Le Port traffic switched "mi-2026". July-Nov 2026 switch of the other direction. Nov 2026-June 2027 finish the interchange, delivered mid-2027. Viaduct works 2027 to early 2030, full commissioning mid-2030.
- Viaduct anchored to max 20 m under the sea, designed for cyclonic swell above 10 m; deck reserves space for a future train.

wikis.title: Two TBMs start boring the second Gotthard road tunnel tube
wikis.summary: Swissinfo/Keystone-SDA (14 Feb 2025): two tunnel boring machines began excavating the second Gotthard road tunnel tube, due for completion in 2030.
wikis.body:
- Published February 14, 2025. Two large tunnel boring machines began excavating the second corridor of the Gotthard road tunnel. Transport minister Albert Rosti called it "a milestone for Switzerland's most important north-south link".
- On Friday Rosti spoke at the launch of the machine "Paulina" in Airolo (150 m long, drill head over 12 m diameter); an inauguration followed in Goeschenen for the machine boring from the north. Both were manufactured in Germany and assembled on site since the previous summer.
- The ~17-km tunnel should be excavated by 2027 and completed in 2030; it will first run two-way traffic for three years so the 1980 tunnel can be renovated; afterwards traffic will use both tunnels in a single lane each.
- Voters approved the second tube in 2016; preparatory work began in 2020. Excavated rock is processed into concrete on site, partly used to cover the freeway in Airolo, partly deposited in Lake Uri for renaturation.

wikis.title: Gotthard Road Tunnel second tube (Structurae)
wikis.summary: Structurae data sheet for the second Gotthard road tunnel tube (2020-2030): dimensions, TBMs, cost, contractors and chronology.
wikis.body:
- Second tube, Goeschenen (Uri) to Airolo (Ticino), A2 motorway; works 2020, completion 2030, under construction. Road tunnel, 2 lanes, 16,900 m; single-shield TBMs for main tube, gripper TBM and single-shield TBM for access tunnel.
- Lot 243/241: access tunnel 3,940 m, main tube 6,885 m, TBM diameters 7.030 m and 12.225 m. Lot 343/341: access tunnel 5,000 m, main tube 7,755 m, TBM diameters 7.400 m and 12.310 m.
- Construction cost (excl. tax) CHF 2,053,000,000. Client: Federal Roads Office ASTRA. Contractors: Frutiger, Implenia, Webuild, CSC Costruzioni (lots 241/243); Marti Tunnel AG (lots 341/343).
- Chronology: 14 February 2025 start of the two TBMs (12.3 m); 29 April 2026 breakthrough in a geologically challenging northern fault zone.
- Imported Wikipedia text (March 2025): 1980 tunnel 16.9 km; second tube approved March 2014 bill, referendum February 2016; access tunnel started September 2021; main contract August 2022; works scheduled complete 2029; original tunnel then refurbished, reopening alongside the new one in 2032.

wikis.title: Carola Bridge, Dresden (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the Carola Bridge over the Elbe in Dresden: its 1971 construction, the 11 September 2024 collapse, demolition and planned replacement.
wikis.body:
- Road and tram bridge over the Elbe. First bridge built 1895, destroyed by the SS on 7 May 1945. Replacement built 1967-1971 (opened July 3, 1971) after a 1965 competition; three prestressed-concrete decks A, B, C (C for trams). Renovation began 2019; declared a protected monument 2022.
- Deck C collapsed between 02:58 and 02:59 (UTC+2) on 11 September 2024; no casualties. District heating pipelines were destroyed; a temporary pipeline was laid across the Augustus Bridge.
- Demolition began the next day, interrupted by the 2024 Central European floods. Decks A and B had shifted and shared structural flaws, so demolition of the whole bridge was approved. Early 2025: unexploded WWII ordnance found; February 2025: cracks detected in steel reinforcement of decks A and B, accelerating demolition. As of June 2025 the entire structure is being demolished.
- Dresden city council approved a new bridge, planned to start in 2027: two spans, four car lanes, tram tracks, extended bike lanes and footpaths.

wikis.title: More sections of Carola Bridge collapse, halting Elbe shipping (gCaptain)
wikis.summary: gCaptain (3 Mar 2025): further steel sections of Dresden's Carola Bridge collapsed, prompting a 72-hour shipping halt on the Elbe.
wikis.body:
- Published March 3, 2025. Additional steel elements collapsed "over the weekend", again halting shipping for 72 hours. The bridge, built 1971 by East Germany, partially collapsed in September 2024 (about 100 m of the central span; a light rail train had just crossed shortly before 3am; no casualties).
- The shipping channel had reopened a month earlier after a four-month closure; since end of January vessels passed single file with authorization.
- If no additional fractures or movement in 72 hours, controlled access under the bridge would resume. Removal of collapsed and standing sections slated to begin in coming weeks, to be completed by end of the year.

wikis.title: Buffalo Bills open new Highmark Stadium on Aug. 15 (preseason vs Panthers)
wikis.summary: Yahoo Sports/USA Today (Aug 3, 2026) on the Bills' first game at the new Highmark Stadium and ticket prices.
wikis.body:
- Published Mon, Aug 3, 2026. The Bills' new stadium, still named Highmark Stadium, opens to fans Saturday, Aug. 15 (1 p.m. ET) against the Carolina Panthers in a preseason game, in Orchard Park, N.Y.
- Tickets starting at $96 (just under $100) at publication; 100-level seating from $142 in Section 149.
- After a Week 1 road game at the Houston Texans, the first regular-season home game is Thursday Night Football vs the Detroit Lions on Sept. 17. The Bills enter 2026 with a new head coach.

wikis.title: Bills to play first regular-season game in new stadium in Week 2 (ESPN)
wikis.summary: ESPN (May 11, 2026): Bills will open their $2.1 billion new Highmark Stadium in Week 2 vs the Lions on Thursday Night Football.
wikis.body:
- Published May 11, 2026. First regular-season game at the new Highmark Stadium: Week 2 vs the Detroit Lions, the season opener for Prime Video's "Thursday Night Football" package. Venue cost $2.1 billion.
- Design: open-air with a roof canopy covering 64% of attendees; first row of one sideline 54 feet closer to the field than the former stadium; new outside area with three bison statues. Field switches from turf to grass, which can be heated.
- Demolition of the former stadium underway; the new one opens for initial events in summer including training camp's Blue & Red practice. The Bills played at the former home since 1973; it was named Highmark Stadium since 2021.

wikis.title: PM Modi inaugurates Chenab Bridge, world's highest rail arch bridge (DD News)
wikis.summary: DD News report (6 June 2025) on Modi inaugurating the Chenab Bridge, Anji Bridge and the USBRL rail link in Jammu and Kashmir.
wikis.body:
- Published 06/06/25. PM Narendra Modi inaugurated the Chenab Bridge, "the world's highest railway arch bridge", during a J&K visit launching projects worth Rs 46,000 crore.
- Chenab Bridge: 359 metres above the Chenab River, 1,315 m long steel arch, built for high seismic and wind loads; cuts Jammu-Srinagar travel time by two to three hours. Also inaugurated the Anji Bridge, "India's first cable-stayed railway bridge".
- USBRL (Udhampur-Srinagar-Baramulla Rail Link) dedicated to the nation: 272 km, about Rs 43,780 crore, 36 tunnels totalling 119 km and 943 bridges, all-weather rail to the Kashmir Valley. Vande Bharat trains flagged off between Shri Mata Vaishno Devi Katra and Srinagar.
- Also road projects (Rafiabad-Kupwara widening on NH-701, Shopian bypass on NH-444; over Rs 1,952 crore), flyovers in Srinagar, and a foundation stone for the Rs 350 crore Shri Mata Vaishno Devi Institute of Medical Excellence in Katra.

wikis.title: Chenab Rail Bridge and Kashmir rail link inaugurated (Gulf News/AP)
wikis.summary: Gulf News (AP, updated 6 June 2025): Modi inaugurated the Chenab Rail Bridge and the 272-km rail line connecting Kashmir to the rest of India.
wikis.body:
- Last updated June 06, 2025. Modi inaugurated the 272-km line running from Udhampur through Srinagar to Baramulla, connecting the Kashmir Valley to the Indian plains by train for the first time; Indian Railways calls it one of the most challenging tracks in the world.
- Line has 36 tunnels and over 943 bridges; total cost about $5 billion per the government.
- Chenab bridge, the world's tallest railway bridge, is 359 metres, 35 metres taller than the Eiffel Tower.
- Modi's first Kashmir visit since a military conflict between India and Pakistan "last month"; line expected to ease movement of troops and public, boost tourism.

wikis.title: Seismic upgrade completed on Salt Lake Temple (Church News)
wikis.summary: Church News (1 July 2026): base isolators freed, interior finishing and reopening preparations at the Salt Lake Temple.
wikis.body:
- Published 1 July 2026. Seismic renovations of about 6.5 years finished; the temple now rests on its base isolation system. Brad Bohne (Jacobsen Construction): "The temple is set free... Free to move now during an earthquake."
- From Thursday June 25 crews removed over 1,500 bolts connecting 392 plates to the 98 base isolators located 20 feet below the temple. Isolators allow the temple to move 5 feet in any direction during an earthquake.
- Interior: carpet in celestial room and study areas, chandelier above east baptistry font, instruction rooms nearing completion; stone paving over snowmelt tubing outside. Refurbished oak doors reinstalled (west early June, east June 23-25).
- Salt Lake Temple Celebration: volunteer/performer applications open through July 15; volunteers commit at least eight weeks.

wikis.title: Timeline of the Salt Lake Temple renovations (Deseret News)
wikis.summary: Deseret News (Aug 3, 2025) timeline from the April 2019 announcement to reopening scheduled for October 2027.
wikis.body:
- Published Aug 3, 2025. Key dates: April 19, 2019 announced; Dec. 30, 2019 temple closes and renovation starts; March 18, 2020 earthquake damages Angel Moroni statue; June 2021 three more floors added; Oct 2021 exterior stones removed; April 11, 2022 Main Street plaza closes; April 2023 completion target pushed back, halfway point April 11, 2023; Feb. 14, 2024 last spire placed; April 2, 2024 Angel Moroni returns; Jan 3, 2025 cable holes drilled; Feb 14, 2025 open house announced; April 2025 interior painting begins; April-October 2027 open house scheduled; October 2027 doors set to reopen.
- Purpose: preservation and earthquake resistance via base isolators under the building, which "will allow it to move 10 feet in any direction" (per this article); interior restored, added floors, a second baptistry and more sealing rooms.
- Reopening scheduled October 2027 after a six-month open house, "the longest temple open house in church history".

wikis.title: Hidroituango Dam threatens collapse in Antioquia, Colombia (FloodList)
wikis.summary: FloodList (20 May 2018): Antioquia declared a public calamity as blocked diversion tunnels at the Hidroituango Dam raised fears for 130,000 people downstream.
wikis.body:
- Published 20 May 2018. The Antioquia government declared Public Calamity as the Hidroituango Dam, on the Cauca river and in the final stages of construction, threatened to collapse.
- On 12 May a sudden release of water flooded Puerto Valdivia and Taraza; around 600 people evacuated. Cause: diversion tunnels blocked; reason unclear, some local media reported landslides. Water building up; fear of collapse threatening more than 130,000 people along the Cauca.
- EPM (Empresas Publicas de Medellin), responsible for construction, said it was working to increase the dam's height. Red Cross: maximum alert downstream (Ituango, Briceno, Valdivia, Caceres, Taraza, Caucasia, Nechi). Preventive evacuation orders in Sucre, Cordoba and Bolivar departments. As of 20 May 2018 around 8,000 people had evacuated between Taraza, Caceres and Caucasia (UNGRD).

wikis.title: Colombia seizes assets of firm behind Hidroituango dam (Colombia Reports)
wikis.summary: Colombia Reports (22 Apr 2021): the Comptroller ordered seizure of Integral SA assets over the Hidroituango dam that nearly collapsed in 2018.
wikis.body:
- Published Apr 22, 2021. The Comptroller General ordered seizure of 13 bank accounts and 12 properties of Integral SA, which designed the dam. The contractors will have to pay $1.7 billion (COP4.2 trillion) to recover alleged damages.
- Integral was founded 1955; co-founder Jose Tejada Saenz proposed a Cauca dam in a 1969 study (he died in 2011). Government approved Hidroituango in 2009; EPM consortium formed 2010; dam was supposed to provide 17% of Colombia's energy in 2018.
- Early 2018 the discharge tunnels blocked and the Cauca's rising waters threatened the project; EPM workers used the turbine tunnel to discharge water and finished the $4 billion dam wall. Authorities relocated more than 100,000 people downstream.
- Aftermath: criminal investigation and probes by the Comptroller and Inspector General; in 2018 the comptroller announced investigations against 18 politicians and former EPM officials.

wikis.title: Disneyland opens, July 17, 1955 (History.com)
wikis.summary: History.com 'This Day in History' entry on Disneyland's opening in Anaheim, with Walt Disney background and later parks.
wikis.body:
- Published Nov 24, 2009; last updated Aug 11, 2026. Disneyland opened July 17, 1955; $17 million park on 160 acres of former orange groves in Anaheim, California. Today more than 18 million visitors a year spending close to $3 billion.
- Construction began 1954 on land bought in Anaheim, about 25 miles southeast of Los Angeles. Invitations were counterfeited so thousands of uninvited people entered on opening day; food and drink ran out, a woman's high-heel shoe stuck in wet asphalt on Main Street USA, the Mark Twain Steamboat nearly capsized.
- Attractions named: the Castle, Mr. Toad's Wild Ride, Snow White's Adventures, Space Station X-1, Jungle Cruise, Stage Coach.
- Later: Walt Disney World opened October 1, 1971 (work began 1965; Disney died 1966); Disneyland Tokyo 1983; Disneyland Paris 1992; Hong Kong September 2005.
- Walt Disney background: born Chicago 1901; Steamboat Willy 1928; Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs (1938).

wikis.title: Disneyland (Wikipedia): origins, construction and opening day to the 1980s
wikis.summary: First part of the Wikipedia article on Disneyland (Anaheim): concept, site, 1954-55 construction, opening day and history through the 1980s.
wikis.body:
- Theme park at Disneyland Resort, Anaheim; first theme park opened by Walt Disney Company and only one built under Walt's direct supervision; opened July 17, 1955. 757 million cumulative visits (as of December 2021); 17.33 million visitors in 2024, second most visited amusement park that year behind Magic Kingdom.
- Origins: idea began watching daughters at Griffith Park merry-go-round; earliest draft memo August 31, 1948 ("Mickey Mouse Park"). Stanford Research Institute (C. V. Wood, Harrison Price) chose the area; Disney bought 160 acres of orange groves and walnut trees in Anaheim in 1953. WED Enterprises founded (precursor of Imagineering). Joe Fowler was "construction boss". Funding via ABC TV show "Disneyland"; owned first five years by Disneyland, Inc. (Walt Disney Productions, Walt Disney, Western Publishing, ABC); by 1960 Walt Disney Productions bought out others.
- Construction began July 16, 1954, cost $17 million; opened one year and one day later. Dedication July 17, 1955 "International Press Preview": 28,000 attended, about half invitees (counterfeit tickets, fence climbers); public opening next day with twenty attractions. Hosts Art Linkletter, Bob Cummings, Ronald Reagan. Known as "Black Sunday" (rides broke down, food ran out, Sleeping Beauty Castle doors unlocked, Mark Twain Riverboat overloaded).
- Later notes: Doritos created at the park's Casa de Fritos (sold regionally 1964); attendance record 82,516 on August 16, 1969; August 6, 1970 Yippie protest, 23 arrests; Bear Country and Main Street Electrical Parade 1972; Space Mountain opened 1977; Big Thunder Mountain 1979; New Fantasyland 1983; September 1984 employee strike. Additions: New Orleans Square 1966, Mickey's Toontown 1993, Star Wars: Galaxy's Edge 2019; Disney California Adventure opened 2001.

wikis.title: ESS completes Beam on Dump 2, advancing toward first neutrons
wikis.summary: European Spallation Source news (July 7, 2026): second accelerator commissioning-to-dump phase (BoD2) completed, with first neutrons planned for early 2027.
wikis.body:
- Published July 7, 2026. ESS completed Beam on Dump 2 (BoD2), started February 2026. First neutrons "planned for early 2027". The accelerator is shut down for the summer; a new commissioning phase starts in the autumn.
- Background: in May 2025 protons were accelerated from the ion source to the tuning beam dump, 542.5 metres down the accelerator tunnel (Beam on Dump), starting full commissioning.
- BoD2: beam through the normal conducting linac, and in March the superconducting linac; since early May the beam has been stably reaching the tuning dump at 800-860 MeV. Now the goal is operating at increasing beam power with stable performance.
- Target: pulsed proton beam with 2 MW average beam power onto a rotating tungsten target wheel, releasing neutrons by spallation. Parameters reached: pulse length 1.5 ms (0.005 ms in May 2025), repetition rate 14 Hz (1 Hz in May 2025), beam current 62.5 mA. 89 RF cavities; more than 500 beam instruments along the linac.

wikis.title: Inside the European Spallation Source neutron research facility (The B1M)
wikis.summary: The B1M video article (12 Nov 2025) explaining how ESS in Lund, Sweden works and how it was built.
wikis.body:
- Published 12 November 2025 (video hosted by Fred Mills; contains paid promotion for Brilliant; 1,426,804 video views). Title: "Inside The $3.5BN Mega-Lab That Will Change The World". Thirteen nations are building it near Lund, Sweden (less than 20 miles from Malmo).
- How it works: a linear accelerator in a ~600 m tunnel fires protons at almost light speed at a target: a stainless-steel wheel weighing almost five tonnes filled with tungsten blocks, 36 radial segments, spinning at 23.3 rpm, helium-cooled. Spallation ejects neutrons; power planned 5 MW, "over twice as powerful as" other such facilities. Accelerator installation began 2017; Ciprian Plostinar (head of accelerator): "we are about to wrap up" in 2025.
- Build details: 6,000+ foundation piles for the Target building; 8 m tall, 6,000-tonne Monolith with 32 stainless-steel blocks placed within +/-0.75 mm; Active Cells Facility with 18 m deep chambers and concrete 60% heavier (iron ore added).
- Neutrons pass a moderator-reflector, then to 15 instrument labs across three halls; data goes to a Data Management and Scientific Computing Centre outside Copenhagen. About 3,000 scientists a year expected. Designed for low visual impact; waste heat to warm around 20,000 people in Lund. Roof by Buro Happold, "ESS Sombrero", cantilevers 35 m. Neutron beam intensity "ten quintillion" neutrons per second. Comparisons: ISIS (UK), Oak Ridge (Tennessee).

wikis.title: BT Tower (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on London's BT Tower (formerly Post Office Tower): construction 1961-65, 1971 bombing, antennas removed, sale to MCR Hotels in 2024.
wikis.body:
- Communications tower in Fitzrovia, London, built 1964 (originally Museum Radio Tower; Post Office Tower, Telecom Tower; BT Tower since 1991). Grade II listed 2003. 177 m main structure, 189 m (620 ft) with aerials. Tallest structure in London until 1980. Owned since 2024 by MCR Hotels.
- Commissioned by the General Post Office for microwave aerials; designed by the Ministry of Public Building and Works (Eric Bedford, G R Yeats); moves no more than 25 cm in 150 km/h winds. Construction began June 1961; topped out 15 July 1964; inaugurated by Harold Wilson on 8 October 1965; cost 2.5 million pounds. First microwave link to Norwich 1 January 1965. Foundations 53 m through London clay. Originally to be 111 m high.
- Opened to public 19 May 1966 (Queen visited 17 May); Butlins revolving restaurant on the 34th floor (one revolution per 23 minutes) until 1980; nearly one million visitors and over 100,000 diners in the first year.
- 04:30 on 31 October 1971 a bomb exploded in the restaurant's men's toilets, claimed by the Angry Brigade; tower closed to the general public afterwards.
- 2009: 360-degree LED screen with 529,750 LEDs added. Last antennae removed December 2011. Two high-speed lifts (7 m/s). 21 February 2024: BT Group announced sale to MCR Hotels, who plan to retain the tower as a hotel.

wikis.title: 8 October 1965: The Post Office Tower opens (MoneyWeek)
wikis.summary: MoneyWeek feature (last updated 8 Oct 2020) on the opening of London's Post Office Tower.
wikis.body:
- Officially opened 8 October 1965 by prime minister Harold Wilson, who made a call to the Lord Mayor of Birmingham. Public opening 19 May 1966 by Tony Benn and Billy Butlin (Butlin's leased the 120-seat revolving restaurant on the 34th floor). Entry 4/- adults, 2/- children.
- Built by the General Post Office for microwave transmission: 150,000 simultaneous telephone connections and 40 TV channels of bandwidth. Construction June 1961, four years, cost "either 2.5m (if you believe Wikipedia) or 9m (if you believe BT)". 189 m (620 ft), Britain's highest building, overtaking St Paul's, until 183 m National Westminster Tower (1980).
- First year: nearly one million visitors, 105,000 diners. An Act of Parliament made it the only building legal to evacuate by lift in a fire.
- 4.30AM 31 October 1971 a terrorist bomb caused extensive damage; closed to casual visitors soon after (4,632,822 had ascended). Restaurant closed 1980; tower used by BT for corporate events; microwave transmitters removed 2011 but still a TV relay centre.

wikis.title: MTA Board approves resubmission of $68.4 billion 2025-2029 Capital Plan
wikis.summary: MTA press release (updated May 28, 2025) on the Board approving the resubmitted $68.4 billion capital plan, focused on state of good repair.
wikis.body:
- Updated May 28, 2025. After funding passed in the New York State budget, the MTA Board approved the plan for resubmission to the MTA Capital Program Review Board in Albany. $68.4 billion; "largest state of good repair investment in MTA history", more than 90% dedicated to rebuilding and improving the system; first informed by a 20-year needs assessment.
- MTA Construction & Development has begun preliminary work on nearly half of projects, including modern signaling on the Fulton and Liberty Lines, preliminary design of the Interborough Express, and Hudson Line resiliency on Metro-North.
- Investments: 2,000 railcars, 60 stations made accessible, 75 miles of signals modernized, new fare gates at 150 stations, Grand Central Artery overhaul, 80+ power stations rebuilt, train shops and yards upgraded.
- In-house work moved to save costs (platform barriers: 19 stations installed so far this year, on track for 100 by year end). MTA C&D says it saved $3 billion over its first five years; plan costs 4% less in inflation-adjusted dollars than the 2020-2024 plan.
- Quotes: Chair/CEO Janno Lieber ("first capital plan based on a comprehensive review"); C&D President Jamie Torres-Springer ("better, faster, and cheaper").

wikis.title: I-45 construction begins in Houston (TxDOT)
wikis.summary: TxDOT news (Oct. 28, 2024): groundbreaking of the $13 billion I-45 North Houston Highway Improvement Project.
wikis.body:
- Published Oct. 28, 2024. TxDOT leadership kicked off construction of the $13 billion I-45 North Houston Highway Improvement Project (NHHIP) at Pitch 25 in East Downtown Houston. Goal: expand capacity, reduce congestion, improve safety along I-45 from I-69 to Beltway 8, and rebuild downtown Houston's freeway system (I-45, I-69, I-10, SH 288), rerouting I-45 parallel to I-69 and I-10.
- Segment 3B-1 (first phase): stormwater management with 12-foot box culverts to detention ponds; St. Emanuel Street as feeder road; completion by 2027; budget $121 million. Segment 3B-2: begins January 2025, complete by 2030; new mainlanes, frontage roads, bike/pedestrian on I-69 between SH 288 and I-45; estimated $695.5 million.
- Whole project expected to take 18 years. Needs: average daily traffic projected to rise as much as 40% between 2015 and 2040; single-direction HOV lane; I-45 is a hurricane evacuation route with flooding at the I-45/I-10 underpass.
- Speakers: Commission Chairman J. Bruce Bugg, Commissioner Steven Alvis ("save people 20 minutes twice a day"). Football-themed event with Vince Young.

wikis.title: TxDOT kicks off I-45 North Houston Highway Improvement Project construction (Texas Contractor)
wikis.summary: Texas Contractor (November 2024) report on the NHHIP groundbreaking in Houston with the $13 billion project's first segments.
wikis.body:
- Dated November 2024. TxDOT officials, Commission Chairman J. Bruce Bugg, Commissioner Steven Alvis, Houston Mayor John Whitmire, Executive Director Marc Williams and 200+ attendees launched construction of the $13 billion I-45 NHHIP at Pitch 25 in East Downtown Houston: Segment 3B-1 (East Downtown) and Segment 3B-2 (Midtown and Third Ward).
- Project: I-45 from I-69 to Beltway 8 North plus rebuilding downtown freeways (I-45, I-69, I-10, SH 288), rerouting I-45 parallel to I-69 and I-10.
- 3B-1: stormwater, 12-foot box culverts, complete by 2027, $121 million. 3B-2: from January 2025 to 2030, $695.5 million. Entire project about 18 years.
- Quotes: Marc Williams "a monumental day for the Houston region"; Whitmire on mobility for "our port, our med center, our retail, our sports venues".

wikis.title: Controlled explosives and rock removal begin on Parliament Hill (Canada.ca)
wikis.summary: Public Services and Procurement Canada media advisory (July 29, 2020) on blasting for phase 2 of the Parliamentary Welcome Centre.
wikis.body:
- Media advisory dated Ottawa, July 29, 2020. Controlled explosives use and rock removal begin in the construction perimeter in front of the Centre Block as excavation continues for phase 2 of the Parliamentary Welcome Centre (the release says both "today" and "tomorrow"). Activity on weekdays during daylight hours.
- Visitors may feel vibrations and will hear horn signals: 3 short horn signals, 1 minute of silence, 1 short horn signal closely followed by the controlled explosion, then 1 long horn signal.
- Once completed the Welcome Centre will offer a curated visitor experience and expanded parliamentary business support.

wikis.title: Blasting starts at Ottawa's Centre Block for Parliamentary Welcome Centre phase two
wikis.summary: Daily Commercial News report that controlled explosives and rock removal begin July 30 in front of Centre Block on Parliament Hill.
wikis.body:
- Public Services and Procurement Canada announced controlled explosives will be employed and rock removal activities will begin July 30 (2020) in the construction perimeter in front of the Centre Block, Parliament Hill, Ottawa.
- The work is part of excavation for phase two of the Parliamentary Welcome Centre.
- Activities take place on weekdays during daylight hours.
- Visitors to Parliament Hill and surrounding areas may feel vibrations and will hear horn signals in order: three short horn signals; one minute of silence; one short horn signal closely followed by the controlled explosion; one long horn signal.
- Once completed, the Parliamentary Welcome Centre will supplement the current tour capability and provide parliamentarians with expanded parliamentary business support, per the release.

wikis.title: Marina Bay Sands $8 billion expansion with Safdie-designed fourth tower
wikis.summary: CNN Style report on the groundbreaking of the $8 billion Marina Bay Sands expansion, a 55-floor fourth tower and 15,000-seat venue expected to open in 2031.
wikis.body:
- Marina Bay Sands (three 650-foot towers joined by a boat-like skybridge, opened 2011) is being expanded with a fourth tower and a new 15,000-seat entertainment venue; the expansion is described as $8 billion.
- The new 55-floor tower broke ground on Tuesday (article published Jul 16, 2025); tower and venue are "expected to open in 2031".
- Architect Moshe Safdie (87) designed it; the Urban Redevelopment Authority repeatedly said "This is our icon" and it could not be compromised. Safdie considered extending the skybridge to the new tower "for a few minutes" but chose a separate adjacent plot.
- The tower adds 570 suites plus luxury retail and meeting space. Its boat-like roof, "Skyloop", will host an observation deck, restaurants, public gardens, cabanas and infinity pools for hotel guests.
- Initial plans in 2019 put the arena on the far side of the tower; about a year earlier, with progress stalled by Covid-19-related delays, Safdie "flipped" the scheme so the arena sits between the new tower and the original three.
- Prime Minister Lawrence Wong joined Safdie at the ceremony (symbolic shoveling of sand) and said the structure "will refresh our skyline".
- Las Vegas Sands says the property drew 38 million visitors and S$2.19 billion ($1.7 billion) in business spending last year.
- Reception online was mixed: Reddit users called it "out of place", sticking out "like a sore thumb"; others said it will "blend in naturally".

wikis.title: Marina Bay Sands expansion: 55-storey tower and 15,000-seat arena, opening Q1 2031
wikis.summary: Mothership.SG report on the July 15, 2025 groundbreaking of Las Vegas Sands' US$8 billion (S$10.27 billion) Marina Bay expansion.
wikis.body:
- Las Vegas Sands held a groundbreaking on Jul. 15 (2025) evening for a US$8 billion (S$10.27 billion) development at Marina Bay Sands.
- Expansion works expected to be completed by 2030; the development is set to open by March 2031, reported The Straits Times (headline: Q1 2031).
- Officiated by PM and Finance Minister Lawrence Wong and Minister Grace Fu; over 220 guests, including Miriam Adelson, chairman/CEO Robert Goldstein and president/COO Patrick Dumont. Wong called it a "new chapter for Marina Bay"; said the government is "not done yet".
- Hotel tower: 55 storeys, 570 suites, rotated 45 degrees, twin wings curving outwards, "biophilic designs", about 200,000 sq ft of premium meeting space, luxury retail, gaming, spa and wellness.
- Skyloop rooftop (76,000 sq ft): lower level with observatory, destination restaurants and gardens; upper level with private cabanas and infinity-edge pools; a cantilevered wellness terrace.
- New podium: 15,000-seat arena "specially designed to host the highest calibre of regional and international touring acts", led by Populous; direct access to Bayfront MRT and linkways to Gardens by the Bay.
- Mentioned alongside the upcoming NS Square.

wikis.title: Eglinton Crosstown LRT (Line 5) opens in Toronto, Feb 8, 2026
wikis.summary: CBC News report on the Eglinton Crosstown LRT opening to riders on Feb. 8, 2026, 15 years after construction began.
wikis.body:
- Line 5 opened Sunday Feb. 8, 2026, 15 years after construction first started; the article calls it controversial. Crowds packed Kennedy and Mount Dennis stations with "Line 5, Line 5, Line 5" chants.
- Phased rollout with limited hours for an "undisclosed amount of time": 5:30 a.m. to 11 p.m. Monday to Saturday, 7:30 a.m. to 11 p.m. Sundays; trains eventually run until 1:30 a.m. at full service. Free of charge on its first official day.
- The inaugural train took 55 minutes from Kennedy to Mount Dennis (19 km), similar to the roughly 10 km Line 6 at launch.
- First-day bumps: a mechanical issue about 30 minutes in (westbound delays at O'Connor), a service stoppage between Pharmacy and Birchmount for an investigation, and westbound delays at Golden Mile; each resumed within minutes. Shuttle buses were sent once.
- The TTC did not have the fanfare or merchandise seen at last year's Finch West LRT opening.
- First operator Gavin Elliott (27 years with the TTC) said the ride was "very comfortable". Riders were reported watching speeds and red lights on the surface section; one 12-year-old estimated it reaches 70 km/h. Trains are Bombardier Flexity Outlooks.
- Rider Marcelo De Oliveira Medina said it cuts his weekly commute from an hour-and-a-half to 30 minutes.
- Related headlines: Metrolinx's ad campaign defending construction cost $2.25M; Monday Feb. 9 was the first weekday rush-hour test.

wikis.title: Ontario marks opening of the Eglinton Crosstown LRT (Line 5)
wikis.summary: ReNew Canada report of the Government of Ontario marking the Eglinton Crosstown LRT opening, which began TTC operation on February 8, 2026.
wikis.body:
- The LRT began operation under the TTC on February 8, 2026; Ontario marked the official opening.
- Line 5 Eglinton: 25 stations and stops along a 19-kilometre line between Kennedy Station and Mount Dennis (Weston Road), with more than 10 kilometres underground. Links to 68 routes, three TTC subway stations and two GO lines.
- Eglinton Crosstown West Extension is under construction: nine kilometres west from Mount Dennis to Renforth Drive.
- After a successful Revenue Service Demonstration, the line achieved substantial completion on December 5, 2025 and full operational control transferred to the TTC.
- Quotes: Premier Ford ("major milestone for commuters in the GTA"); Metrolinx CEO Michael Lindsay; Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow ("The opening will be phased and service levels will increase over time, alongside greater signal priority"); Infrastructure Ontario CEO Angela Clayton ("one of the most complex projects in the city's transit history").

wikis.title: Drone strike on Chernobyl's New Safe Confinement, IAEA statement
wikis.summary: UN News report that a Russian drone strike damaged the protective shield over Chernobyl reactor unit 4 on 14 February 2025, with radiation levels reported normal.
wikis.body:
- Ukrainian authorities said on Friday (article dated 14 February 2025) that a Russian drone with a high explosive warhead struck the former Chernobyl nuclear power plant overnight, damaging the New Safe Confinement (NSC) built after the 1986 disaster. Russia has denied any responsibility.
- IAEA Director General Rafael Mariano Grossi: the on-site team heard the explosion at 1:50am local time, followed by smoke and fire; fire crews arrived within minutes and the blaze was intermittently visible for several hours.
- Radiation levels inside and outside the NSC "remain normal and stable"; no reports of casualties or radiation leak.
- IAEA team saw a breach of the outer layer of the NSC; Ukraine's regulator confirmed outer cladding damage, with investigations ongoing on the inner cladding.
- Grossi: "There is no room for complacency, and the IAEA remains on high alert"; he called for "maximum military restraint around Ukraine's nuclear sites". The strike followed increased military activity near Zaporizhzhya NPP.
- Background: Russian forces briefly occupied Chernobyl after invading Ukraine and it was recaptured in March 2022.

wikis.title: Drone strike damages Chernobyl's New Safe Confinement (WNN)
wikis.summary: World Nuclear News report on the 14 February 2025 drone strike on Chernobyl's New Safe Confinement, with background on the structure.
wikis.body:
- Friday, 14 February 2025: the IAEA (via X) said its team heard an explosion around 01:50 local time from the New Safe Confinement (NSC); photos showed flames near the top. Staff were told a drone caused the damage. "radiation levels inside and outside remain normal and stable"; no casualties; "no indication of a breach in the NSC's inner containment" at that time.
- Plant operators (ChNPP): the arch was struck at a height of 87 metres, above premises housing equipment for remote operation of the Confinement; both external and internal cladding were damaged, along with Main Cranes System equipment; local fire on the cladding was put out. Due to the cladding breach, "limits of safe operation" in the NSC regulations were violated; no release of radioactive substances, "the situation is under control".
- NSC facts: largest moveable land-based structure ever built; span 257 m, length 162 m, height 108 m, weight 36,000 tonnes; designed for about 100 years; completed in 2019 after being built in two halves and moved on rails; covers the original 1986 shelter, which still holds the molten core and an estimated 200 tonnes of highly radioactive material. Two layers of cladding about 12 metres apart; designed for -43C to +45C, a class-three tornado and a magnitude 6 earthquake.
- Context: Chernobyl is about 130 km north of Kyiv and 20 km south of Belarus; 30-km exclusion zone. Russian forces held the plant from February 2022 until 31 March 2022.
- Ukraine blamed Russia; Russia denied responsibility and blamed Ukraine. The IAEA has not attributed blame, Grossi saying proof is needed. Grossi: "there is no room for complacency, and the IAEA remains on high alert".

wikis.title: EBRD: remediation to begin at Mailuu-Suu uranium legacy site, Kyrgyz Republic
wikis.summary: EBRD news release (16 May 2023) on a EUR 23 million ERA grant to remediate the Mailuu-Suu uranium tailings over seven years.
wikis.body:
- 16 May 2023: grant agreement signed by Boobek Ajikeev (Kyrgyz Minister of Emergency Situations) and Balthasar Lindauer (EBRD Director, Nuclear Safety Department).
- EUR 23 million grant from the Environmental Remediation Account for Central Asia (ERA), managed by the EBRD; the largest since the ERA was established. Work at Mailuu-Suu to begin in 2023 and take seven years.
- Will stabilise and cover more than 2 million cubic metres of radioactive tailings along the Mailuu-Suu River; about 350 thousand cubic metres must be relocated to a safe disposal site. Soil covers 2 metres thick. Prevents dispersal into the river system of the Fergana Valley (more than 15 million people); relief for more than 100,000 people in and around Mailuu-Suu. Also funds rehabilitation of contaminated land and water.
- Third such site in the Kyrgyz Republic after Shekaftar and Min-Kush (completed spring 2022); to serve as a model for Central Asia.
- ERA established in 2015 on the EU's initiative; EU is biggest donor, with Belgium, Lithuania, Norway, Spain, Switzerland and the USA.

wikis.title: Remediation of Kyrgyz uranium legacy site at Mailuu-Suu to start (WNN)
wikis.summary: World Nuclear News, 19 May 2023: EUR 23 million (USD 25 million) ERA grant starts seven years of remediation at Mailuu-Suu.
wikis.body:
- Grant of EUR23 million (USD25 million) from the ERA, managed by the EBRD; agreement signed 16 May (2023); allows seven years of remediation; the largest since ERA's founding.
- Background: uranium was mined and milled at Mailuu-Suu between 1946 and 1967 under the Soviet nuclear programme; some 10,000 tonnes of uranium oxide produced; five mine fields, three shafts. Kara Balta Mining Combine set up in the 1950s near Bishkek.
- Radioactive material sits in 23 tailings ponds (about 2 million cubic metres) and 13 mining debris heaps (about 0.9 million cubic metres) along the Mailuu-Suu River, which feeds the Syr Darya. Some tailings have been damaged by landslides, mudslides and floods.
- Plan: 2-metre-thick soil covers; about 350,000 cubic metres relocated to safe disposal; contaminated land and water rehabilitated.
- Third such Kyrgyz site after Shekaftar and Min-Kush (spring 2022). Most Central Asian mines closed by 1995 with little remediation.
- ERA set up by EBRD in 2015 at European Commission request, operational 2016; funded by EC, Belgium, Lithuania, Norway, Spain, Switzerland, USA. Kyrgyz government ratified the framework agreement in August 2017 (signed January 2017).

wikis.title: UK approves 'mega' Chinese embassy at Royal Mint site in London
wikis.summary: Gulf News/AFP, 20 Jan 2026: UK government grants planning permission for China's embassy on the former Royal Mint site.
wikis.body:
- On Tuesday (article dated January 20, 2026) the UK government approved China's "mega embassy" in London, eight years after the process began. Housing minister Steve Reed granted planning permission after multiple delays over "national security concerns"; decision "now final unless it is successfully challenged in court".
- The 20,000-square-metre (235,000 sq ft) site would be the largest embassy complex in the UK by area and one of the largest in the heart of a Western capital.
- Government spokesperson: intelligence agencies involved throughout; China agreed to consolidate its seven current London sites into one.
- Activists and China-hawks have protested; Luke de Pulford (Inter-Parliamentary Alliance on China) previously predicted an "embarrassing and potentially catastrophic" legal challenge from residents.
- Starmer is expected to visit China later this month (unconfirmed), which would be the first UK prime-minister visit since 2018.

wikis.title: UK approves Chinese embassy in London despite security fears (Al Jazeera)
wikis.summary: Al Jazeera, 20 Jan 2026: the UK approved China's embassy at Royal Mint Court, eight years after Beijing bought the site.
wikis.body:
- Housing Minister Steve Reed granted planning permission on Tuesday (20 Jan 2026) for what is described as the largest embassy in Europe, near the Tower of London on the two-century-old Royal Mint Court, ahead of Starmer's expected China visit.
- China bought the site in 2018; the local council rejected the plans in 2022 over safety and security concerns; plans stalled three years over opposition from residents, lawmakers and Hong Kong pro-democracy campaigners, who fear harassment or detention of opponents. Politicians in Britain and the US warned of spying use.
- Xi Jinping asked Starmer to intervene last year; the government repeatedly postponed after alleged Chinese spying cases. In November MI5 warned lawmakers of "targeted and widespread" Chinese recruitment efforts; Beijing called this "pure fabrication and malicious slander".
- Security Minister Dan Jarvis: "I am assured that the UK's national security is protected". Residents plan to challenge the approval in court.

wikis.title: 400 Lake Shore tower nears 66th floor pour, January 2026
wikis.summary: Chicago YIMBY progress update (Jan 5, 2026) on the 72-story 400 Lake Shore North Tower on the former Chicago Spire site.
wikis.body:
- The 66th floor is ready to pour at the 72-story 400 Lake Shore North Tower in Streeterville; "just a handful of stories from topping out". Contractors: LR Contracting and BOWA construction. Exterior glass reaches up through the 47th floor.
- North Tower: 858 feet, 635 dwelling units (127 affordable), about 300 underground parking spaces.
- South Tower: about 765 feet, 465 residences, not expected to start until the first is complete; parking shared.
- DuSable Park buildout, approved by the Chicago Plan Commission in October, expected to start in the spring. Openings for tower and park slated for 2027.
- Sixth and final crane jump scheduled for the coming weekend (five sections, Liebherr crane); November jump was delayed by heavy winds.
- Renderings by SOM. Photos taken January 2, 2026.

wikis.title: 400 Lake Shore (Wikipedia): two-tower residential complex on the former Chicago Spire site
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the 400 Lake Shore development in Streeterville, Chicago, its history since the failed Chicago Spire, and construction status.
wikis.body:
- Skyscraper complex under construction in Streeterville, Chicago, on the site of the previously proposed Chicago Spire; two connected residential towers plus buildout of DuSable Park. Developer Related Midwest; lead designer David Childs of Skidmore, Owings and Merrill.
- Heights: north tower 875 ft (267 m), 72 floors, 635 apartments (one-fifth affordable); south tower 765 ft (233 m), 64 floors, 500 units (per description). North tower completion scheduled for 2027; south tower TBA.
- History: Chicago Spire (Garrett Kelleher/Shelbourne) failed in the Great Recession; courts handed the site to a receiver in 2010; NAMA put it up for sale in 2013; Related gained full control in 2014.
- Planning: Gensler "Gateway Tower" renderings 2016; May 2018 plan of 1,100-ft and 850-ft towers with 300 condos, 175 hotel rooms, 500 rental apartments; Alderman Brendan Reilly's office rejected it in October 2018; revised March 2020 (heights cut, hotel scrapped, all residential); Chicago City Council approved in June 2020, with Related pledging $10 million to finish DuSable Park matched by $5 million from the city.
- Construction: crane permit January 2024; groundbreaking June 17, 2024; facade panel installation (362,000 sq ft) began end of April 2025 with the frame at the 22nd floor; by August 2025 a floor slab about every three days. Infobox status: North Tower topped-out, South Tower proposed (June 2026 photo).

wikis.title: Goldin Finance 117 (Wikipedia): Tianjin supertall, topped out 2015 and being revived
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the 597 m Goldin Finance 117 tower in Tianjin, its halted construction and 2025-2026 revival.
wikis.body:
- Supertall skyscraper in Xiqing District, Tianjin, China, nicknamed "Walking Stick"; topped out 8 September 2015 at 597 m (1,957 ft), 128 storeys (117 for housing, hotel, commercial, hence the name), floor area 370,000 m2, 89 lifts. Designed by P&T Group; owner Goldin Financial Holdings.
- Construction began 2009 (text also says 2008) with 2014 completion planned; suspended January 2010 after the Great Recession, resumed 2011; suspended again December 2015 after the owner's financial difficulties following the June 2015 Chinese stock market crash. Certified by Guinness World Records as the World's Tallest Unoccupied Building.
- On April 25, 2025 a new construction permit was announced; completion set for 2027.
- 2026: January 4, Tianjin leaders met CITIC, China State Construction Engineering and China Cinda on revitalizing the "117 Project"; 29 January it was included in Tianjin's 15th Five-Year Plan outline; 4 February another site inspection. CNOOC, CITIC Group (28 March), sixteen companies (30 March, incl. Lenovo, DiDi) and six central state-owned enterprises (24 April) signed agreements to buy floors or office space.
- Failed projects like this reportedly contributed to a Chinese ban on buildings over 500 metres.
- 2015 and 2016 urban explorers climbed it; a 2016 video by Ivan Beerkus and Angela Nikolau got over 922,000 views as of April 2023.

wikis.title: Goldin Finance 117 nears completion (SCMP)
wikis.summary: SCMP, 5 Apr 2026: Tianjin's once-abandoned Goldin Finance 117 is in the homestretch after a year of resumed work.
wikis.body:
- Once dubbed the world's tallest abandoned skyscraper, Goldin Finance 117 in Tianjin appears in the homestretch after nearly a decade of dormancy and a year of resumed work, despite a struggling property market.
- Late last month (March 2026), workers began installing a diamond-shaped crown on top, per state media; designed to be 596 metres (1,955 feet) tall upon completion.
- Eighteen years after construction began; the saga underscores the collapse of China's property market and retreat from supertall pursuits. Article notes a state-backed revival to rebuild confidence (paywalled teaser only).

wikis.title: Gran Torre Santiago (Pelli Clarke & Partners)
wikis.summary: Architect's project page for Gran Torre Santiago, the 300 m tower in Santiago, Chile, completed 2014.
wikis.body:
- Tallest tower in South America at 300 meters (980 ft); anchors the Costanera Center complex in Providencia, Santiago; public observatory on upper floors with 360-degree views.
- Design: obelisk form of faceted glass walls that fold at the centerline and taper, ending in a latticed crown that glows softly at night. Cesar Pelli quote: "No human-built form can compete with the power of these mountains."
- LEED Gold; recycled steel, natural cooling with water from the San Carlos Canal, high-performance glass coatings; structural system for earthquake protection.
- Facts: client Cencosud, S.A.; size 1,200,000 sq ft / 110,000 sq m; completion 2014. Architect of record Alemparte Barreda Wedeles Besancon; structural Rene Lagos Engineers / Thornton Tomasetti. Awards: 2013 International Property Awards (Highly Commended for Chile High Rise; 5 Star for Mixed-Use).

wikis.title: Gran Torre Costanera (Wikipedia): South America's tallest building
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the 300 m Gran Torre Costanera in Santiago, Chile, and its construction timeline.
wikis.body:
- 62-story (infobox; text says 64 plus 6 basement floors) skyscraper in Santiago, Chile; tallest in South America, second tallest in Latin America, 300 m (984 ft) architectural height; part of the Costanera Center complex (largest shopping mall in Latin America, two hotels, two other towers). Cost US$1 billion; developer Cencosud; architects Alemparte Barreda & Asociados, Cesar Pelli (Pelli Clarke Pelli) and Watt International; builder Salfa Corp.
- Construction began 18 June 2006, expected finish 2010, put on hold January 2009 (Great Recession), resumed 17 December 2009. Overtook Titanium La Portada in November 2010 (205 m); passed Caracas's Twin Towers in 2011 (226 m). Structural work done July 2011; topped out 14 February 2012 at 300 m; completed 2013.
- Planners estimated some 240,000 people per day to and from the site.
- "Sky Costanera" observation deck opened 11 August 2015 on floors 61 and 62.

wikis.title: 432 Park Avenue (Skyscraper Museum Supertall!)
wikis.summary: Skyscraper Museum profile of 432 Park Avenue, New York, tallest residential building in the Western Hemisphere.
wikis.body:
- At 57th Street on "Billionaire's Row"; described as currently the tallest residential building in the Western Hemisphere. Designed by Rafael Vinoly; architect of record SLCE; structural WSP Cantor Seinuk; developers CIM Group and Macklowe Properties.
- White grid of exposed concrete split into six sections by open mechanical floors; 93 sq ft floor plate (as printed), 12.5 ft ceilings, slenderness ratio 1:15; 10 ft by 10 ft windows; 1 to 4 units per floor; amenities in the lower section.
- Facts: proposed 2011, construction started 2011, completed 2015; height 425.7 m / 1397 ft; 85 floors; GFA 65,497 m2.

wikis.title: 432 Park Avenue (Wikipedia, part 1): site, architecture and structure
wikis.summary: Wikipedia on 432 Park Avenue, Rafael Vinoly's residential tower on Billionaires' Row in Manhattan: history, form, facade and structure.
wikis.body:
- 1,396-foot (425.5 m) residential skyscraper at 57th Street and Park Avenue, Midtown Manhattan; developed by CIM Group and Harry B. Macklowe, designed by Rafael Vinoly; SLCE Architects architect of record; interiors by Deborah Berke and Bentel & Bentel; structural WSP Cantor Seinuk; contractor Lendlease. 125 condominiums; median unit sells from 10.5 to 90 million dollars.
- At completion in 2015 it was the third-tallest building in the US and tallest residential building in the world; as of 2025 sixth-tallest in the US, fifth-tallest in NYC, third-tallest residential building in the world. 84 numbered stories plus mezzanine (top story labelled 96).
- Site: former Drake Hotel, sold to Macklowe in 2006; five years of delays from lack of financing and site assembly; plans approved 2011, excavation next year, sales launched 2013, topped out October 2014 (infobox October 10, 2014), completed December 23, 2015. Residents later complained of mechanical and structural problems, leading to multiple lawsuits in the 2020s.
- Form: 12-story blocks separated by open double-story mechanical windbreaks; facade a white Portland cement concrete lattice of 10-foot-square apertures, inspired per Vinoly by a 1905 trash can by Josef Hoffmann; height-to-width ratio 15:1; after completion the facade experienced excess wind forces that cracked concrete. Nightly illumination of the windbreaks began November 14, 2016.
- Structure: 30-by-30-foot reinforced concrete core with 30-inch walls; perimeter columns taper from 5 ft 4 in to 20 in.
- Reviews described as mixed (slenderness, symbolism of ultra-wealthy housing).

wikis.title: Room With a View: 432 Park Avenue (The B1M)
wikis.summary: The B1M video page (14 September 2016) on how 432 Park Avenue was built and its engineering.
wikis.body:
- Site: tight lot between East 56th and 57th Streets on the former Drake Hotel (built 1926), bought by Harry Macklowe in 2006 and demolished in 2007; Macklowe paid USD $440M for the title.
- Height 426 m, 104 apartments over 96 levels; width-to-height 1:15; design by Rafael Vinoly (said to be inspired by a Josef Hoffman wastepaper bin), square geometry with six square windows per side of each floor plate.
- Structure: solid concrete core at centre, reinforced-concrete grid at perimeter; two floors in every 12 left open for wind, holding mechanical services; two large tuned mass dampers; poured in-situ using a climber rig that rose up the lift shafts.
- Residences from a 33 m2 studio to penthouses on floors 91 to 96 designed by Deborah Berke; amenities include golf training, private dining and cinema rooms; the foremost apartment "almost USD $95M".
- Controversy: called an eyesore casting shadows over Central Park; seen as catering to the super-rich and the wealth divide. Video views listed: 1,128,334.

wikis.title: Gelephu Mindfulness City (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Bhutan's planned Gelephu Mindfulness City special administrative region.
wikis.body:
- Planned economic hub and special administrative region (GeSAR) in Gelephu, Sarpang District, Bhutan, on the border with India; 2,500 km2 ("three times the size of Singapore"), announced 17 December 2023 by King Jigme Khesar Namgyel Wangchuck at the 116th National Day; own Basic Law; leader listed Mun Leong Liew.
- Aim: business-friendly hub integrating sustainability, Bhutanese culture and spirituality; low-rise eco buildings, organic food, renewable electricity, cycling, AI innovation; diversify beyond hydropower and tourism.
- Plan by Bjarke Ingels Group, Arup, Cistri and MQDC: eleven mandala-inspired neighbourhoods linked by green corridors and inhabitable bridges. Eight core industries; target 100,000 jobs by 2030.
- Infrastructure: international airport, first phase about 1.3 million passengers annually, expansion to 5.5 million; Bhutan's first domestic bond offering in 2025 to fund it; high-speed rail links to India mentioned.
- January 2025: announced cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin and Ether in strategic reserves. Volunteer programme hand-clearing the airport site brought 7,050 people; October 2025 third wave over 5,600 people, king established the pelsung youth programme. As of September 2025 "Innovate for GMC" had over 1,700 applicants.

wikis.title: Gelephu Mindfulness City official website
wikis.summary: The official gmc.bt homepage describing Gelephu Mindfulness City, Bhutan's autonomous Special Administrative Region.
wikis.body:
- GMC is His Majesty The King's vision of "an oasis of mindfulness and prosperity", under "One Country, Two Systems"; established by Royal Charter in February 2024 as a highly autonomous SAR with full executive and legislative powers and an independent judiciary.
- Located in Bhutan's southern plains bordering Assam, India; spanning over 4,046 km2, 10% of Bhutan (the site states this figure).
- Eight core priority industries: Spiritual Health and Wellness, Education and Knowledge, Agri-Tech and Forestry, Green Energy and Technologies, Finance and Digital Assets, Aviation and Logistics, Tourism (as listed on the page).
- Quote from the King's National Day Address, 17th December 2023: "This project is not just an infrastructure development—it is a People's Project".
- News items listed: GMCA awards first purpose-built workers' dormitory under 25-year public-private partnership (September 18, 2026); GMC-Japan Partnership to Transform Gelephu Town (September 12, 2026); Golden Mandir for GMC (September 8, 2026). Project 108: 108 Jangchub Chortens.

wikis.title: History of the High Altitude Research Station Jungfraujoch
wikis.summary: Foundation page on the history of the Jungfraujoch research station, from 19th-century alpine exploration through the Jungfrau Railways to the 1930s station.
wikis.body:
- Station at 3500 m above sea level, year-round access via the Jungfrau Railways; more than half of projects concern environmental and climatic questions.
- Early exploration: de Saussure's 1787 Mont Blanc ascent; Louis Agassiz's 1838-1841 expeditions with the "Hotel des Neuchatelois".
- Railway: plans 1860-1890 (Koechlin, Trautweiler, Locher); decisive idea 1893 by Adolf Guyer-Zeller, electric, from Kleine Scheidegg; physiologist Hugo Kronecker's tests supported altitude safety; construction started 1896; Guyer-Zeller died six months after the first section opened; a 30-ton dynamite explosion in 1908; completed 1912, nine years late. Over 1,000,000 visitors a year; UNESCO World Heritage status 2001. The concession required support for high-altitude research.
- Science: Alfred de Quervain drove the founding of the Jungfraujoch Commission in 1922; meteorological pavilion 1926; astronomy from 1922-1927 (E. Schar); Chalonge's ozone measurements 1928; cosmic ray expeditions by Kolhorster and von Salis in 1925 and 1926.
- W.R. Hess led the founding of the International Foundation in 1930; station inaugurated a year later; the Sphinx observatory completed 1937; first astronomical cupola 1950; two Gornergrat observatories in the late 1960s.

wikis.title: Sphinx Observatory (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the Sphinx Observatory above the Jungfraujoch, Switzerland, at 3,571 m.
wikis.body:
- Astronomical observatory above the Jungfraujoch, Valais, Switzerland; 3,571 m (11,716 ft), established 1937; one of the highest observatories in the world; the public viewing deck is the second highest observation deck in Switzerland. An elevator tunnelled through the mountain rises from the Jungfraujoch railway station (highest in Europe).
- Facilities: two large laboratories, weather station, workshop, two terraces, astronomical and meteorological cupolas; astronomical dome has a 76 cm telescope with Cassegrain and Coude focus. Views of the Jungfrau, Monch and Eiger.
- Science: solar spectrometer work for the University of Liege institute; LIDAR experiment by EPFL; in 1949 nuclear emulsion plates exposed to cosmic rays provided first precise evidence for the charged K-meson.
- In media: The Grand Budapest Hotel, The Hero: Love Story of a Spy, Krrish 3, The Amazing Race season 22, the video game Steep, The Pentaverate, Crash Landing on You (episode 16), and as inspiration for the "Voussoir Facility" in Abiotic Factor.

wikis.title: Ciudad Real International Airport (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Spain's Ciudad Real International Airport (CQM), opened 2009 at a cost of EUR 1.1 billion and closed in 2012.
wikis.body:
- Private international airport and long-storage facility south of Ciudad Real (formerly Central Airport CR, Don Quijote Airport, South Madrid Airport); cost EUR 1.1 billion; opened in 2009 as Spain's first private international airport. Operations ran until April 2012 when the management company went bankrupt; closed seven years, reopened September 2019 without scheduled passenger traffic.
- Facilities: single runway 4,100 m by 60 m (can take the A380); terminal designed for two million passengers a year (up to ten million with modules); cargo up to 47,000 tonnes a year; planned industrial zone over 8 km2; a 300 m footbridge to the Madrid-Seville high-speed line was built but the station never started.
- Flights: Air Berlin to Palma (ended 30 May 2010), Air Nostrum; Ryanair from London Stansted from June 2010 (three weekly, ended 11 November 2010 after about 22,000 passengers, 22 jobs lost); Vueling until 29 October 2011. By 13 April 2012 all operations shut; debt above EUR 300 million (per this page).
- Reasons for failure: siting in a Bird Special Protection Area and a volcanic field, delaying opening four years (2008 instead of 2004); Madrid Barajas's 2006 expansion to 70 million passengers a year; no high-speed station; Spain's financial crisis; main shareholder Caja Castilla-La Mancha was the first Spanish bank bailed out.

wikis.title: Don Quixote airport: cost EUR 1bn, now could sell to China for EUR 10,000 (Guardian)
wikis.summary: Guardian, 17 July 2015: a Chinese-led consortium is the only bidder for Ciudad Real airport at EUR 10,000.
wikis.body:
- Ciudad Real airport, cost EUR 1bn (GBP 694m) to build, was on sale at a knockdown EUR 40m, but a Chinese-led consortium (Tzaneen International, set up in March with EUR 4,000 capital) was the only bidder at public auction with an initial EUR 10,000 outlay for the land and most buildings incl. runway and control tower. Rival bidders had 20 days to come forward because the offer was far under 70% of the asking price.
- Auction asking price cut from EUR 100m (last year) to EUR 80m to EUR 40m. Tzaneen says it may invest up to EUR 100m and wants to buy the unfinished terminal and car parks; plans a cargo hub "with special attention to the Chinese market".
- Airport: runway able to land an A380, terminal for 10m travellers a year; opened to international flights in 2010 and shut two years later. Administrators said backers never did an investment analysis. Went into administration with debts of EUR 529m; biggest creditors are savings banks owed EUR 233m; locals claim a further EUR 106m for compulsory purchase; Castilla-La Mancha savings bank held 68% and went bankrupt.
