- History: originally Edo; political prominence from 1603 as seat of the Tokugawa shogunate; by mid-18th century over one million people. After the Meiji Restoration (1868) the capital moved to Edo, renamed Tokyo ("Eastern Capital"). Damaged by the 1923 Great Kanto earthquake and WWII bombing; rapid reconstruction from the late 1940s fueled the "Japanese economic miracle".

wikis.title: Millau Viaduct (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the Millau Viaduct, the cable-stayed motorway bridge across the Tarn gorge in France.
wikis.body:
- Multiple-span cable-stayed viaduct carrying 4 lanes of the A75 autoroute over the Tarn valley at Millau-Creissels, Aveyron. Designers: Norman Foster (architect) and Michel Virlogeux (structural engineer). Concrete and steel.
- Total length 2,460 m; width 32.05 m; max pylon height 343 m above ground; main span 342 m (spans 204 m, 6 x 342 m, 204 m); deck about 270 m above the valley below. Design life 120 years.
- Cost EUR 394 million; construction began 16 October 2001 (infobox); inaugurated 14 December 2004; opened to traffic 16 December 2004; toll from EUR 8.30. Builder and maintainer: Compagnie Eiffage du Viaduc de Millau.

wikis.title: Eiffage Genie Civil: Millau Viaduct
wikis.summary: Eiffage's page on building the Millau Viaduct in three years (2001-2004).
wikis.body:
- Eiffage says it took exactly three years to build the world's highest viaduct, enabled by the steel deck it proposed and installed. Delivered December 2004.
- Multi-span cable-stayed bridge designed by Sir Norman Foster with engineer Michel Virlogeux; 343 m high, 2,460 m long, 7 concrete piers and a steel deck; 85,000 m3 of concrete and 36,000 tonnes of steel; 14 years of preparation and 3 years of construction (2001-2004); 600 master craftsmen at peak.
- Inaugurated 14 December 2004 by President Jacques Chirac. IABSE Outstanding Structure Award 2006, praising an "elegant, slender bridge ...constructed using an innovative launching procedure".
- Key stages: 14 December 2001 first stone (Transport Minister Jean-Claude Gayssot); 25 March 2003 first deck stretch launched; 24 November 2003 piers completed; 28 May 2004 northern and southern deck halves met 268 m above the Tarn; 14 December 2004 inauguration.

wikis.title: Sands Macao (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the Sands Macao hotel and casino resort in Macau.
wikis.body:
- Hotel and casino resort in Se, Macau, owned and operated by Las Vegas Sands; designed by Steelman Partners (infobox lists Aedas as architect). 229,000 sq ft casino, 289-suite hotel; theme "Desert".
- Opened 18 May 2004 at a cost of $240 million [clarification needed]; mortgage bonds paid off May 2005. 2006 expansion took the casino from 165,000 to 229,000 sq ft; new hotel tower opened late 2007, bringing rooms to 289.
- At opening Sheldon Adelson said the company would soon be a mainly Chinese enterprise and Las Vegas should be called "America's Macau". On 12 February 2007 a Las Vegas Sands executive predicted Macau gaming revenue had topped the Las Vegas Strip and would more than double by 2010.

wikis.title: Sands Macao 20 years: stories from long-serving team members
wikis.summary: Sands China partner feature (17 May 2024) on Sands Macao's 20th anniversary and Macao's transformation.
wikis.body:
- Sands Macao opened 20 years earlier as Macao's first Las Vegas-style integrated resort, after the government ended the local gaming monopoly; Sheldon Adelson envisioned Macao as the "Las Vegas of Asia".
- The article says Sands Macao was a US$265 million investment that broke even in just nine months; Adelson then built Cotai resorts, The Venetian Macao (3,000 rooms and suites), The Plaza Macao, Sands Cotai Central, and more.
- Three staff recall: Amy Lee (payroll manager from 2003, now VP of human resources) recalls no proper offices before opening and the first 4,000-person payroll; also Armindo Goncalves and Raymond Ho.
- Claims tourism, real estate values and GDP per capita rose while unemployment fell. A partner feature, not independent reporting.

wikis.title: Railway Gazette: Hamburg-Berlin line reopens after 10-month closure
wikis.summary: Railway Gazette (19 June 2026) on DB's reopening of the Hamburg-Berlin main line and the criticism of the corridor blockade model.
wikis.body:
- DB InfraGO reopened the 278 km Hamburg-Berlin corridor, the largest Generalsanierung project yet, after a closure from 1 August 2025 lasting 10 months and two weeks versus an initial six-month plan (revised to nine months). CEO Philipp Nagl cited "extended construction work due to the harsh winter".
- Works: 165 km track and 249 turnouts replaced, 47 km overhead line renewed, seven crossovers, six new and 19 modernised signal boxes (ETCS-ready), FRMCS preparation, 28 stations refurbished.
- Reopening: northern section (Hamburg-Hagenow Land-Schwerin) 15 May; southern section 14 June. Speed restrictions and timetable adjustments to 30 June.
- Criticism: Die Gueterbahnen said the closure meant "well over 300 days of complete closure on 1% of the German rail network" and the concept "failed its primary test"; alleged chaos on diversions via Uelzen, Hannover and Bremen. Dispute over replacement buses: DB Fernverkehr ran 170 buses covering 25 million km; DB refused to fund buses on Hamburg-Schwerin.
- Generalsanierung introduced June 2022; launch parameters aimed to limit closures to five months.

wikis.title: Generalsanierung Hochleistungsnetz (German Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: German Wikipedia on the Generalsanierung, a German government and DB InfraGO programme to renew main rail corridors through months-long full closures.
wikis.body:
- Programme (now also called Korridorsanierung): comprehensive renewal of Germany's busiest rail lines classed as high-performance corridors; between 2024 and 2035 over 4,000 route-km are to be renovated during multi-month full closures, replacing the earlier approach of many small projects under traffic.
- Background: in the first half of 2022 long-distance punctuality fell from 80.9% in January to under 60% in June to August; below 70% is DB's "red line". In 2021 41.6% of freight trains were late. From 3 June to 28 August 2022 DB Netz listed 20,712 construction measures.
- Announced 22 June 2022 by Transport Minister Volker Wissing with DB CEO Richard Lutz: works to start 2024 and lead to a high-performance network by 2030. The network of about 3,500 km (about 10%) was already at 125% utilisation; train numbers about 47,000 (2010), 51,000 (2022), over 59,000 expected for 2030.
- Pilot: Riedbahn (Mannheim-Frankfurt), begun September 2022 planning.

wikis.title: Jewel Changi Airport (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Jewel Changi Airport, the entertainment and retail complex at Singapore Changi Airport.
wikis.body:
- Entertainment and retail complex in Singapore; soft opening 17 April 2019 and official opening 18 October 2019 (about 50 million visitors in six months per Straits Times).
- Owners: Changi Airport Group and CapitaLand (Jewel Changi Airport Trustee). Size 3.5 ha; floor area 135,700 m2; 12 levels (5 above ground, 7 basement).
- Architect Moshe Safdie with RSP Architects Planners & Engineers; other designers PWP Landscape Architecture, ICN Design, Ove Arup, Benoy, Lighting Planners Associates; main contractors Obayashi Corporation and Woh Hup.

wikis.title: CBC: Toronto's The One condo project placed into receivership
wikis.summary: CBC News (20 Oct 2023) on the receivership of The One, an 85-storey Yonge-Bloor condo tower with $1.6 billion in unpaid debt.
wikis.body:
- The One, an 85-storey tower at Yonge and Bloor, was taken over by a court-appointed receiver after lenders' financiers defaulted on more than $1.2 billion in loans; about $1.6 billion in unpaid debts; costs have ballooned to more than $2 billion.
- Developer Sam Mizrahi bought the land for $300 million almost a decade earlier; plan for 85 storeys and 416 residential units. Broke ground 2017; retail planned for 2018, hotel and condos by 2022 at the latest.
- Lender filing cites delays, cost overruns and infighting between Mizrahi and investor Jenny Coco (50% stakes each). Main lender: a division of KEB Hana Bank (more than $315 million next payment); $130 million owed to Aviva; $182 million to China-East Resources Import & Export Corporation. Project delayed at least two years and needs hundreds of millions more.
- A planned 19,000-square-foot Apple Store flagship fell apart in 2021.

wikis.title: One Bloor West (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on One Bloor West (The One), the supertall skyscraper under construction in Toronto.
wikis.body:
- Supertall mixed-use (residential, retail, hotel) tower at 1 Bloor Street West, Toronto; 85 floors; height 1,012.4 ft; tallest in Canada from 2025 to 2026 per infobox, surpassing First Canadian Place; estimated completion 2028; status topped-out. Architects Foster and Partners with Core Architects; structural engineer RJC Engineers.
- Developer Mizrahi Developments, with Tridel since May 2025. Groundbreaking 23 August 2017; cost CAD 2 billion (estimated $1 billion in planning).
- Sam Mizrahi bought the land in October 2014 for CA$300 million; city approval 12 September 2016. Placed into receivership October 2023.
- First 18 storeys: retail, restaurants and a 160-room Andaz Toronto hotel (floors four to sixteen). Apple sued in March 2022 to end its lease, claiming $6.9 million in delay damages; press reports say Apple will not move in. Final design dropped the exoskeleton but keeps diagonal hangers.

wikis.title: Techo International Airport opens in Phnom Penh (press release)
wikis.summary: PR Newswire release (3 Oct 2025) on the 9 September inauguration of Cambodia's Techo International Airport.
wikis.body:
- Techo International Airport (IATA KTI, ICAO VDTI) was inaugurated 9 September in Phnom Penh, described as Cambodia's largest aviation infrastructure project; first commercial flight operated by Air Cambodia.
- Developed by Cambodia Airport Investment Co., Ltd. (CAIC), a joint venture of the State Secretariat of Civil Aviation and Overseas Cambodian Investment Corporation (OCIC). First-phase capacity 15 million passengers annually. Built with more than 200 Cambodian engineers and 17,000 workers.
- Terminal designed by Foster + Partners with roof canopies on structural "trees" inspired by the rumduol flower; nine-meter Buddha statue. Partners: Vinci Airports, Lagardere Travel Retail, Newrest, SIAEC. Within first month two new routes opened and Cathay Pacific temporarily hosted some of its fleet during Typhoon Ragasa.

wikis.title: AeroTime: Kansai Airport is sinking
wikis.summary: AeroTime (7 Feb 2025) on why Japan's Kansai International Airport is sinking faster than predicted.
wikis.body:
- Kansai (KIX) opened in 1994, the world's only truly floating airport per the article, costing more than $20bn. In 2024 it had 169,774 aircraft movements and 25.9 million passengers (29.4 million pre-pandemic). Operator: Kansai Airports (Orix-Vinci).
- Built on alluvial clay seabed in water over 60 feet deep; sand drains used to speed settling. By 1990 it had sunk 27 feet, 50% more than the expected 19 feet (per Smithsonian).
- Further $150 million spent on strengthening and raising the seawall; hydraulic jacks with iron plates raise the foundation in stages. Sinking rate: over 19 inches per year at opening, 2.8 inches per year by 2008, 2.3 in 2023. Some engineers predict sections could be below sea level as soon as 2056.
- Causes: loose clay and silt compressing under the 69.5 square miles of fill, incomplete consolidation, underestimated settlement.

wikis.title: NASA Earth Observatory: Kansai Airport (2004 image of the day)
wikis.summary: NASA Earth Observatory Image of the Day (12 Feb 2004) on Kansai International Airport, Osaka Bay.
wikis.body:
- KIX is described as the world's first ocean airport, built on a landfill island in Osaka Bay, opened 1994, entirely artificial island.
- Built on compacted fill, it subsides, sinking 2-4 centimeters per year.
- Terminal 1.7 km long, designed by Renzo Piano; linked by a 3.7 km bridge; serves Osaka, Kobe and Kyoto. Survived the magnitude 6.7 Kobe earthquake four months after opening with minor damage.
- ASTER image acquired 19 September 2003, scene 48.5 x 55.5 km.

wikis.title: New Administrative Capital Stadium / Misr Stadium (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Egypt's 93,940-capacity Misr Stadium in the New Administrative Capital.
wikis.body:
- Also called Egypt Stadium or New Capital Stadium; capacity 93,940, largest in Egypt and second largest in Africa; part of Egypt International Olympic City. Cost E 900 million; built 2019-2023; opened 22 March 2024; tenant Egypt national football team.
- Designed by Italian firms SHESA Architects and MJW Structures with Cosmos-E; Orascom Construction main contractor. Elliptical plan; roof based on Nefertiti's headdress and necklace.
- First match 22 March 2024: Egypt 1-0 New Zealand (attendance 30,200). ACUD Cup final 26 March 2024: Egypt 2-4 Croatia, attendance 85,350 (record).
- Complex to include training ground, two indoor halls (one 15,000 arena), Olympic pool, built with an eye toward Olympic or World Cup bids.

wikis.title: StadiumDB: Egypt Stadium
wikis.summary: StadiumDB entry on Egypt Stadium in the New Administrative Capital.
wikis.body:
- Capacity 93,940; inauguration 22/03/2024; construction 2019-2024; cost EGP 900 M ($19.3 M); design SHESA; contractor Orascom Construction PLC. Whole complex cost 2.28 billion Egyptian pounds.
- Initially scheduled for 2022, then June 2023, not ready until early 2024; Egypt trained there in January 2024 before the Africa Cup of Nations. First match 22 March 2024, Egypt 1-0 New Zealand.
- Elliptical plan, hybrid turf and athletics track, three tiers with blue folding seats; largest in the Middle East and second largest in Africa after FNB Stadium; roof with 32 tall masts and membrane; blue/turquoise facade resembling Nefertiti's headdress.
- Meant to replace Cairo International Stadium as national stadium and support Olympic or World Cup bids. Complex includes two arenas, Olympic pool, hippodrome, tennis and squash facilities.

wikis.title: One London (formerly 1 Undershaft): construction start set for 2028
wikis.summary: Construction Enquirer reports that construction of the City of London's tallest tower, renamed One London, is set to start in 2028, with completion in 2033.
wikis.body:
- Construction is set to start in 2028 on the City of London's tallest tower; a main contractor is due to be appointed "later this year".
- The site formerly known as 1 Undershaft has been renamed One London by the team behind it.
- Aroland Holdings, Stanhope and Eric Parry Architects said the scheme will rise to 309.6 metres and hold 1.2 million sq ft of office-led space on completion in 2033.
- Full planning consent was given by the City of London Corporation in December 2025; the site is at the junction of Leadenhall Street and St Mary Axe.
- Deconstruction of the existing building, St Helen's Tower, is already underway by Keltbray.
- Level 73 will house Europe's highest publicly accessible viewing gallery at just over 300 metres, operated by London Museum. Level 72 has educational 'classrooms in the sky'.
- Stanhope CEO David Camp: "One London will be a striking addition to the capital's skyline and serve as a symbol of its enduring global pre-eminence."

## Project team
- Owner: Aroland Holdings (a consortium of Southeast Asian investors), advised by Perennial Holdings (Singapore-based)
- Development manager: Stanhope; architect: Eric Parry Architects
- Civil/structural, MEP and sustainability: WSP; landscape: SLA
- Leasing adviser: Newmark; deconstruction contractor: Keltbray

wikis.title: City of London Corporation approves 1 Undershaft, the Square Mile's tallest tower
wikis.summary: City of London Corporation press release of 13 December 2024 announcing planning approval of the 74-storey, 309.6m 1 Undershaft office tower.
wikis.body:
- Published 13 December 2024. The Planning Applications Sub-Committee approved proposals for what will become the City's tallest tower.
- 74 storeys, 309.6m high office tower known as 1 Undershaft, planned between the 'Gherkin' and the Leadenhall building; the tallest point of the City Cluster.
- Ties to the Corporation's target of a minimum of 1.2 million square metres of new office space by 2040. The proposals revise a previously consented scheme to respond to post-pandemic office needs and 'City Plan 2040'.
- 154,156 sqm of Grade A office space.
- A 1,000 sqm free-to-visit elevated public space and children's education space on levels 72 and 73, operated with the London Museum, open 7 days a week and into evenings.
- A 2,500 sqm publicly accessible podium garden 42 metres above street level with a structural glass floor, food, drink, retail and cultural attractions across levels 10 to 12.
- Ground-level public realm from St Mary Axe to parts of Leadenhall Street to become step-free with greening, seating, wayfinding and a large digital screen for events.
- Context cited: Sky Garden, 120 Fenchurch, The Lookout at 8 Bishopsgate and Horizon 22 have collectively greeted more than 13 million people; Deloitte Crane survey says City construction activity edged up 7 per cent; Knight Frank says availability in new City offices fell to 0.5 per cent and prime rents rose 16 per cent over 12 months.

wikis.title: Collapse of the Francis Scott Key Bridge, 26 March 2024 (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia account of the 26 March 2024 strike by the container ship Dali on the Francis Scott Key Bridge in Baltimore, the second-by-second timeline, damage and background.
wikis.body:
## Overview
- On March 26, 2024 (1:28:49 a.m. EDT per the infobox) the main spans and three nearest northeast approach spans of the Francis Scott Key Bridge over the Patapsco River collapsed after the container ship Dali, which had suffered catastrophic power outages impairing its control systems, struck a pier.
- Six members of a maintenance crew working on the roadway were killed; one was rescued from the river and an inspector was rescued from the remaining structure.
- The collapse blocked most shipping to and from the Port of Baltimore for 11 weeks. Governor Wes Moore called it a "global crisis" affecting more than 8,000 jobs; economic impact of the closure was estimated at $15 million per day.
- Maryland officials "plan to replace the bridge by late 2030"; initial cost estimates of $1.7-1.9 billion were later revised to $4.3-5.2 billion.

## Background
- Bridge: steel arch-shaped continuous truss, opened 1977, 1.6 miles long, second-longest of its type in the US; carried I-695 with four lanes and some 34,000 vehicles a day (3,000 trucks), many hauling hazardous materials barred from the harbor tunnels.
- Port of Baltimore in 2023: more than 444,000 passengers and 52.3 million tons of foreign cargo worth $80 billion; leading US port for automobiles for 13 straight years (847,000+ vehicles); employed 15,000 and indirectly supported 140,000.
- Dali: Singapore-registered Neopanamax container ship completed 2015, 980 ft long, 157 ft beam; operated by Synergy Marine Group, owned by Grace Ocean Private Ltd; crew of 20 Indian nationals and one Sri Lankan; loaded with 4,700 forty-foot containers.
- In 1980 a ship about one-third Dali's size struck and lightly damaged a pier. Anonymous former agency officials told the Washington Post that the Maryland Transportation Authority (MDTA) did not consider studying a collision with a larger ship.
- AASHTO did not specify ship-collision strength until 1994; existing bridges were exempted from the 1991 updated regulations by a grandfather clause. Experts debate whether protection could have prevented the collapse given Dali's size. Preliminary NTSB report noted March 2021 and May 2023 inspections found the bridge satisfactory.

## Collapse
- Dali left the port at 12:44 a.m. bound for Colombo, Sri Lanka, with two local harbor pilots. At 1:24 a.m. it suffered a "complete blackout" and drifted from the channel; a mayday was made at 1:27 a.m.
- Traffic was stopped by MDTA Police; the ship dropped anchor before impact. It struck the southwest pier of the central truss span at roughly 8 knots (timeline table: 6.4 knots at 01:29:09).
- Timeline highlights (NTSB-based): 01:24:59 low-voltage power lost about 3,200 ft from the bridge; 01:25:58 power restored by manual breaker closing; 01:27:04 generators underperform for lack of fuel, breakers open; 01:29:22 pier 17 collapses; 01:29:51 all approaches reported shut.
- Emergency teams got 911 calls from 1:30 a.m.; 50 public safety divers in eight teams were dispatched.

## Damage
- Impact force estimated by New York Times writers at 27-52 million pounds-force. The bridge was fracture critical, with no redundancy. The whole trussed section fell within 30 seconds.
- 13 of 4,700 containers were damaged, two fell into the water (no hazardous substances). Dali was impaled by an estimated 3,000-4,000 tonnes of wreckage but stayed watertight.

wikis.title: NTSB investigation of the Dali strike on the Francis Scott Key Bridge
wikis.summary: NTSB investigation page giving what happened on 26 March 2024, the probable cause and the safety recommendations after the Key Bridge collapse in Baltimore.
wikis.body:
## What happened
- On March 26, 2024, about 0129 local time, the 984-foot Singapore-flagged containership Dali, leaving Baltimore Harbor, lost electrical power, propulsion and steering and struck Pier 17, the southern pier supporting the central span of the Francis Scott Key Bridge.
- A substantial portion of the bridge collapsed; parts fell onto the vessel's bow and forwardmost container bays.
- A seven-person road maintenance crew and one inspector were on the bridge. Six highway workers died, one was seriously injured, the inspector was unharmed. One of 23 people aboard the Dali had a minor injury.
- Damage to the Dali exceeded $18 million; cargo damages undetermined; bridge replacement costs were unavailable at the time.
- Over 34,000 vehicles a day (10% trucks) must take alternate routes; hazardous-materials vehicles, barred from the tunnels, face extended detours.

## Probable cause (NTSB)
- Loss of electrical power (blackout) due to a loose signal wire connection to a terminal block stemming from improper installation of wire-label banding, leaving the vessel without propulsion and steering close to the bridge.
- Contributing: limited time to recover propulsion; no countermeasures against vessel impact because the Maryland Transportation Authority had not done a vulnerability assessment recommended by AASHTO; no effective, immediate communications to tell workers to evacuate.

## Recommendations
- Four urgent recommendations (H-25-1 to H-25-4). FHWA, with the Coast Guard and Army Corps of Engineers, to set up an interdisciplinary team advising bridge owners on vessel-collision risk (H-25-1, H-25-2).
- A long list of bridge owners to calculate the AASHTO Method II annual frequency of collapse for identified bridges and report to the NTSB (H-25-3), and develop risk reduction plans where above threshold.

wikis.title: The Clock Towers (Abraj Al Bait), Mecca (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the Clock Towers hotel complex in Mecca, Saudi Arabia, home of the Mecca Royal Clock Tower (601 m).
wikis.body:
- The Clock Towers (formerly Abraj al-Bait) is a government-owned hotel complex of seven skyscraper hotels in Mecca, part of the King Abdulaziz Endowment Project to modernize the city for pilgrims.
- Central Mecca Royal Clock Tower: fourth-tallest building and sixth-tallest freestanding structure in the world; per Guinness World Records the tallest clock tower, and the complex of seven buildings the world's second most expensive building. Its clock faces are the largest in the world; the top four floors hold the Clock Tower Museum.
- Complex is 300 m from the Great Mosque of Mecca; built after demolition of the Ajyad Fortress, an 18th-century Ottoman citadel.
- Developer and contractor: Saudi Binladin Group. Architects/structural engineers: SL Rasch GmbH and Dar Al-Handasah.
- Cost: US$15 billion. Construction started 2002, completed 2011, opened 2012.
- Heights: architectural/tip 601 m (1,972 ft); antenna spire 93 m; roof 508 m; top floor 494 m; observatory 484.4 m. 120 floors, 96 elevators (with mall).
- Floor area: tower 310,638 m2; development 1,575,815 m2.
- Tallest building in Saudi Arabia since 2012 (preceded by Kingdom Centre). Tower contains a five-star Fairmont hotel.
- Materials: reinforced concrete lower part, steel/concrete composite, steel upper part; cladding of glass, marble, natural stone and fibre-reinforced plastic.

wikis.title: The B1M: how the Makkah Royal Clock Tower was built
wikis.summary: The B1M video article (25 September 2024) on the engineering of the Makkah Royal Clock Tower, described as a roughly USD $16BN, 600 m minaret and clock tower.
wikis.body:
- Published 25 September 2024 by The B1M (host Fred Mills). The site notes it depicts on-site health and safety and labour culture different from what The B1M advocates.
- Tower: 35 times the size of Big Ben with the world's largest clock; estimated cost USD $16BN; about 600 m high; still holds the highest occupied man-made space (prayer room at 600 m vs Burj Khalifa's highest occupied floor at 585 m and Shanghai Tower's at 583 m).
- Firms from over ten countries worked on it; many engineers and architects could not visit because only Muslims may enter Mecca. Some glazing experts (from Germany and Poland) converted to Islam to work on site, per Mustafa Rasch of SL Rasch.
- Hotel originally planned at 450 m (construction began 2002); extended to 600 m to serve as a minaret and clock tower when half the hotel was already built, so foundations limited weight to 82,000 tonnes (Shanghai Tower, 632 m, is 575,000 tonnes). Engineers used an Eiffel-Tower-inspired lightweight steel and concrete framework on five transfer slabs, with floors about 12 m apart behind the clock and voids cut in floors.
- Clock intended to set a second time standard beside Greenwich Mean Time, showing atomic time in Mecca.
- Clock face is green and white, lit by more than 2M LEDs (105 mm pixel spacing), legible from more than 8 km.
- Facade: 98M mosaic glass tiles (20 x 20 mm), 13 colours, one-third with 24 carat gold leaf; a Venetian company automated production with a robotic system (gold tiles had been 15-20 sq m a month versus 250-300 needed).
- Much was prefabricated in Dubai, including a quarter of the clock, then trucked three days to Mecca. The crescent top is described as the biggest carbon fibre structure ever built, with three floors including the highest prayer room; lifting it was at the limit of the tower crane (about 220 m plus) and wind made it spin. The king pressed a button to turn on the lights at opening.
- Hajj: up to 3M Muslims travel to Mecca; religious tourism contributes about $12BN annually to the kingdom's economy, per the video.

wikis.title: Lakhta Center, Saint Petersburg (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the 462 m, 87-storey Lakhta Center in Saint Petersburg, tallest building in Russia and Europe, covering planning, construction, design and proposed follow-on towers.
wikis.body:
- 87-storey (plus 3 below ground) skyscraper in Lakhta, Saint Petersburg; 462 m (1,516 ft); tallest building in Russia and Europe, sixteenth-tallest in the world, and the northernmost skyscraper. Owner Gazprom; cost US$1.77 billion; floor area 163,000 m2; observatory at 357 m.
- Construction started 30 October 2012; topped out 29 January 2018; completed 2019 (infobox). It passed the Federation Towers' Vostok Tower as tallest in Russia and Europe on 5 October 2017.
- Designers/builders: RMJM (until 2011), then Gorproject; main contractor Rönesans Holding (selected 22 April 2014); project management AECOM; glazing by Josef Gartner.
- Planning: it replaced the earlier Okhta Center plan, moved after UNESCO's World Heritage Committee opposed a 400 m tower in the historic centre.
- Schedule facts: 2,080 piles in total (264 for the tower); 19,624 cubic metres of concrete in the foundation raft; passed 300 m in April 2017; 374 m on 5 October 2017.
- Certified LEED Platinum on 24 December 2018. Gazprom completed re-registration in Saint Petersburg in August 2021.
- Facilities: offices, co-working, sports centre, children's science centre, conference centre, 1,500 sq m exhibition space, planetarium (140 capacity), public observation deck at 357 m. Anti-icing measures on the spire (metal gauze in place of glazing, heated glass).
- Awards: Emporis Skyscraper of the Year 2020; CTBUH facade engineering award 20 May 2021, plus two Awards of Excellence; Grand Prix at 100 + Awards, October 2021.
- Future (announced, uncertain): Lakhta Center II, 703 m / 150 floors (announced May 2021); Lakhta Center III, 555 m (announced December 2021, "no major news" since).

wikis.title: Lakhta Center officially commissioned (Archinect, October 2018)
wikis.summary: Archinect news item from 19 October 2018 reporting that Saint Petersburg officials authorised commissioning of the 462 m Lakhta Center, with construction and wind details.
wikis.body:
- Dated Oct 19, 2018. Local officials in Saint Petersburg granted the RMJM-designed Lakhta Center complex authorization for commissioning after final inspections that week.
- The 462 m (1,516 ft) tower already holds the title of Europe's tallest building and world's northernmost skyscraper, with the fastest elevators in Russia; grand opening as Gazprom's HQ was "still another year out".
- Final fit-out by operators and tenants "will take at least a year". Planned for visitors: Europe's highest panoramic restaurant at 315 m, sky deck at 360 m, spherical planetarium (10 million stars), sports facilities with panoramic pool, children's education centre, exhibition space, coast amphitheater and concert hall with 15 transformations. Two elevated roads with cycle-pedestrian paths were built across Lakhta harbor.
- Foundation: raft area of the multifunctional building more than 2 hectares; the tower's box foundation lower slab poured (19,624 volume) in 49 hours, described as a world record.
- Wind: gusts of 120-140 km/hour recorded; storm warnings numbered 159 in 2015, 258 in 2016, 176 in 2017; 18 days of strong wind hit spire installation. Construction was completed on time.
- Anti-icing system for the spire tested in Russia and Canada: passive grid facade plus active heating elements, described as having no analogs.

wikis.title: LTA page: Singapore's Cross Island Line
wikis.summary: Land Transport Authority overview of the Cross Island Line's phases, expected completion years and the alignment options studied near the Central Catchment Nature Reserve.
wikis.body:
- The Cross Island Line (CRL) is Singapore's eighth MRT line, the longest fully underground line at more than 50 km, with 11 interchange stations, serving east, west and north-east corridors (Jurong Lake District, Punggol Digital District, Changi region).
- Phase 1 (CRL1): 29 km, 12 stations from CR2 to CR13 Bright Hill; more than 100,000 households to benefit; expected completed by 2030.
- Phase 2 (CRL2): about 15 km, six underground stations (interchanges at King Albert Park with Downtown Line and Clementi with East-West Line); stations opening by 2032.
- CRL-Punggol Extension: 7.3 km linking Pasir Ris/Tampines North with Punggol and Sengkang; expected 2032.
- Phase 3 (CRL3): about 10 km, four underground stations from CR19 Jurong Lake District to CR23 Gul Circle; two interchanges (Jurong Region Line at JS12, East-West Line at Gul Circle); construction "expected to commence in 2027", stations targeted "by the late 2030s"; up to 50 minutes saved for western commuters. A second depot of about 23 hectares at the former Raffles Country Club site, co-located with a bus depot.
- Alignment near the Central Catchment Nature Reserve (CCNR): two-phase EIA by Environmental Resource Management (ERM). Direct option: 2 km tunnel beneath the CCNR (about 70 m deep, in hard granite, no surface structures), about 6 minutes less commuting time, about 15% lower fares, estimated daily ridership above 600,000 initially and over one million longer term. Skirting option: about 45 m deep, 9 km tunnel under roads and buildings. An International Panel of Advisors concluded tunnelling on either alignment is safe; the EIA found both feasible with residual impacts "largely moderate or below".

wikis.title: Cross Island Line (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Singapore's under-construction Cross Island Line MRT, covering its history, phases, alignment controversy and planned opening years.
wikis.body:
- High-capacity MRT line under construction in Singapore, running east-west from Changi to Pioneer with a Punggol branch; 67 km when fully operational (about 26 stations), to replace the East-West Line as the longest on the network. Uses CRRC Qingdao Sifang CR151 trains (six-car, stations built for eight-car), Siemens Trainguard CBTC, GoA 4 driverless operation, overhead 1,500 V DC.
- Long-term ridership expected over one million daily; estimated cost S$40.7 billion.
- First announced by Transport Minister Lui Tuck Yew on 17 January 2013 (then planned as 50 km, opening 2030).
- Alignment controversy: Nature Society Singapore called for tunnels to avoid the Central Catchment Nature Reserve; ERM's EIA (phase 1 report February 2016, phase 2 September 2019). On 4 December 2019 the Ministry of Transport chose the direct route beneath the reserve, tunnelling deeper with no surface works; cost expected $2 billion lower than alternatives.
- Phase 1: 29 km, 12 stations, Aviation Park to Bright Hill; announced 25 January 2019; construction officially began 18 January 2023; opening pushed from 2029 to 2030 due to COVID-19. 57-hectare Changi East Depot.
- Punggol Extension: 7.3 km, announced 10 March 2020, delayed from 2031 to 2032.
- Phase 2: 15 km, six stations Turf City to Jurong Lake District, confirmed 20 September 2022, expected 2032; groundbreaking at Clementi 7 July 2025.
- Changi Terminal 5 extension (5.8 km): confirmed 14 May 2025 and announced by LTA 25 July 2025, mid-2030s.
- Phase 3: studies concluded March 2026; on 31 July 2026 four stations over 10 km announced (Jurong Pier and Gul Circle interchanges); second depot at former Raffles Country Club; construction slated 2027, completion "late 2030s".
- December 2022: bored tunnel contract between Fairways Drive and Sin Ming Walk awarded to Obayashi and Shanghai Tunnel Engineering for $758 million.

wikis.title: Land Transport Guru: Cross Island Line phases and timeline
wikis.summary: Fan-run transport site's summary of the Cross Island Line's phases, opening dates, rolling stock, station lists and dated announcement history.
wikis.body:
- Phases and dates: Phase 1 (2030) Aviation Park-Bright Hill, 12 stations, 29 km; Punggol Extension (2032) Pasir Ris-Punggol, 3 stations, 7.3 km; Phase 2 (2032) Turf City-Jurong Lake District, 6 stations, 15 km; Changi Terminal 5 (mid 2030s), 1 station, 5.8 km; Phase 3 (late 2030s) Jurong Lake District-Gul Circle, 4 stations, 10 km. About 67 km when complete.
- Fully automated driverless line; CRRC Sifang CR151 six-car trains (possible eight-car); 1500V DC overhead; depots at Changi East and a western depot (phase 3).
- Timeline: announced 17 Jan 2013 (Land Transport Master Plan 2013); EIA Aug 2014-end 2016; Phase 1 announced 25 Jan 2019 (then due 2029); direct alignment chosen 4 Dec 2019; Punggol extension announced 10 Mar 2020 (then due 2031); delays to 2030 and 2032 attributed to COVID-19 supply and manpower disruption (March 2021 press release); Phase 2 announced 20 Sep 2022, works started 2023; Terminal 5 station announced 14 May 2025 and 25 Jul 2025; engineering studies for Phase 3 completed 4 Mar 2026; Phase 3 formally announced 31 Jul 2026, construction to start 2027.
- Station names other than interchanges are working names. Phase 1 stations: Aviation Park, Loyang, Pasir Ris East, Pasir Ris, Tampines North, Defu, Hougang, Serangoon North, Tavistock, Ang Mo Kio, Teck Ghee, Bright Hill.

wikis.title: National Gas to invest 870 million pounds in the East of England
wikis.summary: National Gas press release (8 January 2026) on an 870 million pound five-year investment in the East of England, centred on its Peterborough regional HQ and compressor station.
wikis.body:
- Dated 8 January 2026. National Gas, owner and operator of Britain's gas network, is investing £870 million in the East of England over the next five years, creating 250 more jobs and safeguarding 300.
- Peterborough is home of the East Region's headquarters (Fleet House, Cygnet Road), covering Cambridgeshire, Essex, Kent, Lincolnshire, Norfolk, Northamptonshire and Suffolk.
- The £870 million is part of a £3.2 billion funding package approved by Ofgem (RIIO-GT3). It will fund projects such as updating control systems at King's Lynn and Diss compressor stations.
- Peterborough's two new compressors are fully installed and operational, with a third in early construction; compatible with methane and blends of hydrogen. Compressors push 99% of Britain's gas through 5,000 miles of pipelines.
- Peterborough was one of three compressor sites sharing a £350 million investment announced in 2025.
- Announced during a visit by Industry Minister Chris McDonald and MPs Andrew Pakes and Sam Carling, who opened the new East Region office. Regional Director Nick Sides: "Peterborough's compressors are the powerhouse of Britain's gas network".
- Graduates and apprentices are set to benefit.

wikis.title: Merdeka 118, Kuala Lumpur (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Merdeka 118 (renamed Merdeka Maybank Tower), the 678.9 m megatall skyscraper in Kuala Lumpur, with its construction history, opening status and design.
wikis.body:
- 118-storey megatall skyscraper in the Merdeka Precinct, Kuala Lumpur, 678.9 m (2,227 ft); described as second-tallest building in the world after the Burj Khalifa; tallest in Malaysia and Southeast Asia (surpassing Landmark 81). Developer: Permodalan Nasional Berhad (PNB); budget RM5 billion, which drew public criticism.
- Announced by Prime Minister Abdullah Badawi on 12 September 2007. Spire completed December 2022; structure completed November 2023; grand opening 10 January 2024 (inaugurated by the Yang di-Pertuan Agong) but not opened to the public as scheduled. Park Hyatt Kuala Lumpur began operation on levels 75 to 112 on 7 August 2025; the rest "remains far behind schedule as of 1 July 2026", with most areas closed.
- Renamed Merdeka Maybank Tower (Menara Merdeka Maybank) in July 2026 for anchor tenant Maybank (article gives both 28 July and 30 July 2026).
- Construction: contract of RM3.4 billion awarded 23 November 2015 to Samsung C&T and UEM Group JV; work halted 18 March 2020 by COVID-19 Movement Control Order, resumed mid-May 2020; concrete core topped out August 2020; topped out November 2021. Engineers Leslie E. Robertson Associates, Robert Bird Group, Arup; Turner International as project management consultant; KONE supplies about 87 elevators and escalators.
- Design: inspired by Tunku Abdul Rahman's outstretched hand chanting "Merdeka!" in 1957; diamond-shaped glass facade (18,144 panels, 114,000 sq m glass); 400,000 sq m of space; highest observation deck in Southeast Asia; 118 Mall (set to open by June 2026 per article); 8,500 parking spaces; Park Hyatt on top 17 floors. Belfield Tunnel (1 km) opened 2 March 2025.
- Security incidents in 2022: an American group trespassed and Russian rooftoppers scaled the spire.

wikis.title: Notre Dame de Paris reopens after the 2019 fire (CNN, 7 December 2024)
wikis.summary: CNN report on the formal reopening ceremony of Notre Dame cathedral on Saturday 7 December 2024, five years after the fire.
wikis.body:
- Published Dec 7, 2024. Notre Dame de Paris formally reopened on Saturday with a two-hour ceremony inside the renovated interior, five years after it was "nearly destroyed" in a fire.
- Attendees with French President Emmanuel Macron included US President-elect Donald Trump, US first lady Jill Biden, Elon Musk and Prince William; Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky was welcomed with a standing ovation. About 170 bishops and priests from each of the 106 Paris parishes took part; Pope Francis did not attend but sent a message of "joy, celebration, and praise".
- Weather (rain, winds near 40 mph) moved the start of the service from the forecourt to inside.
- Estimated restoration cost €700 million ($739 million); captions say some 250 companies and hundreds of experts were mobilised. Centuries of grime were wiped away, leaving a Gothic church that "glistens".
- Macron: "We rediscovered what great nations can do: accomplish the impossible." More than 2,000 congregants attended.
- Security: an extra 6,000 officers; Ile de la Cite closed to all but residents, law enforcement and attendees.
- Captions: first Mass held Sunday December 8; first glimpses of the interior given on Friday November 29; Archbishop of Paris Laurent Ulrich led prayers; the cathedral is described as 860 years old.

wikis.title: Olympic rings installed on the Eiffel Tower for Paris 2024
wikis.summary: KIRO 7 (Cox Media Group) report of 7 June 2024 that the five Olympic rings were mounted on the Eiffel Tower 50 days before the Paris Games.
wikis.body:
- June 07, 2024: the Olympic rings were mounted on the Eiffel Tower at the 50-day mark before the Games, per the AP; placed between the first and second floors on the south side facing the Seine.
- Created by ArcelorMittal in coordination with the tower, from recycled French steel. Each ring is 30 feet in diameter, 30 tons total, lit by 100,000 LED bulbs through the Paralympic Games.
- Paris 2024 president Tony Estanguet: "It is wonderful. There are a lot of emotions..."
- The Seine boat parade of Olympians to the opening ceremony is on July 26. The tower is a backdrop for events including volleyball at the temporary Eiffel Tower Stadium at its foot.
- Each Olympic and Paralympic medal will have a small piece of iron from the tower embedded.

wikis.title: Nuuk International Airport officially opens with a new runway (Simple Flying)
wikis.summary: Simple Flying report on the opening of Nuuk International Airport's new 2,200 m runway and terminal, and the first widebody flight to Greenland's capital.
wikis.body:
- Nuuk International Airport (GOH) officially opened to the public ("today" in the article; no date given in the text) after a $300 million project: a new 2,200 m (7,200 ft) runway, new terminal and Instrument Landing System, making transatlantic and intercontinental flights possible.
- Capacity 800 passengers per hour. First flight out was an Air Greenland Dash 8 to Paamiut at 07.35; first widebody arrival was an Air Greenland Airbus A330neo from Copenhagen, greeted by over 2,000 people.
- Previously the airport (opened September 1979) had a 950 m (3,100 ft) runway suited only to turboprops; long-haul jets used Narsarsuaq or Kangerlussuaq (former US air bases handed over in 1956 and 1992). Contractors blasted over 240 million cubic feet of rock.
- New cargo facilities aim at seafood exports. Greenland Airports CEO Jens Lauridsen called it "a truly historic milestone"; airport communications director Mikkel Lund said over two dozen carriers had shown interest and talks were held with at least 30 airlines.
- Announced routes: United from Newark next summer (first US direct link); SAS from Denmark and AirSeven next year; Icelandair to upgrade Reykjavik flights to the 737 MAX.
- Two more airports, at Ilulissat and Qaqortoq, are part of the wider project (given as "$800", figure as written) and expected to open in 2026.

wikis.title: Bohunice V1 reactors fully dismantled (World Nuclear News)
wikis.summary: World Nuclear News item reporting that the two VVER-440 V-230 reactors at Bohunice V1 in Slovakia have been fully dismantled, per the EBRD.
wikis.body:
- The two VVER-440 V-230 reactors at Bohunice V1, Slovakia, were decommissioned and disassembled on site, the first time this has happened for this reactor type, per the EBRD.
- Funded by the Bohunice International Decommissioning Support Fund, more than EUR650 million (USD660 million) as of mid-2018 from the European Commission, Austria, Denmark, France, Ireland, the Netherlands, Spain, Switzerland and the UK; managed by the EBRD. Work completed "on schedule and within budget".
- Preparation began in 2012. Remaining equipment to be taken apart by 2025; buildings demolished and site ready for redevelopment by 2027.
- Reactors date to the 1970s, the first of their kind outside the Soviet Union; closed at end of 2006 and 2008 under Slovakia's EU accession terms (2004).
- Steam generators were removed to make room for decontamination pools. Total plant mass about 800,000 tonnes. JAVYS project manager Tibor Rapant named the reactor pressure vessels, internals and steam generators as the key challenge.
- Slovakia has four reactors generating half its electricity and two more under construction.

wikis.title: EBRD: Bohunice reactors decommissioning milestone (2022)
wikis.summary: EBRD news release on the full dismantling of the two VVER-440 reactors at Bohunice, Slovak Republic, funded through the EBRD-managed BIDSF.
wikis.body:
- The two VVER-440 pressurised water reactors at Bohunice NPP have been fully dismantled and components decontaminated for safe storage and recycling.
- Work by JAVYS and a Westinghouse-led consortium including VUJE, funded through the Bohunice International Decommissioning Support Fund (BIDSF), managed by the EBRD, established 2001.
- First time reactors of this type were decommissioned and disassembled directly on site. Twelve 160-tonne steam generators were removed from the turbine hall, allowing two 1250 m3 pools for underwater sectioning. Around 95 per cent of waste and metals already processed, decontaminated and released.
- Decommissioning of the two reactors began May 2020 and April 2021 and took 18 and 11 months. EBRD's Steve White: "an impressive achievement".
- Remaining equipment to be processed by 2025; buildings demolished and area redevelopment-ready by 2027.
- Slovakia agreed to early shutdown of Units 1 and 2 in 2006 and 2008 under EU accession; the EU provided more than €800 million in assistance. BIDSF donors: EU, Austria, Denmark, France, Ireland, Netherlands, Spain, Switzerland, UK.

wikis.title: Queensland government commits to rebuild Paradise Dam wall in place (ABC, 7 July 2026)
wikis.summary: ABC News report that Queensland's government will restore the existing Paradise Dam wall rather than build a new wall downstream, with $60 million allocated in this year's budget.
wikis.body:
- Posted Tue 7 Jul 2026. Premier David Crisafulli, in Bundaberg, said the state committed $60 million in this year's budget, predominantly for geotechnical works, to rebuild the Paradise Dam wall where it is instead of a new wall downstream. "I don't accept the nonsensical argument ... an inferior, smaller wall downstream."
- Background: Paradise Dam (Burnett River near Bundaberg) had safety concerns raised in 2019; the wall was lowered 5.8 m in 2020; $1.2 billion in joint state and federal funding was committed to rebuilding.
- In 2024 operator Sunwater said there were too many issues to repair and recommended a new downstream wall at an estimated cost of at least $4.4 billion. In May (2026), a leaked letter from Sunwater chairman Jeff Seeney recommended scrapping the new-build plan as "grossly disproportionate".
- The Sunwater business case on how the wall would be rebuilt is "yet to be delivered".
- Irrigators: Bundaberg Regional Irrigators Group's Dale Hollis said the regional economy is about $10 billion a year, about $2.5 billion from intensive irrigated agriculture; grower Judy Plath wants detail and speed, noting the dam is "only half its original size" and an El Nino is predicted.
- Timeline: promised 1998; approved 2002; $200 million project, construction completed 2005; first filled 2010; 2013 flood damage, repairs over $23 million; 24 September 2019 wall to be lowered, capacity reduced to 42 per cent; December 2019 report found spillway well below safety guidelines.

wikis.title: Seoul announces 'Seoul Twin Eye' twin Ferris wheel plan at Peace Park
wikis.summary: Seoul Metropolitan Government announcement of a proposed 180 m twin-ring Ferris wheel, tentatively 'Seoul Twin Eye', in Pyeonghwa (Peace) Park, Sangam-dong.
wikis.body:
- SMG announced a 180 m Ferris wheel tentatively named "Seoul Twin Eye" in Pyeonghwa (Peace) Park inside World Cup Park, Sangam-dong, Mapo-gu, billed as the world's first twin Ferris wheel with two intersecting rings. The city plans to seek Ministry of Economy and Finance approval "in the early next year".
- Part of the Great Hangang Project; SMG announced in March a private investment project for a spokeless Ferris wheel and the legal basis was set in September.
- The Seoul Twin Eye Consortium (SH Corporation, TheRitz and three other corporations) submitted a proposal on Nov. 29 following a contest that began in September.
- Proposal: world's largest spokeless design, 64 capsules, 1,440 passengers per cycle, raised 40 m above ground; lower section for performance and exhibition halls (13,126 m2), convenience facilities (7,853 m2) and support facilities (2,296 m2), plus fountains, zip lines and monorails. Nanji Pond to host a fountain show; a monorail is planned from World Cup Stadium Station (Line 6).

wikis.title: Seoul's 'Seoulling' giant Ferris wheel plan (Asia Business Daily)
wikis.summary: Asia Business Daily article on Seoul's planned ring-shaped Ferris wheel in Peace Park, with construction aimed for next year and completion as early as 2028.
wikis.body:
- The article (dated 31 January 2025 in its URL; no date in the text) says the ring-shaped Ferris wheel 'Seoulling' is expected to be unveiled as early as 2028, with construction aimed to start "next year".
- Design: two 180 m diameter rings intersecting in an 'X' shape, the largest ring-shaped Ferris wheel without spokes in the world, in the Peace Park within World Cup Park, Sangam-dong.
- Process: Seoul began a strategic environmental impact assessment last year and held a public hearing; then the KDI's PIMAC eligibility evaluation, a Ministry of Economy and Finance private investment review, Seoul Metropolitan Council approval, and a third-party announcement to select an operator within the year.
- Cost: budget rose from 400 billion KRW to 1.08 trillion KRW after the design changed from a single ring to two intersecting rings and the site moved from Sky Park to Peace Park; SH Corporation's involvement drew criticism that citizens' taxes are indirectly invested.
- A fast-track procedure shortens administrative steps by up to about 10 months (normally about three years before construction).
- Comparisons cited: London Eye (135 m, 3.5 million visitors annually), Osaka 115 m (2016), Ain Dubai which ceased operations about a year after its October 2021 completion. A Seoul official said the city will monitor environmental, traffic and feasibility issues.

wikis.title: The Henderson, Hong Kong (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on The Henderson, the Zaha Hadid Architects-designed 36-storey, 190 m office tower at 2 Murray Road, Central, Hong Kong.
wikis.body:
- 36-storey, 190 m (623 ft) skyscraper in Central, Hong Kong, designed by Zaha Hadid Architects; about 465,000 sq ft (citation needed per the page). Developer Henderson Land Development.
- The site at 2 Murray Road was reportedly the world's most expensive plot, worth US$3 billion when bought in 2017, replacing a car park. Construction began in 2019 and was completed in 2024.
- Occupancy reached 90% as of January 2026. Tenants include Point72, Coller Capital, General Atlantic, Cohen & Steers, Akin Gump, Nishimura & Asahi, Audemars Piguet (a whole floor, about 12,000 sq ft), Christie's (four floors, about 50,000 sq ft; Asia Pacific HQ) and Carlyle (about 20,000 sq ft).
- Design: curved silhouette inspired by a Bauhinia bud in full bloom.
- Awards: 2025 CTBUH Overall Category Winner (Best Tall Building, Asia, and Facade Award) plus Awards of Excellence; Quality Building Award 2024; HKIA Medal of the Year 2024; Green Building Award 2021; "World's Best Property" at the International Property Awards. 10 sustainability and smart accreditations including LEED, BEAM Plus, WELL. Its restaurants Akira Back, Hana no Kumo and Peridot are on the Prix Versailles 2026 list. First commercial building in APAC to partner with Forbes Travel Guide.

wikis.title: Dezeen: Zaha Hadid Architects' Henderson skyscraper nears completion (January 2024)
wikis.summary: Dezeen article of 8 January 2024 on The Henderson in Hong Kong's Central district, nearing completion on a reportedly record-priced site.
wikis.body:
- Dated 8 January 2024. The 36-storey Henderson office tower by Zaha Hadid Architects is nearing completion beside Chater Garden, near Bank of China Tower and the HSBC building.
- Site at 2 Murray Road reportedly the world's most expensive plot when Henderson Land bought it in 2017, at £764,000 per square metre.
- Construction "has overshot its intended 2023 completion date"; most curved glass panels are in place.
- Form informed by buds of the Hong Kong orchid; facade of more than 4,000 double-laminated glass panels with 1,000 different curvatures. Building raised above ground, linked to raised walkways, two MTR stations and Chater Garden; two open-air balconies, an enclosed sky garden with running track, top-floor banquet hall. Column-free plans supported by six "mega-columns" and a one-sided steel core.
- As of September only half the office space was leased, tenants including Audemars Piguet and Christie's (Asia Pacific HQ across four floors); a record 13 million sq ft of workspace sits empty across the city.
- Second Hong Kong project of Zaha Hadid Architects after the Jockey Club Innovation Tower.

wikis.title: Intuit Dome, Inglewood (Wikipedia)
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on Intuit Dome, the Los Angeles Clippers' arena in Inglewood, California, covering its approval fights, construction, opening and features.
wikis.body:
- Multi-purpose indoor arena in Inglewood, California, south of SoFi Stadium and the Kia Forum; home of the LA Clippers, who previously shared Crypto.com Arena (1999-2000 to 2023-24). Groundbreaking September 17, 2021; opened August 15, 2024; newest NBA arena; to host basketball at the 2028 Summer Olympics; hosted the debut of WWE Monday Night Raw on Netflix.
- History: in 2017 Inglewood approved an exclusive negotiating agreement with the Clippers. Lawsuits by Uplift Inglewood (Surplus Land Act) and IRATE (legal fees paid by Madison Square Garden Company, owner of The Forum) opposed it; Uplift's suit was rejected in November 2019; California Air Resources Board approved it in December 2019. Steve Ballmer bought The Forum for $400 million (announced March 2020, completed May) to settle litigation.
- Naming rights: 23-year deal for at least $500 million with Intuit. Bruno Mars opened the arena with shows on August 15 and 16, 2024. First preseason game October 14 (110-96 over Dallas); first regular season game October 23 vs Phoenix (lost 116-113 in overtime, 18,300 fans); first playoff game April 24, 2025 (117-83 over Denver).
- Design by AECOM; 18,000 seats; 85,000 sq ft practice facility, 55,000 sq ft team offices, 25,000 sq ft sports medicine clinic, 40,000 sq ft retail, 260,000 sq ft outdoor plaza. "The Wall" seating section (51 rows); over 1,100 toilets and urinals; Daktronics halo board of 38,375 sq ft at 4K.

wikis.title: Construction Dive: Intuit Dome opens with Bruno Mars concert (August 2024)
wikis.summary: Construction Dive report that the $2 billion Intuit Dome opened with a Bruno Mars concert, with build, sustainability and entry-technology details.
wikis.body:
- The Intuit Dome opened to the public on a Thursday night with a Bruno Mars concert; construction finished "this month" (article undated in text; context is August 2024). The Clippers will take the court "this fall".
- Built by an AECOM Hunt and Turner joint venture, which broke ground on the $2 billion venue in September 2021; AECOM also designed it.
- Facial-recognition entry problems left thousands of fans outside and delayed the concert (per ABC 7); patrons register in an app and create a "Game Face ID".
- 17,700 seats, five basketball courts, practice facility and training center, outdoor plaza; the world's largest "Halo Board", a double-sided 4K scoreboard roughly an acre in size.
- Sustainability (per mechanical engineer Henderson Engineers): 2 MW rooftop solar, 11 MW battery storage, all-electric, heat pumps, under-seat air supply; LEED-Platinum certified.
- Slated to host the 2026 NBA All-Star Game and 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.

wikis.title: First Johor Bahru-Singapore RTS Link train unveiled (MOT Singapore)
wikis.summary: Singapore Ministry of Transport release on the unveiling of the first RTS Link train at the Singapore Rail Test Centre, with testing progress and a December 2026 service target.
wikis.body:
- Singapore's Acting Minister for Transport Jeffrey Siow and Malaysia's Transport Minister Anthony Loke unveiled the first RTS Link train at the Singapore Rail Test Centre (SRTC); the article gives no date.
- At the start of service the RTS Link will have eight four-car trains from CRRC Zhuzhou Locomotive Co., each carrying more than 600 passengers; peak capacity up to 10,000 passengers per hour per direction.
- Offsite systems integration testing at SRTC by RTS Operations Pte Ltd (RTSO, a joint venture of Prasarana RTS Operations and SMRT RTS) over the next few months, expected complete in the fourth quarter this year; then onsite testing with the other seven trains.
- InfraCos have granted RTSO access to civil structures since end of 2024; track spans about 5.3 km from Wadi Hana Depot to Bukit Chagar and on to Woodlands North; rail system works about 56% complete.
- Links Bukit Chagar (Johor Bahru) and Woodlands North; about five minutes' journey; "targeted to commence passenger service by December 2026". Co-located CIQ facilities at both stations, so only one immigration clearance at the departure point.

wikis.title: Loke: RTS Link on track to start January 1, 2027 (Malay Mail, 11 January 2024)
wikis.summary: Malay Mail report from Johor Baru on 11 January 2024 that Malaysia's transport minister was confident the RTS Link would start on January 1, 2027.
wikis.body:
- Dateline JOHOR BARU, Jan 11 (2024). Transport Minister Anthony Loke said the government is positive the RTS Link will be fully operational on January 1, 2027, and that development is on schedule.
- Progress he cited: marine viaduct 68% complete, terrestrial viaduct 31%, stations 41%, Customs, Immigration and Quarantine (CIQ) complex 3.22%. "We are 100 per cent confident..."
- Said at a press conference after the span completion ceremony connecting Malaysia and Singapore, officiated by Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim and Singapore's Lee Hsien Loong at the marine viaduct.
- The RTS Link: light commuter rail of four kilometres with two stations (Bukit Chagar and Woodlands North), about 10,000 passengers per hour each way, on a viaduct 25 metres above the Tebrau Straits. Expected to draw 35 per cent of the 350,000 people crossing the Johor Causeway daily; expected to benefit the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone.

wikis.title: ERR: Rail Baltica to be finished 2030 in Estonia but with reduced scope
wikis.summary: ERR report on a Ministry of Climate presentation saying Rail Baltica's Estonian section keeps a 2030 completion date but with a slashed first-phase scope and a large funding gap.
wikis.body:
- The official completion date remains 2030 (per Deputy Secretary General Sander Salmu), with the railway operational from Tallinn to the Lithuania-Poland border but "with significant compromises"; over the next two years more than €400 million is needed and not yet secured.
- Compromises: whole Estonian section single-track (originally double), with sidings; Muuga-Soodevahe (freight only) single-track; traffic control built to 80% and electrification to 70%; 11 to 13 viaducts not built in the first phase; all 12 local stops minimal (no full station buildings). Ulemiste and Parnu passenger terminals still to full specification by 2030; Ulemiste terminal building construction to begin this year.
- Throughput capacity and connection speed said to remain on par with the full-scale solution.
- Cost of the first phase: €3.1 billion, about €1.5 billion funded; another €272 million for supporting activities and launch of regional passenger services; unfunded portion €1.756 billion. In 2025 nearly €290 million is planned; about €1.1 billion of works under contract. Funding shortfall of €160 million next year and €255 million the year after; Estonia hopes for about €1.25 billion of EU funds in 2028-2030; debt is an option "if those funds prove insufficient". New trains need €60-75 million in the 2026-2029 budget strategy.

wikis.title: EU auditors: Rail Baltica will miss 2030 deadline (LRT)
wikis.summary: LRT report that the European Court of Auditors says Rail Baltica will not be completed by 2030 and has no final completion date.
wikis.body:
- The European Court of Auditors said (on a Monday; article text gives no date) the long-delayed, increasingly costly Rail Baltica will not be completed by 2030 and there is no final deadline for the full line.
- Auditor Annemie Turtelboom: "Now, 2030 is the envisaged date to complete only a first phase, and therefore, there is no timeline for the full project."
- Estimated cost of the European standard-gauge project has risen 2.6 times over six years to 23.8 billion euros, nearly four times the initial estimate. Causes: lack of maturity, repeated scope changes, design alterations and splitting into two phases.
- The EU goal of completing the core TEN-T network by 2030 is no longer achievable. Total cost of eight major EU infrastructure projects reviewed rose 24% over six years, driven largely by Lyon-Turin and Rail Baltica.

wikis.title: Hong Kong opens Kai Tak Sports Park (HKFP/AFP, 2 March 2025)
wikis.summary: HKFP (AFP) report on the opening of the HK$30 billion Kai Tak Sports Park and its 50,000-seat stadium on Saturday 1 March 2025.
wikis.body:
- Hong Kong opened the HK$30 billion ($3.86 billion) Kai Tak Sports Park on Saturday (March 1, 2025), centred on a 50,000-seat stadium with a purplish facade dubbed "Pearl of the Orient" and a retractable roof.
- The 28-hectare park is on the site of the former Kai Tak Airport in Kowloon. Also includes a 10,000-seat sports centre, a 5,000-seat public sports ground and three shopping malls.
- Chief Executive John Lee: it ushers in a "state-of-the-art new stage for Hong Kong". Stadium expected to host the Hong Kong Sevens later in March and Coldplay concerts in April.
- An Olympic-standard stadium was floated in the 2000s, but construction only began in 2019 and was beset with delays. The city seeks to regain its standing for major events after political upheaval and COVID curbs; Taylor Swift's Eras Tour skipped Hong Kong for Singapore. Opening ceremony featured Donnie Yen and fencer Vivian Kong.

wikis.title: SCMP: Kai Tak Sports Park to open in first half of 2025
wikis.summary: Short SCMP teaser saying Hong Kong's Kai Tak Sports Park is set to open in the first half of next year, with an official rejecting noise and traffic fears.
wikis.body:
- Hong Kong's Kai Tak Sports Park is set to open "in the first half of next year" (the text gives no date; the headline says 2025).
- Chief Secretary Eric Chan Kwok-ki said on Friday authorities were satisfied with progress; construction of major facilities, including the 50,000-seat main stadium, was largely complete.
- He said there will be trial events before the formal opening, was "confident" events would not cause traffic or noise problems, and noted the site is well served by public transport, including two nearby MTR stations.

wikis.title: One Wall Street condo conversion completed and welcoming first residents
wikis.summary: CityRealty tour of One Wall Street, New York's largest office-to-residential conversion, as the first residents prepare to move in.
wikis.body:
- Article dated Friday, Mar 3, 2023, by CityRealty Staff.
- Plans for the residential conversion of One Wall Street (built as headquarters of the Irving Trust Company) date back to 2014, when Macklowe Properties bought the building. The pandemic and lockdown slowed the conversion; building and amenity construction are now complete and first residents are getting ready to move in.
- Sales launched in September 2021. Availabilities range from a studio at $1.13 million to a five-bedroom combination at $19.05 million.
- All units: high ceilings, wide-plank French oak floors, high-tech kitchens with marble countertops, warm stone primary baths, in-unit Miele washer/dryers.
- At 1.25 million sq ft it is "New York's largest office-to-residential conversion to date". Original design by Ralph Walker; Robert A.M. Stern Architects added a five-story addition on the non-landmarked annex and restored the limestone facade.
- The White Room (shell ceiling imported from the Philippines) will be part of the penthouse (not listed). The Red Room mosaic by Hildreth Meière will be part of the first US outpost of Printemps (54,000 sq ft, "rumored" to include an experiential concept). A Whole Foods in the base is the first in the Financial District and the largest grocery there. A Life Time Fitness outpost gives residents complimentary membership.
- Collections: Harbor Collection (eight units facing the harbor; three-bedroom model listed at $9,750,000), Loft Collection (new glass overbuild), Terrace Collection (46 residences with private outdoor space), Tower Collection (floors 40-48).
- Amenities: One Works coworking (6,500 sq ft), 75-foot Sky Pool by MdeAS Architects, private restaurant by Deborah Berke, 4,500 sq ft terrace, children's playroom, teen lounge, pet grooming.
- Quote, Harry Macklowe (CEO, Macklowe Properties): "The completion of One Wall Street embodies our vision for luxury living in Downtown Manhattan".

wikis.title: One Times Square property page (Jamestown)
wikis.summary: Jamestown's property page describing One Times Square and its $500 million redevelopment into a visitor center.
wikis.body:
- One Times Square is a 26-story building in Times Square, New York City, built as headquarters of The New York Times in 1904.
- Home to the New Year's Eve Ball Drop; central to New Year's Eve traditions since 1907. Its advertising signage is described as "among the most valuable signage in the world".
- In April 2022 Jamestown announced a $500 million redevelopment to modernize the building into a 21st century visitor center for New York City, opening much of the interior to the public for the first time in decades.
- Planned elements: viewing deck, museum experience, 12 floors of technology-enabled brand activations, and space and services for wedding ceremonies, vow renewals and proposals.
- Address: One Times Square, New York, NY 10036.

wikis.title: Sandoy Tunnel set to open December 21st, 2023
wikis.summary: Local.fo article on the festivities, toll-free period and costs as the Sandoy Tunnel in the Faroe Islands opens on 21 December.
wikis.body:
- Article by Alda Nielsdóttir, December 18, 2023.
- The Sandoy Tunnel (Sandoyartunnilin) opens to the public on December 21st, connecting Sandoy and Streymoy; driving is toll free for a period.
- It comes about 20 years after the Faroes' first road tunnel, the Vagar Tunnel; two more subsea tunnels were added in 2006 (Northern Tunnel) and 2020 (Eysturoy Tunnel). Sandoy is the fourth subsea tunnel and the longest road tunnel in the Faroes, up to 10.8 km between Gamlarætt (Streymoy) and Traðardalur (Sandoy).
- Sandur councillor Hanna á Reynatúgvu: residents hope to change the downward population trend; Tórshavn will be "just half an hour's drive".
- Teitur Samuelsen (CEO, Eystur- og Sandoyartunlar): toll free for the first 23 days, until January 12th, 2024, as with Eysturoy Tunnel; toll rate same as Eysturoy Tunnel.
- Combined cost of the Eysturoy and Sandoy tunnels approx. 2.6 billion DKK (349 million EUR).
- New bus route between Sandoy and Tórshavn announced by SSL. Retiring ferry Teistin makes final trips between Gamlarætt and Skopun on opening day; open to the public at Skopun 4 to 6 PM.
- Opening ceremony in the afternoon of December 21st near the mouth at Traðardalur, with speeches, a public run through the tunnel, a bicycle race, exhibitions and open houses.

wikis.title: Sandoyartunnilin (Sandoy Tunnel), Faroe Islands
wikis.summary: Wikipedia article on the undersea road tunnel between Streymoy and Sandoy, its specifications, history and traffic.
wikis.body:
- Undersea road tunnel connecting Streymoy with Sandoy, crossing Skopunarfjørður from Gamlarætt to Traðardalur. Owner: Faroese government; operator P/F Eystur- og Sandoyartunlar; tolled.
- Specs: length 10,785 m (10.8 km); 2 lanes; 80 km/h; max elevation 50.7 m; clearance 4.6 m; width 10.5 m; depth below water 155.1 m; max grade 5.0%.
- Estimated cost 860 million DKK.
- Work began 27 June 2019; halfway mark September 2020; two sides connected in a ceremony on 3 February 2022; opened 21 December 2023, after which ferry Teistin ceased the Gamlarætt-Skopun route.
- Financially linked to the Eysturoyartunnilin (opened 19 December 2020), which will partially finance it by cross subsidisation; tolls pegged to it.
- Tunnel debris used for a new residential and industrial area at Velbastaður and bypass roads in Runavík and Strendur.
- Bus route 650 runs Sandur to Tórshavn daily. A branch to Hestur was lobbied for but deprioritised due to costs.
- Traffic: 1,057 vehicles per day (twelve months to Oct/Nov 2025); planning projected 300-400 per day; the ferry averaged 195 vehicles per day in 2021; Feb and Mar 2024 saw 783 and 919 vehicles per day.

wikis.title: Thames Tideway super sewer fully connected
wikis.summary: Tideway press release announcing the last of 21 connections between the Victorian sewers and the 25km Thames Tideway Tunnel.
wikis.body:
- Press release dated 14/02/25: after ten years of construction the last of 21 connections has been made between the original Victorian sewers and the new 25km Thames Tideway Tunnel, bringing the whole system online. 95 per cent of spills are now being stopped.
- Connection sites include Putney Embankment, Chelsea and Victoria Embankments, Blackfriars Bridge and King Edward Memorial Park, Wapping.
- 5,500,000 m³ of sewage captured to date, "the equivalent of 2,200 Olympic-sized swimming pools"; a new tracker at tideway.london publishes updates.
- Next step: test in storm conditions over the coming months. The system connects to the 6.9km Lee Tunnel to form the London Tideway Tunnel (LTT), capacity 1.6m m³. The project is "on track to be fully complete (with testing complete) later this year", after which Thames Water will operate it.
- Earlier: first four connections captured 589,000 tonnes in one rainy 24 hours (autumn 2024); 848,365 tonnes captured on November 27th.
- Timeline: work began 2016 at two dozen sites from Acton to Abbey Mills; first tunnelling machine started 2018; primary tunnelling completed 2022; secondary lining complete by autumn 2023; heavy civil engineering complete spring 2024; connected to Lee Tunnel May 2024.
- Contractors: west BAM Nuttall/Morgan Sindall/Balfour Beatty; central Ferrovial Agroman/Laing O'Rourke; east Costain/Vinci/Bachy Soletanche; system integration Amey.
- Quotes: Tideway CEO Andy Mitchell, Environment Secretary Steve Reed, Mayor Sadiq Khan, Thames Water CEO Chris Weston ("built for four million people but today, it serves over nine million"; funded by Thames Water customers), Environment Agency's Alan Lovell, Ofwat's David Black.

wikis.title: King officially opens the Thames Tideway Tunnel
wikis.summary: Greater London Lieutenancy record of HM The King's visit to the Thames Tideway Undercroft site to open the tunnel.
wikis.body:
- Dated 07 May 2025 (updated 22 Jan 2026): HM The King officially opened the Thames Tideway Tunnel in London.
- He was received at Westminster Millennium Pier by the Lord-Lieutenant of Greater London (Sir Kenneth Olisa) and TfL's Andrew Lord, and travelled downstream on the passenger ferry MARS CLIPPER to Blackfriars Pier.
- Received there by Environment Secretary Steve Reed, Tideway Chairman Michael Queen and Chief Executive Andrew Mitchell.
- Visited the Thames Tideway Undercroft work site, viewed footage and data from inside the tunnel, met staff, viewed the ventilation columns and walked to the newly-created planted walkway, Bazalgette Embankment, at 15 Victoria Embankment.

wikis.title: Silvertown Tunnel opening confirmed for 7 April 2025
wikis.summary: New Civil Engineer report on the confirmed opening date, funding, buses and construction timeline of London's Silvertown Tunnel.
wikis.body:
- 07 Jan 2025, by Rob Hakimian: TfL and the Riverlinx consortium announced the Silvertown Tunnel will open on 7 April 2025. The new £179M crossing links Newham to the Greenwich Peninsula; the tunnel is 1.4km long; construction started 2020.
- Opens with new bus routes free for the first year, including Superloop SL4 (Canary Wharf to Grove Park); buses crossing the Thames in the area rise from six to 21 per hour. A cycle-shuttle runs every 12 minutes daily 06:30-21:30.
- Funded primarily by private finance raised by Riverlinx (abrdn, Invesis, Cintra, SK Ecoplant); built by Riverlinx CJV (BAM, Ferrovial Construction, SK Ecoplant). A user charge will manage traffic, repay costs and maintain Silvertown and Blackwall tunnels. Aim: relieve congestion at the Blackwall Tunnel.
- Project announced 2012; over 1.8Mt of material moved by river; more than 120 apprenticeships.
- Timeline: pandemic pause March-June 2020; launch chamber completed Nov 2021 (Keltbray); TBM parts arrived Dec 2021 (82m long, 1,200t, 11.87m diameter, largest in UK to date); 9,000+ precast segments from March 2022; TBM launched early Sept 2022; fire later that month, tunnelling resumed 20 Oct; first drive ended Feb 2023; TBM "Jill" turned 180° in Greenwich (a UK engineering first) and relaunched April 2023, back in Silvertown early August 2023; connections between approaches and main tunnel finalised May 2024; fit-out and testing since.
- Quote, TfL's Stuart Harvey: "the Silvertown Tunnel will open on 7 April 2025".

wikis.title: Paris inaugurates Austerlitz storage basin to clean the Seine for the Olympics
wikis.summary: France 24/AP report on the Austerlitz wastewater storage basin opened 2 May 2024 to make the Seine swimmable for Paris 2024.
wikis.body:
- 2 May 2024: officials inaugurated the Austerlitz wastewater and rainwater storage basin, meant to help make the Seine the venue for marathon swimming and the swimming leg of triathlons.
- Last year swimming test events were cancelled due to poor water quality after heavy rain overwhelmed old sewers.
- The reservoir holds the equivalent of 20 Olympic swimming pools of dirty water, which will be treated instead of spilling into the river.
- Prefect Marc Guillaume: "We are on time." Mayor Anne Hidalgo promised to swim in the Seine herself before the Olympics.
- During the Games water will be tested at 3 a.m. daily; events could be delayed a few days if standards are not met.
- Cleanup cost estimated at 1.4 billion euros ($1.5 billion), paid by state and local authorities. About 35 fish species live in the Paris section, up from three in the 1970s. Swimming has been mostly illegal since 1923; bathing sites planned for the public from next year.
- A water treatment plant at Champigny-sur-Marne was inaugurated the previous month.

wikis.title: The Seine reopens: how the Olympics helped Paris reclaim its river
wikis.summary: IOC article on Paris's three new Seine swimming sites opened 5 July 2025 and the Olympic legacy of the cleanup.
wikis.body:
- Three natural swimming sites at Bras Marie, Bercy and Grenelle opened on 5 July 2025, just over a year after the Olympic triathlon and marathon swimming; about 1,000 swimmers a day until end of August.
- Swimming was banned in 1923 due to pollution; cleanup origins date to the early 90s; in 2015 the Greater Paris Sanitation Authority announced the plan to make the Seine swimmable by the Games.
- The Austerlitz underground basin holds over 50,000 cubic metres, roughly twenty Olympic pools.
- Sites have lifeguards, showers, sun decks, kayaks at Grenelle; water tested daily; removable modular structures. More public swimming spots planned along the Seine and Marne.
- The Games accelerated efforts already in progress. Quotes from Mayor Anne Hidalgo and IOC Head of Legacy Tania Braga.

wikis.title: Hyper-Kamiokande main cavern excavation completed
wikis.summary: Kavli IPMU press release that excavation of the Hyper-K detector cavern finished on 31 July 2025.
wikis.body:
- 5 August 2025: on July 31, 2025 the University of Tokyo completed excavation of the cavern for Hyper-Kamiokande, a water Cherenkov detector under construction in Hida City, Gifu, Japan, about 600 m underground.
- Led by University of Tokyo and KEK; about 630 researchers from 22 countries (July 2025). Fiducial volume 8.4 times Super-Kamiokande; over 20,000 new photodetectors. Aims: measure neutrino properties, search for proton decay. Project began February 2020.
- Cavern: dome about 69 m diameter, 21 m high, plus cylinder 73 m high; about 330,000 cubic meters of rock removed; finished about six months behind original schedule. Dome excavation began November 2022; cylinder October 2023, using a pre-dug 3.4 m vertical shaft.
- Next: from August 2025 convert to tank of 260,000 cubic meters of ultra-pure water; two-layer detector structure begins 2026; all in-tank components installed by 2027; operation scheduled to begin 2028. KEK upgrades the J-PARC beam and a new intermediate detector in Tokai.

wikis.title: Hyper-Kamiokande construction status and prospects
wikis.summary: Frontiers in Physics perspective (March 2024) on Hyper-K's goals and the excavation progress of its underground facility.
wikis.body:
- Published 26 March 2024 (Front. Phys. 12), by Ko Abe and Hide-Kazu Tanaka for the Hyper-Kamiokande collaboration.
- Hyper-K: international neutrino and nucleon decay experiment with a next-generation underground water Cherenkov detector plus upgraded J-PARC neutrino beam, hosted by University of Tokyo and KEK; about 560 researchers from 101 institutes in 21 countries at time of writing. Budget approved by the Japanese Diet January 2020; operation "expected to start in 2027".
- Located about 600 m underground beneath the Kamioka Mine, Hida City, Gifu; overburden 592 m at the top of the main cavern and 650 m at detector center. Detector 71 m high, 68 m diameter, 0.260 million metric tons of ultra pure water (fiducial mass 0.188 million tons, an order of magnitude more than Super-K).
- Physics goals: leptonic CP violation (covering 60% of parameter space at 5 sigma or better after 10 years; over 8 sigma if delta CP = -pi/2), proton decay (p -> e+ pi0, potential beyond 1e35 years), neutrino mass ordering, solar and supernova neutrinos.
- Excavation: yard prepared from 6 May 2021 (~10,000 m2); 2.0 km access tunnel (1979.5 m, 5 m x 5 m, done in 9 months, completed February 2022, max 15 m/day); approach tunnels 385 m, 413 m, 154 m (March-August 2022); 445 m circular tunnel with sub-cavities in about 4 months; water purification cavity 101 x 17 x 16 m completed May 2023.
